column33: poultry litter (11.25 t ha-1)
column38: The research was conducted from 2001 to 2005 at the USDA-ARS J. Phil Campbell Sr. Natural Resource Conservation Center in Watkinsville, GA (83°24´ W, 33°54´ N) on 12 large (10 bt 30 m2) nearly level (<1.5% slope) plots with drainage tiles set at about a meter depth from the surface. The soil is Cecil sandy loam with about a 20-cm thick brown sandy loam Ap-horizon, underlain by a 5- to 10-cm thick BA-horizon of a red sandy clay loam to clay loam texture. e experiment was a randomized complete block split plot design with three replications. Nitrogen fertilizer subplots were either CF applied as ammonium nitrate/sulfate vs. PL. Conventional tillage consisted of 30-cm deep chisel plowing followed by one to two diskings to 20-cm depth and a subsequent 8-cm deep disking with a tandem-disk to smooth the seed bed. The only soil disturbance in no-tillage was planting with a four-row notillage planter. The no-tillage treatment started in fall of 1991. From 1996 to 2000 cotton research was conducted under the same two tillage and fertilizer regimes (Endale et al., 2002a; Endale et al., 2002c). The cropping regime consisted of cereal rye (cv. Hy-Gainer [2001 and 2002]; Penington WinterGrazer [2003 and 2004]; Wrens Abruzzi [2005]) grown in late-fall to early spring followed by corn (cv. Pioneer 3223 [2001 to 2003]; Pioneer 33V15 Poncho Treatment Em250 [2004 and 2005]) from mid-spring to mid-fall. Corn planting and harvest dates consecutively from 2001 were: 24 May and 9 October; 22 May and 4 October; 29 May and 22 October; 12 April and 9 September; and 11 May and 20 October. Corn was planted in 76-cm rows with density target of seven to eight plants per row meter. Nitrogen fertilization for corn was at a rate of 168 kg available N ha–1 in all but the third year. In all but the third year, this meant a PL application of 11.25 Mg ha–1 at about 30% moisture assuming 50% mineralization (Vest et al., 1994; CAES, 2007b) during the corn season (i.e., the litter contained about 336 kg N ha–1 but only half of this became available). In the third year the N application rate was doubled in both tillage treatments (336 ka available N ha–1; litter 22.5 Mg ha–1) because of interest for detecting potential levels of the hormones estradiol and testosterone coming off the field in runoff or drainage from litter (Jenkins et al., 2004). Conventional N fertilizer was applied as ammonium nitrate or sulfate (depending on availability) in split applications (Gandy 10T series, pull behind drop fertilizer spreader, Gandy Company, Owatonna, MN)1, one-third a day or two before planting, and two-thirds about 33 d later. The rye cover crop in the PL treatment was fertilized with litter at 124 kg N ha–1 in 2001, 67 kg N ha–1 in 2002 and 2003, and with ammonium nitrate or sulfate at 67 kg N ha–1 the rest of the period. Since litter application was based on assumption of 50% N mineralization in the current year, residual N mineralization could have increased the amount of N available to corn in subsequent years in the PL treatment. But we expect less and less N to become available each succeeding year from one litter application. Twenty to 30 ears were then sampled from each plot to determine shelled corn weight. Grain yield was determined in proportion to the whole ear yield of each plot and expressed at moisture equivalent of 155 g kg–1. Corn plants remaining after harvest were shredded with a rotary mower. Operations for the cover crop followed after that with same tillage regimes and a no-tillage drill used to plant the rye in both tillage treatments. In 2004 the rye was chemically killed early before the usual spring surge of biomass accumulation to make way for a rainfall simulation study on part of each plot, and the residue averaged only 0.36 Mg ha–1 across plots. Mean rye residue yield across all treatments for the remaining 4-yr varied in the narrow range of 3.45 to 3.97 Mg ha–1 with no difference among treatments.

column38: Field plots were established in 1981 and 1982 on a Canisteo soil (fme-loamy, mixed calcareous, mesic, Typic Haplaquoll) near Ames, lA. The Canisteo soil is 30% sand, 42% silt, and 28% clay with 5.0% organic matter and a pH of 8.0. The area was moldboard plowed after each maize crop and disked after soybeans. Maize was grown in 1980. Surface plant residue cover was determined by using the photographic method (Williams, 1979). This field polyfactorial trial with soybean (variety Quito) was performed at the research site of the Research Institute of Agroecology in Milhostov (altitude: 101 m, average temperature: 9.0°C, sum of precipitation: 559 mm) on gleyey alluvial soil in 2006–2008. Soil pH/KCl ranged from 6.3 to 6.6 (slightly acid – neutral soil reaction) during the trial period. Temperatures and sums of precipitation during the growing seasons were evaluated according to Kožnarova and Klabzuba (2002) and are presented in Tables 1 and 2. Two-rowed barley was a preceding crop. A seeding amount of 650 000 viable seeds/ha and a row spacing of 180 mm were used. Seed was not inoculated. Three tillage systems: conventional tillage (stubble cleaning followed by mouldboard ploughing in autumn and seedbed preparation followed by drilling in spring), reduced tillage (spring shallow cultivation by a stubble cultivator to a depth of 100 mm followed by drilling) and no-tillage, and two starting doses of nitrogen: 50 kg N/ha and 25 kg N/ha applied before drilling, were tested in the trial. The doses of PK fertilizers were estimated on the basis of soil tests and also applied before drilling. The trial was organized in a complete randomized block design with four replicates. A plot seed yield, harvested from the area of 1.5 × 23 m, was adjusted to moisture of 14% and expressed in t/ha.

column33: Urea + 228 kg P2O5 ha-1 as superphosphate
column38: The field was under no-tillage for 2 yr before the study began and included a self-contained drainage system. Winter wheat was grown in the year before the experiment and the wheat plants were harvested by hand at maturity this allowed the accurate implementation of tillage and mulching treatments for the experiment. In conventional tillage (T), the straw from the previous wheat crop was not returned to the plots after grain harvest. the wheat straw from previous crops was cut to 5- to 6-cm lengths using a hay cutter (ZHADAO model, Shandong Machinery Inc., Taian, China) after the winter wheat was threshed, and then the chopped straw (6750 kg ha−1) was returned to the original plots immediately. The irrigation occurred on 4 November, 5 May, 28 May, and 12 June during the 2005–2006 growing season, and on 5 November, 7 May, 29 May, and 13 June during the 2006–2007 growing season. The field was sown on 16 Sept. 2005 and on 18 Sept. 2006 with a seed rate of 337.5 kg ha−1 and the crop was harvested on 18 July 2006 and on 14 July 2007. Nitrogen as urea at 365 kg N ha−1 and P as superphosphate at 228 kg P2O5 ha−1 were applied to plots each year. Fertilizer was applied at 192 kg N ha−1 and 138 kg P2O5 ha−1 at planting, 130kg N ha−1 and 69 kg P2O5 ha−1 when plots were irrigated at early jointing, and 43 kg N ha−1 and 21 kg P2O5 ha−1 at early heading when the third irrigation occurred. In the no-tillage with wheat stubble standing treatment (NTSS), a 25- to 30-cm (in height) wheat stubble was left standing in the fi eld at harvest, and the rest of the wheat straw was removed off the plots. glyphosate at 0.84 kg ha−1 and 2,4-D at 1.10 kg ha−1 were applied to the no-tillage plots (NT, NTSS, and NTS) to control weeds.

A two-year measuring campaign was carried out on a long-term field study (initiated in 2010) at the CERZOO experimental station, in Piacenza (45°00′21.6″N, 9°42′27.1″E; altitude 68 m), Po Valley, Northern Italy. This site is representative of intensive agriculture in northern Italy. It is characterised by a temperate climate with an annual mean temperature of approximately 12.2 °C, and precipitation of 778 mm. The soil is a fine, mixed, mesic Udertic Haplustalf, with a silty clay loamy texture (sand 122, silt 462, and clay 416 g kg−1) in the upper layer (0–30 cm), well drained and non-saline. The main physico-chemical properties at the beginning of the experiment were: pH 6.8, soil organic carbon 12.8 g kg−1, total N 1.2 g kg−1, available P 32 mg kg−1, exchangeable K 294 mg kg−1, and cation exchange capacity 30 cmol+ kg−1. The experiment was laid out in a randomized complete block design, with four blocks (replicates) and three treatments: CT, NT with hairy vetch (Vicia villosa Roth) as CC (NT vetch), and NT with rye (Secale cereale L.) as CC (NT rye). The plot size was 1430m2 (65m×22 m) with buffer rows of 4m between plots. In 2015 the main crop was soybean (maturity group 1-), which was planted in May and harvested at the end of October. Eighteen days before planting soybean, both CCs were terminated in NT plots by spraying 2.4 l ha−1 of Glyphosate. No fertilizer was applied during the CCs and soybean cropping seasons. In both years, soybean and maize were sprinkler-irrigated to prevent water stress. The field experiment was established in 2010 to compare: (i) conventional tillage (CT), which included autumn plowing (30 cm depth) with crop residues incorporation into the soil and two spring rotating harrowing (15 cm) to provide a suitable seedbed. In the NT plots, after harvesting soybean (2015) and maize (2017), crop residues were left on the soil surface (the whole plant aboveground biomass except the grain biomass). Fungicidal treatment 27/07/2015.

The experiment was laid out in a randomized complete block design, with four blocks (replicates) and three treatments: CT, NT with hairy vetch (Vicia villosa Roth) as CC (NT vetch), and NT with rye (Secale cereale L.) as CC (NT rye). The plot size was 1430m2 (65m×22 m) with buffer rows of 4m between plots. In 2015 the main crop was soybean (maturity group 1-), which was planted in May and harvested at the end of October. Eighteen days before planting soybean, both CCs were terminated in NT plots by spraying 2.4 l ha−1 of Glyphosate. No fertilizer was applied during the CCs and soybean cropping seasons. In both years, soybean and maize were sprinkler-irrigated to prevent water stress. The field experiment was established in 2010 to compare: (i) conventional tillage (CT), which included autumn plowing (30 cm depth) with crop residues incorporation into the soil and two spring rotating harrowing (15 cm) to provide a suitable seedbed. In the NT plots, after harvesting soybean (2015) and maize (2017), crop residues were left on the soil surface (the whole plant aboveground biomass except the grain biomass). Intensive initial sampling 0–20 cm revealed a grey-black clay (47% clay, 18% silt and 35% sand), with a bulk density of 1.4 g cm_3 and 0.03 and 1.5 MPa gravimetric water contents of 34.0 and 19.8%, respectively. Organic matter content was 2.4%, total nitrogen 0.126%, Olsen available phosphorus 50 ppm, exchangeable potassium 507 ppm, cation exchange capacity of 24.8 meq/100 g, pH in water 6.5, and electrical conductivity and exchangeable sodium very low. seeding of a uniform barley crop in late July. This was harvested in November. application of a broad spectrum contact herbicide 1 month after the rains began. Two comprised continuous cropping, either with wheat (WW) or maize (MM), and four were binary (2 years) rotations, namely maize–wheat (MW, WM), vetch (Vicia sativa L.)–wheat (VW, WV), vetch–maize (VM, MV), and medic (Medicago polymorpha) pasture–wheat (PW, WP). two levels of N fertilisation were allocated at random: N1, no fertilisation, and N2, supplemental N between 35 and 45 days after seeding. The amount of N applied varied from 50 to 100 kg/ha depending on seasonal prospects. In 1995 both N1 and N2 fertiliser sub-plots were further split into three portions, and each portion allocated at random to levels of 0, 60 and 120 kg/ha fertiliser N in order to test for both current and residual effects of fertiliser. Nitrogen fertiliser was supplied as urea, broadcast on the soil surface just before rain.

column5: Parana, Londrina, Embrapa Soybean experiment station
column19: winter wheat- summer soybean; winter lupine - summer maize; winter oat - summer soybean
column33: Urea + 28-75 kg P2O5 ha-1 (triple superphosphate) + 34-60 kg K2O ha-1 (potassium chloride)
column38: The experiment was installed on an Oxisol (Eutroferric Red Latosol, in the Brazilian classification; or Rhodic Eutrudox, in the USA classification) with 710 g clay kg−1 soil, 82 g silt kg−1 soil, and 208 g sand kg−1 soil. two crop systems [(1) wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) in the winter and soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr) in the summer; a procedure that was repeated at each year, and designated as crop succession (CS); and (2) a 4-year crop rotation (CR), with the following species in winter–summer: white lupine (Lupinus albus L.) – maize (Zea mays L.); black oats (Avena strigosa Schreb.) – soybean; wheat – soybean; wheat –soybean]. The 6th crop rotation cycle will be ended in the 2012/2013 crop season. Each plot had the measures of 7.5 m in width × 30.0 m in length, thus totaling 225 m2. Every three years, an average of 2 Mg ha−1 of lime was applied to the soil surface to reach a saturation of bases of 60% and to increase the pH in water to approximately 5.5. The fertilizers (N, P2O5, and K2O) were simultaneously applied 0.05 m below and at the side of the seeds, during the sowing procedure. For the wheat and maize, the N was not applied as topdressing fertilization. To the cover crops (black oats and white lupine), fertilizer was not applied. In the NT system, the vegetation present in the area prior to the sowing of the crops was desiccated with the herbicide glyphosate (at dosage of 720 g a.i. ha−1) mixed with mineral oil (0.5 L ha−1). The plots cultivated with wheat and the winter cover crops (white lupine, or black oats) were sown in the month of April in all agricultural years. The soybean was sown in November of every crop season. The maize was also sown in November in all agricultural years, throughout the experiment. NT, sowing directly performed through the residues of the previous crop, by opening only a narrow furrow in the sowing row

During the first 3 years, treatments included all combinations of three tillage systems, three irrigation regimes and four N-rates. The tillage systems did not include any crop residue as it is removed at harvest and used as cattle feed or as raw material in agro-based industries. Nitrogen rates were 0 (No), 50 (N50), 100 (N100) and 150 (NIso) kg ha-1. This experiment included two tillage systems, NT and CT, and four N-rates, 0, 80, 120 and 160 kg ha- 1. Irrigation regimes, experimental design and size of the subplots were the same as in the first 3 years. Other fertilizer nutrients, 26 kg P (single super-phosphate ), 25 kg K (muriate of potash) and 5 kg Zn (ZnSO4) ha-1, were drilled befoie seeding. Weeds were controlled by spraying 600 ml of (2,4-dichlorophenoxy) acetic acid (34% EC) in 500 1 water ha- 1, 40- 45 days after seeding.

column19: soybean-winter wheat-maize with vetch and rye cover crop
column33: Urea, ammonium nitrate
column38: Low-input is defined here as a farming system lacking the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides as applied with conventional management. The CONV and LI farming systems each had a basic soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.]-winter wheat-corn (Zea mays L.) rotation, with the inclusion of hairy vetch (Vicia villosa Roth.) and rye (Secale cereale L.) cover crops in the low-input system. Management of the field during the 15 years prior to the establishment of the trial included diverse field crop rotations (corn, soybean, small grains, and hay crops), animal manures, and mechanical weed control. No synthetic chemical fertilizers or pesticides were used. Rotary hoeing and cultivation were the only means of weed control prior to the start of the field trial. Nitrogen fertilizer [urea (30-34%)-ammonium nitrate (40-44%)] was applied at a rate of 67 kg N ha-1 on 14 April 1993 in the CONV plots. No N was applied to the LI plots. This farming system relied upon residual N from N fixation by soybean (before wheat) and hairy vetch (prior to corn) and retention of N by the rye cover crop (before soybean).

The study was conducted at the Michigan State University, Kellogg Biological Station (KBS), a long-term ecological research site (LTER). Four agronomic management systems comprised the treatments: tilled with conventional chemical inputs (CT); no-till with conventional chemical inputs (NT); tilled with low chemical inputs (LI), and tilled with no chemical inputs (ORG). The dominant soil types were well-drained Kalamazoo silt loam (Typic Hapludalfs) and Oshtemo sand loam (Typic Hapludalfs) (Davis et al., 2005). The site was established in 1988. The experiment was designed as a randomized complete block and each treatment had six replicates (more information can be found at http://lter.msu.edu/data). From 1993 to 2006, a rotation of corn–soybean–winter wheat was grown at the site. Among those years, soybean was grown in 1994, 1997, 2000, 2003, and 2006 (the information of soybean varieties and planting and harvest dates can be found in Table 1). A more detailed description of these four management systems and site history can be found in Smith et al. (2007). A total of 120 soybean grain samples were collected from six reps with four treatments over fi ve soybean rotational years: 1994, 1997, 2000, 2003, and 2006. Soybean grain was collected at harvest, ground, and stored at 4°C. Average growing season daily (maximum, mean, minimum) temperature and total precipitation was obtained from the KBS LTER Meteorological Station. Management practices, including tillage, fertilizer input, and plant rotation, have been reported to have significant effects on agricultural systems, including weed community

In rice, T1 (CT-TPR rice), T4 (bed-TPR), and T6 (ZT-TPR) plots were irrigated (5-cm depth of standing water) daily for the fi rst 2 wk, and thereaft er irrigation (5-cm depth of standing water) was applied at the appearance of hairline cracks on the soil surface. Wheat was sown in the fi rst week of November at 90 kg ha−1 on raised beds and 120 kg ha−1 in fl at beds using ZT drill. In rice, all plots received 150 kg N, 26 kg P, 50 kg K, and 8.75 kg Zn ha−1. Rice was drill-seeded in the first week of June. additional dose of 22.5 kg N ha−1 at 20 DAS was applied in all DSR plots. A full dose of P and K and 1/4-dose of N were applied using a ZT seed-with-fertilizer drill at the time of seeding in DSR and were broadcasted manually at the time of transplanting in TPR. In wheat, all treatments received 150 kg N, 26 kg P, and 50 kg K; and full P, K, and 1/4 of N were applied using a ZT seed-with-fertilizer drill at sowing. Th e remaining N was applied in three equal splits at just before fi rst irrigation (CRI), second irrigation (tillering), and third irrigation (fl owering initiation), respectively. In both rice and wheat, the plots were kept weed free by controlling with the use of appropriate herbicides and hand weeding. Crop stubbles were incorporated in to soil during conventional puddling and tillage, but in ZT plots, seeding was done in the standing stubbles.

column33: Urea + calcium ammonium nitrate + 17 kg P ha-1 as songle superphosphate  + 16 kg K ha-1 as potash
column38: The soil ranged in texture from sandy loam near the surface (110 g kg -1 clay and 760 g kg -1 sand) to loam in the lower layers (170 g kg -1 clay and 600 g kg-1 sand) with pH of 8.0 and organic carbon content of 3 g kg -1 soil. The soil was classified as fine loamy Fluventic Ustochrept by Soil Taxonomy (Raj-Kumar et al., 1998) and as Eutric/Dystric Fluvisols by FAO. Water retention at -33 kPa pressure ranged from 135 to 207 g kg -1 and at ÿ1500 kPa pressure from 41 to 75 g kg -1, in different layers of 0±1.8 m soil. minimum tillage . residue of the previous crop left on the surface as mulch at 3 Mg ha -1 (MTR) minimum tillage without residue (MT), conventional tillage without residue (CT). Maize (cv. Megha) was sown in July (when soil moisture in the surface layer stabilized with the first two or more rain events) and harvested in October the same year. A basal application of 40 kg N ha -1 as calcium ammonium nitrate, 17 kg P ha -1 as single superphosphate and 16 kg K ha -1 as muriate of potash was applied at the time of maize sowing. A month later, 40 kg N ha -1 as urea was side-dressed. Two hoeings were conducted at 1 and 2 months after planting maize to control weeds in conventionally tilled plots, while the weeds were hand-pulled in minimum till plots. No herbicide was used in minimum till plots so as to have a similar practice of controlling weeds physically under both tillage systems. Wheat (cv. PBW 175) was sown in November with five rates of N (0, 40, 80, 120 and 160 kg N ha -1) in subplots. The crop was harvested in April of the following year

Water retention at -33 kPa pressure ranged from 135 to 207 g kg -1 and at ÿ1500 kPa pressure from 41 to 75 g kg -1, in different layers of 0±1.8 m soil. minimum tillage . residue of the previous crop left on the surface as mulch at 3 Mg ha -1 (MTR) minimum tillage without residue (MT), conventional tillage without residue (CT). Maize (cv. Megha) was sown in July (when soil moisture in the surface layer stabilized with the first two or more rain events) and harvested in October the same year. A basal application of 40 kg N ha -1 as calcium ammonium nitrate, 17 kg P ha -1 as single superphosphate and 16 kg K ha -1 as muriate of potash was applied at the time of maize sowing. A month later, 40 kg N ha -1 as urea was side-dressed. Two hoeings were conducted at 1 and 2 months after planting maize to control weeds in conventionally tilled plots, while the weeds were hand-pulled in minimum till plots. No herbicide was used in minimum till plots so as to have a similar practice of controlling weeds physically under both tillage systems. Wheat (cv. PBW 175) was sown in November with five rates of N (0, 40, 80, 120 and 160 kg N ha -1) in subplots. The crop was harvested in April of the following year

column2: Journal of Soil and Water Conservation
column38: Five conservation tillage treatments were randomly applied within four replicated blocks in each field. The intermediate single pass treatments comprised a Claydon hydrid drill with tines operating at a depth of 150 mm (labelled “150T”), a Mzuri Pro-Til drill with wing tines at 150 mm (labelled “150WT”), and a Sumo Deep Tillage Seeder with tines at 177 mm (labelled “177T”). The width of the tines ranged from 15 mm for the "177T” to 215 mm width for the Farm System. The experiment was undertaken in two 4 ha fields, of contrasting soil type, at Lamport Hall Estate (52°35'85"N 0.87°25'63"W), 14 km north of Northampton in the United Kingdom. One field, labelled “Clay loam” had a clay loam soil, whilst the second field labelled “Clay” had a clay soil. The experiment ran over three cropping seasons with crops planted between August and September in 2013, 2014 and 2015. Over the three years, the mean annual rainfall was 626 mm and the mean annual temperature 10.5°C. The clay field contained substantial blackgrass infestations when planted to winter wheat in year 1 and 3 and the spatial distribution of the blackgrass was assessed in June 2014 and 2016, when wheat was in the grain development stage. Areas of blackgrass were delineated by walking around the border of each infestation with Trimble Geox 6000 GPS unit (45 cm precision) to create a polygon shape, ensuring closure of the polygon at the end. Blackgrass plants and heads counts were also measured to get a clearer picture of its distribution and density. Blackgrass was not a problem in the clay loam field or when the clay field was planted with oilseed rape. There was no statistically significant difference between the capacity of the conservation tillage treatments to control blackgrass on the clay soil, indicating that other measures are needed to control this competitive weed

column33: 200 kg ha-1 ammonium nitrate (46% N)
column38: The experiment was conducted at Domboshawa Training Center, which  situated at the north-east of Harare (Zimbabwe), during the 2015/2016 crop season. This site is characterized by moderately deep Arenosols and Luvisols under FAO classification. It has approximately 5% clay content and is derived from granite parent material . The climate conditions correspond to the Zimbabwean agro-ecological region II [30], with generally long dry periods (April to October), in which April to July is cool and August to October is warm. This region receives an average rainfall of between 700 and 1000 mm and mean maximum daily temperatures of 32°C during summer. Seven maize drought tolerant commercial hybrids (SC621, Pan53, 30G19, Zap55, Pristine601, PGS61, and Zap61) and one drought-sensitive commercial control variety (SC513) were manually planted on 14 December 2015 in plots of 23 m2 (5 _ 4.6 m) with four lines per plot. Two differential plot management regiments have been applied to the field since 2009. One half was managed using no-tillage and the application of 2.5–3.0 Mg ha-1 of maize stover to all the plots. Rotation, a critical component for CA, was not practiced in this trial. Weed control was done by applying a combination of 2.5 L ha-1 of glyphosate, 3 L ha-1 of atrazine, and 1 L ha-1 of dual immediately after planting, if there were weeds present. The other half was conventionally ploughed and without any residue management. applying a combination of 2.5 L ha−1 of glyphosate, 3 L ha−1 of atrazine, and 1 L ha−1 of dual immediately after planting, if there were weeds present. The other half was conventionally ploughed and without any residue management. Both cropping systems were fertilized twice equally with 200 kg ha-1 using Compound D (7:14:7) as a basal NPK dressing and top dressed ammonium nitrate (200 kg ha􀀀1, 46% N) in a split application four weeks and seven weeks after seeding. Maize plants seeded at different density sub-treatments were applied: one low-planting density (44,444 plants ha-1) and one high-planting density (53,333 plants ha-1). Each sub-treatment was repeated in three replicates in which varieties were ordered in a completely randomized block design. A total of 96 plots were studied (2 agricultural practices _ 2 density conditions _ 8 varieties _ 3 replicates, 24 plots per growing conditions).

column33: N-P2O5-K2O
column38: A long-term study was set up in 2002. The soil is classified as a Typic Pellustert. It has a pH1:2H2O of 6.7, an organic matter content of 2.24% and a clay texture. The region has an average of 610 mm of rain, mainly between June and August, with a mean annual temperature of 19_C (maximum average of 30_C and minimum average of 10_C). wheat–maize rotation with conventional tillage (CT) and burning of residues (W-M/CT/B, regional control); wheatbeans rotation with CT and incorporation of residues into the soil (W-P/CT/I); wheat-maize rotation with CT and incorporation of residues into the soil (W-M/CT/I); maize-beans rotation bi-annual, 1 year bean and the next maize, fallow in the autumn–winter cycle with CT and incorporation of residues into the soil (M-P/CT/Bi); wheatmaize rotation, no tillage (NT) and residues left on the soil surface as mulch (W-M/NT/S). All treatments received 240-40-00, 60-40-00, and 300-80-00 kg N–P2O5–K2O ha-1 to spring maize, spring beans and winter wheat, respectively.  The N-fertilizer was equally split at sowing and 40 days later, all of the P-fertilizer was applied at sowing. The farming practices for sowing, fertilization, irrigation, and pest and weed control were performed following the recommendations of the National Research Institute on Livestock and Agriculture (INIFAP).

The KBS is located in the northern portion of the midwestern Corn Belt in southwest Michigan. Soils at the KBS LTER are co-occurring Kalamazoo fine loam and Oshtemo coarse loam (Crum and Collins, 1995). Although the clay content in these soils is typically between 15 and 20%, the silt content is high ( 40%). The crop rotation consisted of corn and soybean grown in 1:1 rotation until 1995 when the rotation was switched to corn–soybean–wheat. Corn was grown in 6 yr, soybean in 5, and wheat in 3. Asterisks indicate significant differences between tillage treatments for a particular crop (n = 6 replicate blocks). At the KBS LTER, starter fertilizer applications are used at a rate of about 30 kg N ha-1 for corn and have likely helped maintain similar soil N concentrations and yields as in the tilled soils.

column33: ammonium nitrate + KNO3+K+Cl
column38: Field experiments were conducted from 1987 to 1990 on a fine sandy loam and a silty clay Orthic Black Chernozemic soil. The land had been sown to cereal crops in the preceding 3 yr. column33: 280 kg ha-1 NH3 + 50 kg P ha-1 + 194 kg K ha-1
column38: The experiments were conducted at the Purdue University Agronomy Farm in central Indiana (40'28' N Lat.) for 12 yr on Chalmers silty clay loam and at the Southeast Purdue Agricultural Center (39'2' N Lat.) for 7 yr on Clermont silt loam. The Chalmers soil has less than 2% slope, is tiled at a 20-m spacing, is well structured, and has an organic matter content in the surface 30 cm of over 40 g kg-1. The Clermont silt loam has less than 1% slope, no tile, a fragipanlike layer at about 86 cm, and 10 g kg-l organic matter in the surface 30 cm. at a rate (kg ha-I) of 20-22-0 (N-P-K) from 1975 to 15179, and 31-14-0 (N-P-K) from 1980 lo 1986. Nitrogen was applied as NH3 preplant at rates of 190 kg ha-' from 1979 to 1978, and 280 kg ha-1 from 1979 to 1986. Bulk P antl K were broadcast biennially in the fall before tillage operations at rates that averaged 50 kg P ha-1 and 194 kg K ha-1. Limestone was applied periodically to maintain soil pH levels at 6.0 or above. Insect control-A soil-applied insecticide was used at planting for all treatments. Carbofuran (2,3-dihydro-2,2-dimethyl- 7-benzofuranyl methylcarbamate; 1 OG) was used from 1975 to 1979, and terbufos (S-([(l,l-dimethylethyl) thio]methyl]O,O-diethyl phosphorodithioate; 1 5G) was used from 1980 to 1986. In addition, chlorpyrifos [O,O-diethy1 0-(3,5,6-trichloro-2-pyridyl)-phosphorothioatew] as applied postemergence for cutworm (Agrostis ipsilon) control in 1981. Weed control-The same pre-emergence herbicides were applied at planting for all treatments. These included an atrazine (2-chloro-4-ethylamino-6-isopropylamin1o,3-, 5 triazine)-cyanazine (24 [ 4-chloro-6-( ethy1amino)-S-triazine-2- yl]amino)-2-methylpropionitrile) -alachlor [2-chloro-2'-6'- diethyl-N-(methoxymethy1)-acetamide] combination from 1975 to 1980, and an atrazine-cyanazine-metolachlor [2- chloro-N-(2-ethyl-6-methyphenyl)-N-(2-methox1y- m ethylethyl acetamide] combination from 198 l to 1986. Either paraquat ( 1,l '-dimethyl-4,4'-bipyridinium ion) or glyphosate [isopropylamine salt of N-(phosphono-methyl)glycine], depending on species and size of weeds, was used preplant for no-till and ridge treatments. Post-emergence herbicides were used in no-till plots when needed; linuron [3-(3,4-dichloropheny1)- 1-methoxy- 1-methylureu] postdirected in 1979, ametryne [2-(ethylamino)-4-isopropylamino-6-methyl-thio- S-triazine] post-directed in 1980, and bentazon [3-( l-methylethy1)- 1H-2,1,3-benzothiadiazin-4(3H)-one 2,2-dioxide] broadcast in 1982. Plow, chisel, and ridge treatments were cultivated once annually. In addition, hand weeding was done as necessary to eliminate weed control as a variable.

column33: N + 60 kg P ha-1
column38: Two field experiments were carried out at Agriculture Research Farm, KPK Agricultural University Peshawar during 2006 and 2007 in RCB design with split-split-plot arrangements replicated three times. Zero and conventional tillage were assigned to main plots, three populations of maize viz., 90000, 60000 and 30000 plants ha-1 to sub-plots and four types of mulches, a hand weeding and a weedy check to sub-sub plots. Each experimental unit comprised of four rows of maize, four m long and 0.75 m apart. In case of conventional tillage, land was prepared by ploughing the field three times and harrowing afterwards. The rate of N and P fertilizers was 100 and 60 kg ha–1 before sowing while 60 kg ha–1 N one month after sowing. Maize variety ‘Azam’ was sown in June 2006 and June 2007 with the help of dibbler to keep uniform plant to plant distance. Additional maize population was maintained for replacing the missing plants in case of no germination to keep the plant population constant. Two rows of mungbean (variety NM-92) were planted as living mulch. The other mulches i.e. black plastic, white plastic and weeds were applied four days after crop emergence. In the weeds mulch, weeds were cut and spread in 4-6 inches layer between maize rows. In hand weeding treatment weeding was done twice (30 and 45 days after crop emergence). All the other agronomic practices were kept uniform during the growing season. Highest grain yield was recorded in the hand weeding (2863 kg) and black plastic mulch (2813 kg), followed by weeds mulch (2460 kg) and white plastic mulch (2398 kg), followed by living mulch (2145 kg) against 1422 kg ha-1 in weedy check . eds were cut and spread in 4-6 inches layer between maize rows.

column33: Urea + 150 kg P ha-1 as diammonium phosphate
column38: The field experiment was conducted at the Wuwei Experimental Station (37°34′N, 102°94′E, 1506m a.s.l.) of Gansu Agricultural University during the 2016 and 2017 growing seasons. This research station is located in the eastern part of the Hexi Corridor of northwestern China, and has long-term (1960–2017) average annual sunshine duration of 2945 h, annual mean air temperature of 7.2 °C, accumulated air temperature above 10 °C of 2985 °C, and a frost-free period of 155 days. Also, the sunshine duration in wheat growing season was 1080 h in 2016 and 1043 h in 2017, respectively. The mean air temperature was 17.9 and 17.3 °C in wheat growing season, in 2016 and 2017, respectively. The soil at the experimental site is classified as an Aridisol. At planting time, the soil contained 17.8 g kg–1, 1.76 mg kg–1, and 12.3 mg kg–1, and 29.0 mg kg–1 of organic matter, NH4 +–N, NO3–N, and Olsen-P in the 0- to 30-cm soil layer, respectively, in CT practice. In NT practice, these values were 18.0 g kg–1, 1.80 mg kg–1, and 12.6 mg kg–1, 29.2 mg kg–1, respectively. The soil and climate of this experimental site is representative of the cropland in the region, which relies on irrigation for production of cereals, namely wheat and maize. During the wheat growing season (late March–late July), precipitation was 107mm in 2016 and 101mm in 2017. The experiment utilized a split plot arrangement of treatments in randomized complete block design with three replicates. The experiment followed plastic film mulched maize in each year (polyethylene film 0.008- mm thick and 140-cm wide, made in Lanzhou Green Garden Corporation of China, Lanzhou). Two tillage practices [no-tillage with previous plastic mulching retained (NT), and conventional tillage with previous plastic mulching destroyed during tillage (CT)] formed the main plots, and a factorial arrangement of two levels of irrigation and three levels of N fertilization formed the subplots From late September to early October in 2015 and 2016, tillage treatments were applied following harvest of maize grain and stover (Fig. 1). This involved moldboard plowing to a depth of 30 cm for the CT treatment and no soil disturbance for the NT treatment. In the following spring prior to wheat planting, fertilizer was applied to all plots, followed by shallow rotary tillage and harrowing in the CT plots only. Spring wheat was planted with a manual duckbill punch roller dibbler. Also, Wheat field weeds were controlled by 2,4-D Butyl Wheat (cv. Long-chun 30) was planted at 4,650,000 seeds ha−1 (200 kg ha−1) on 28 Mar. 2016 and 26 Mar. 2017. column33: 300 kg ha-1  N-P-K-S-B 5-7.9-8.3-8-0.25% + 250 kg ha-1 ammonium nitrate 34.5%
column38: Irrigated wheat is grown in winter (May–August) when temperatures are low and favourable for grain yield and quality, followed by irrigated cotton in summer (November– April). The soils are predominantly sandy loam (11% clay, 11% silt, 78% sand) overlying sandy clay loam (20% clay, 12% silt, 68% sand) derived from granitic alluvium. Prior to the study, the whole experimental site was grown to low-input rainfed maize under conventional tillage for five consecutive seasons. At the start of the experiment in winter 2000, crop residues from the previous maize crop were left on the experimental site before implementing the tillage treatments. (a) conventional tillage (CT),—disc ploughing to 25 cm-depth followed by discing using tractor-drawn rotary disc, wheat straw and cotton stalks were completely buried; (b) minimum tillage (MT),—disturbing the soil to a depth of 15 cm using a tractor-drawn tine ripper, with partial covering of wheat straw and cotton stalks; (c) no-till system (NT)—wheat straw and cotton stocks were left on the soil surface, a hand hoe was used to open planting stations. Basal fertilizer was applied at a rate of 300 kg ha-1 Compound D (8–6.2–7– 5.4%; N–P–K–S) for wheat, and 300 kg ha-1 Compound L (5–7.9–8.3–8–0.25%; N–P–K–S–B) for cotton. A top dressing of 250 kg ha-1 ammonium nitrate (34.5% N) was applied for each crop at 12 weeks after emergence. In all tillage systems, weeds were controlled by hand hoeing, which is the common practice in the region. Pest and disease management were done according to recommended procedures for the two crops.

column33: UAN
column38: The corn was sprinkler-irrigated with a linear-move system as needed [determined weekly by the feel method. Triple superphosphate (0–46–0) was applied to the entire plot area before corn planting at 56 kg P ha-1 in 1999 and 28 kg P ha-1 in 2004. The soil had a pH of 7.6 (soil:0.01MCaCl2 solution ratio 1:2), organic matter content of 21 g kg-1, electrical conductivity of 0.7 dS m21 (soil:water ratio 1:1), sodium bicarbonate extractable P content of 17 g kg-1, and a clay and silt contents of 33 and 27%, respectively, in the 0- to 15-cm depth. Due to only a minimal grain yield response to N fertilization at the N6 rate in 2000, the fertilizer N rate was reduced to 168 kg N ha-1 in 2001, increased back to 202 kg N ha-1 in 2002, and then increased to 224 kg N ha-1 in 2003 and 2004 due to obvious N shortage in the NT system with each additional corn crop. The same rate of N was applied to the same plots each year with the exception of the N6 treatment. The N source was UAN (32–0-0), which was applied with a liquid fertilizer applicator that banded the N about 5 cm below the soil surface in bands spaced 33 cm apart (parallel to the corn row, but at varying distance from the corn row) the day before corn planting. Starter P and K fertilizer was applied directly with the seed at planting except in 2001. Corn hybrid Pioneer Brand 38B22 Bt LL was planted with a 76-cm row spacing on 27 Apr. 2000, DeKalb DK440 RR/YG on 30 Apr. 2001, Pioneer Brand 37H26 LL on 24 Apr. 2002, DeKalb DKC44–46 RR/YGCB on 28 Apr. 2003, and Pioneer Brand 38P04 LL on 27 Apr. 2004 in the plot area. Planting rates were approximately 84 000 seeds ha21 in 2000, 2003, and 2004; 91 000 seeds ha21 in 2001; and 96 000 seeds ha21 in 2002. The corn planter was equipped with residue managers or trash whippers to facilitate planting in the NT system. Corn hybrid was changed from year to year to allow herbicide rotation. In 2000 and 2001, N level in the water was not monitored but was assumed to be similar to that in 2002–2004. The total N contribution from the irrigation water to the plot area was estimated to total about 12 kg N ha-1 in 2000, 12 kg N ha21 on CT plots and 10 kg N ha-1 on the NT plots in 2001, 14 kg N ha-1 in 2002, 15 kg N ha-1 in 2003, and 8 kg N ha-1 in 2004 during irrigation of the corn with a very small amount. Crop residue cover on the soil surface was estimated each spring just before planting using the line-transect method. Residue cover did not vary with N rate in the NT system but varied slightly with N rate in the CT system.  Irrigation: 414 342 484 505 411 362 mm for 2000CT 2000 NT and 2001 to 2004

The experiments were designed by scientists, influenced by farmers’ interests and constraints in managing weeds effectively without additional weeding or herbicide applications. All treatments were arranged in a split-plot design with four replications. column33: ammonium nitrate + 15 kg P ha-1 as triple super phosphate + 0/28/56/112 kg K ha-1
column38: Field investigations were initiated in 1991 and continued through 1994 at the West Tennessee Experiment Station, Jackson, TN, on a Lexington silt loam (Typic Paleudalf, fine-silty, mixed, thermic) and at the Milan Experiment Station, Milan, TN, on a Loring silt loam (Typic Fragiudalf, fine-silty, mixed, thermic). Mehlich IEK in the 0-15 cm soil layer was evaluated during the fall of 1990. Extractable K for the CT and NT sites was 193 and 225 kgha1, respectively, for the Lexington soil and 221 and 188 kgha1, respectively, for the Loring soil. These levels of EK are classified as high (Univ. of Term., Plant and Soil Sei. Handbook). The cultivar 'D&PL 50' was planted by mid-May each year in 97 cm rows at Jackson and 102 cm rows at Milan. All plots were fertilized with 90 kg N ha1 using ammonium nitrate and 15 kg P ha1 using triple super phosphate. The CT plots were disked after fertilization and before planting. The NT cotton was planted by setting the planter gauge wheel on top of the previous year's cotton stubble. The experimental design was a split plot arrangement of treatments in a randomized complete block with five replications. Main plot treatments were 0, 28,56, and 112 kg of soil applied K ha1. Muriate of potash was broadcast before planting in both tillage systems. Foliar sub-plot treatments included a non-foliar check, KNO3, and Ca(NO3)2. Potassium nitrate was applied at 4.1 kg K ha'-application1. Calcium nitrate was applied at 1.6 kgNha1 to equal theN in the KNO3 foliar treatment. Foliar treatments were applied four times during the growing season in 94 Lha1 water. Individual sub-plots were 9.1 m long and 4 rows wide. Treatments were applied annually to the same plots. Foliar treatments were applied in 1991 and 1992 at 14, 28, 42, and 56 days after mid-bloom using a multi-line boom. In 1993 foliar treatments were applied at mid-bloom and repeated 14, 28, and 37 days after mid-bloom. The 1994 treatments were applied at early bloom with additional applications 14,23, and 32 days later. The application interval was reduced to improve treatment effectiveness. Petioles were collected from the two center plot rows before each foliar application. Twenty fully expanded leaves, generally the fourth leaf from the terminal, were collected from each sub-plot. Petioles were not collected in 1991 from the Loring site prior to the fourth foliar application. The petioles and leaves were separated, rinsed in tap water, rinsed twice in distilled water, and oven dried at 64°C. After grinding, petioles were extracted with a 2% acetic acid solution (Baker et al., 1994), and K concentrations were determined on an atomic absorption spectrophotometer.

column33: Urea
column38: Three factors comprised of two tillage types, five compaction levels, and two N fertiliser (urea) treatments were included in a strip-split-plot design. The various combinations of two tillage (horizontal strips) and five compaction treatments (vertical strips) resulted in 10 intersection plots (3.6m×6.0 m), each with two split subplots of urea (+/–) treatments. The experiment was replicated in four blocks. After spraying off previous pasture, NT and IT were used to establish the forage oat crop (Avena sativa L.) on 21 April 2016. For the NT treatment, forage oats were sown with a Taege® direct drill (Taege Engineering Ltd, Christchurch, New Zealand). In each intersection plot, urea was broadcast at 400 kg N ha−1 in one subplot (+Urea) to simulate the high rate of urinary-N inputs from livestock grazing of forage crops, whereas the other sub-plot received no urea (–Urea). Five millimetres of water was applied in both subplots immediately after application to dissolve the urea and minimise ammonia volatilisation. On 27 September 2016, all plots were surface cultivated prior to establishing a barley crop (Hordeum vulgare L.) with the Taege® direct drill. The cultivation involved two passes with a grubber (< 0.15m depth) followed by alternating passes of a grubber/ crumbler (Clough Maxitill), tine harrow, and Cambridge roller. Irrigation and N fertiliser applications varied between the three phases (Fig. 1). During the forage crop phase, a total of 189mm water (142mm rainfall and 47mm irrigation) and 40 kg N ha−1 was applied, the latter as base fertiliser at sowing (21 April 2016). During the barley phase, a total of 166mm water (90mm rainfall and 76mm irrigation) was applied. At sowing (28 September 2016), 37.5 kg N ha−1 was applied to all plots. Side dressings of 80 and 50 kg N ha−1 were made on 8 November and 21 November 2016, respectively.

column19: early season rice - later season rice - fallow
column38: The data is above ground biomass, A fixed field experiment was carried out at the Experimental Farm of Hunan Agricultural University (28_110N, 113_040E), Hunan Province, China, from 2008 to 2011. The soil of the experimental field was a Fluvisol with the following properties: pH = 5.83, organic matter = 27.7 g kg−1, total N = 1.59 g kg−1, available P = 12.6 mg kg−1 and available K = 107 mg kg−1. The cropping system evaluated was doubleseason rice in rotation with fallow. Two tillage methods were set as the experimental treatments: CT and NT. CT operation was performed using a rotary plough, whereas NT involved applying herbicide (paraquat) and soaking. Plots were arranged in a randomized complete block design with four replications and a plot size of 45 m2. Once assigned, the NT versus CT soil management was maintained for the duration of the experiment. Transplanting was carried out by hand with two seedlings per hill. In the early season, 67.5, 30, 30 and 15 kg N ha−1 were applied at basal (1 day before transplanting), early tillering (7 days after transplanting), panicle initiation and booting, respectively. In the late season, 75, 30, 30 and 15 kg N ha−1 were applied at basal, early tillering, panicle initiation and booting, respectively. In both the early and late seasons, 67.5 kg P2O5 ha−1 were applied as basal, and 135 kg K2O ha−1 were split equally at basal and panicle initiation. After harvesting the late-season rice (20 October to 4 November), weeds were naturally grown without any management activities. The dominant fallow weed was Japanese foxtail (Alopecurus japonicus).

N was split-applied: 90 kg ha−1 as basal, 45 kg ha−1 at mid-tillering, and 15 kg ha−1 at panicle initiation. P was applied as basal and K was split equally at basal and panicle initiation. In CT plots, the basal fertilizer was broadcast after the first harrowing and incorporated with the second harrowing. Weeds, insects and diseases were controlled as required to avoid yield loss. whether NT causes soil acidification may be determined by the effect of NT on bulk density, which differs under different conditions such as time since last tillage, residue coverage, soil type and cropping system.

column33: Urea + 45.9 kg P ha-1 as calcium super phosphate
column38: The site had a Huangmian soil (Chinese Soil Taxonomy Cooperative Research Group, 1995), aligning with a Calcaric Cambisols in the FAO soil map of the world (FAO, 1990). It is a sandyloam with lowfertility soil organic carbon below7.63 g/kg and Olsen P below 13.3 mg/kg. The site had a long history of continuous cropping using conventional tillage. The crop prior to the experiment commencement in 2001 was flax. Phase 1 started with spring wheat, followed by field pea and phase 2 started with field pea, followed by spring wheat. sow the seeds and apply fertilisers in one operation. For both CT and NT, some of them, stubble are retained and some are removed. Nitrogen and phosphorus were applied at 105 kg N/ha as urea (46% N) and at 45.9 kg P/ha as calcium superphosphate (6.1% P) for spring wheat, and 20 kg N/ha and 45.9 kg P/ha for field pea. No farm manure was used in this experiment. Field peas were not inoculated when sown as no appropriate rhizobia were available on the market. However, the site had history of field pea in the previous 3 years. Roundup1 (glyphosate, 10%) was used for weed control during fallow after harvesting as per the product guidelines. During the growing season, weeds were removed by hand. Pests and diseases were monitored and controlled as per conventional practice in the area.

column33: 200 kg ha-1 adiammonium phosphate + 200 kg urea
column38: This study was conducted in the 911-ha Robit-Bata watershed, located 10 km north of Bahir Dar, near Lake Tana. Rainfed crops include maize, teff, millet, and barley. Soils are volcanically derived and predominantly consist of chromic Vertisols in the lower watershed, with clay content ranging between 64% and 82% and organic matter ranging from 0.3% to 1.7%, and Eutric Nitosols in the upper watershed with clay content between 30% and 78% and organic matter from 0.6% to 2.2%. Depending on the crop, land preparation generally begins in May, at the start of the rain phase, with sowing in June. Land preparation was undertaken by an oxen-driven Maresha plough to a depth of 10–15 cm. Plots were ploughed three to five times prior to planting, depending on crop and soil type. Weed management is primarily manual, although some herbicides may be used. Between cropping seasons, animals are allowed to graze, which may contribute to soil compaction. In June 20, 2016, the sowing rate was adjusted to 20 cm by 70 cm, as per the recommendation of the Office of Agricultural within the district. Fertilizers were broadcasted at a rate of 200 kg ha􀀀1 diammonium phosphate (DAP consisting of 18% N-NH4+, 46% P-PO4 3-) during sowing and 200 kg ha􀀀1 urea (46% N-NH4+) 60 days after planting. Weed management was done manually in all plots four times from planting to harvest.

column19: continuous silage maize - winter rye cover; silage maize - winter rye.forage sorghum - winter triticale - alfalfa
column38: The field trial was located at the Experimental Field Station at ZALF Müncheberg, 40 km east of Berlin, Germany. The experimental field is located at 52°515′N and 14°07E at an altitude of 62 m. The ground is even, and the soil is sandy (Eutric Cambisol) with a high sand proportion of more than 83% at a depth of 0–60 cm. The experimental field size was 320m by 110 m. It had a split-plot design started in 2008 with 3 management factors, tillage, irrigation and cropping system, as treatment factors with 3 replications. The whole field was subdivided evenly into three cropping system blocks (3 replications) with two subblocks (21 m x 45 m each) for the irrigation treatment. As a result, there were 24 plots (21 m x 38 m each). The amount of irrigation was controlled and modeled by BERSIM and BEREST 90. Crop rotation also had two treatments: continuous silage maize (CMaiz) from 2008 to 2016 with a catch crop of winter rye in between and a 4-year crop rotation system (4ZCR) with the crop sequence of silage maize (2011, 2015, 2016) – winter rye/forage sorghum – winter triticale – alfalfa. All crops were harvested on whole mature as silage; thus, no crop residues were left on the field. Silage is popular as an important source of livestock feeding and bioenergy producing. As a result, we conducted repeatable measurements at the same plots during studying period from 2008 to 2016. PT buries or manipulates previous crop residues, helps to loosen the soil, mixes fertilizer and lime throughout the upper 20 cm and provides a reliable means of weed control. Indeed, in 2015, lucerne hindered maize-growing significantly in the no-till plots, an effect that was not observed in the plowed plots.

column19: wheat-rice-vinyl sheets covered wheat from April to June in 2001/2002 and 2002/2003
column27: weed controlled but no pest control
column28: weed controlled but no pest control
column38: Wheat and rice were grown under upland and paddy conditions, respectively, by draining the excess water through a channel between the plots. In the no-tillage plots, the soil was undisturbed except for the planting holes and surface scraping for weeding Half of the replicates were covered with transparent vinyl sheets from April to June to protect the fi eld from rainfall (dry treatment). The other half of the replicates were under natural rainfall (wet treatment). During the growth period in 2001/2002, the wet plots, however, were irrigated occasionally to avoid drought The crops were grown for six successive cropping seasons from 2000/2001 to 2002/2003. The vinyl shade was removed after wheat harvesting. From June to October 2000, rice was cultivated as the preparatory cropping before the experiment began. The topsoil in the fi eld was heavy clay (sand 22.3%, silt 47.6%, clay 30.2%). Wheat was sown between mid-November and the beginning of December, and rice between mid and late February. Ten g and 15 g of dry seeds per m2 were sown for wheat and rice, respectively. For wheat, the basal fertilizer was mixed with soil during tilling, and applied on the soil surface for the notillage treatment. For rice, the basal fertilizer was applied to the planting holes together with the seeds. Topdressing was broadcast on the soil surface in all treatment and crops. Fertilization was done according to the prefecture guidelines as follows. For wheat, 6, 4, and 6 g/m2 of N, P2O5 and K2O, respectively, were applied as a basal dressing using a compound synthetic fertilizer (N, 0.14 g g-1; P2O5, 0.10 g g-1; K2O, 0.14 g g-1). An additional application was conducted by oneto two-time split dressing to supply 6 g/m2 of N using ammonium sulfate. When the rice was sown, a slowlydissolving (controlled release) nitrogen fertilizer (LP-S100: LP-S120=4:6) at the rate of 13.3 g N/m2 was applied to the planting ridge. Pest management was not conducted for either crop.

column33: N + 150 kg P ha-1 + 105 kg K ha-1
column38: Four mulch levels used were control (no mulch application) and mulch at 2, 4 and 6 Mg ha- 1  (1) Zero tillage (or no till): the field was not tilled and herbicides were used to control weeds. (2) Minimum tillage: the field operations comprised two ploughing and two planking operations. Hoeing along with herbicides controlled weeds. (3) Conventional tillage (CT): consisting of one disk ploughing, four cultivations and two plankings. Hoeing along with herbicides was used to control weeds, (4) Deep tillage (DT): the field operation comprised two 0.3- 0.4 m deep chiselings with three shovels spaced 0.45 m apart followed by four narrow tine cultivations and two plankings with a wooden planker. Weed control was similar to that in conventional tillage. Mulch was applied after complete germination of maize, 15 days after Planting. Seed rate was 28-30 kg ha-1. Recommended doses of N, P and K (200-150-105 kg ha-1) were applied.

column24: mulch 4.8 t ha-1 with maize stover 30% cover of the soil surface
column33: Urea + 100 kg P2O5 ha-1 as phosphorus + 100 kg K2O ha-1 as potassium
column38: Field experiments were conducted at the Nuclear Institute for Agriculture and Biology, Faisalabad (31°23′ N, 73°2′ E; 184m above mean sea level), Pakistan. The soil (Typic Ustocrept, Hafizabad series) is a deep, well-drained loam developed in mixed calcareous medium-textured alluvium derived from Himalayas. Continuous maize-maize cropping sequence was followed with Springmaize grown during mid-February–early May (growing period, 110–115 days) and Fall-maize during mid-July–early November (growing period, 105–110 days). Maize (Zea mays L. cv. EV-77) was planted with row–row and plant–plant distances of 75 and 20 cm, respectively (plant density, 89,000 ha−1). Phosphorus (P2O5, as triple superphosphate) and potassium (K2O, as potassium sulfate) were applied at 100 kg ha−1 each at land preparation before sowing. In treatments receiving N fertilizer, urea was applied at 165 kg N ha−1 in three equal splits along with irrigation or rain (1st split, 10–15 days after sowing (DAS); 2nd split, 25–38 DAS; and 3rd split, 50–58 DAS). In treatments receiving mulch, maize stover (chopped to ca. 30 cm) was applied at 4.8 t ha−1 to cover 30% of the soil surface. Under CT, mulch was applied at the soil surface after tillage. For non-mulched plots, crop residues from the previous crop were completely removed. In addition to the pre-sowing irrigation (depth, 75 mm), the crop received 6–8 irrigations during the growing season (depth, 50 mm). Weeds were removed manually. At crop maturity, four sub-samples (1m2 each) were taken from each replicate plot and pooled to determine the dry matter yield.

column33: N + green manure + 100 kg K ha-1 as Kcl
column38: The NT plots were undisturbed until planting. Corn was planted about 10 May each year with a no-tillage planter equipped with fluted coulters. The seeding rate was such that a final stand of —50 000 plants ha-1 was obtained. All plots were sprayed at corn planting with a mixture of herbicides described by Blevins et al. (1983b). Muriate of potash (KC1) was broadcast on the soil surface periodically during the term of the experiment at the rate of 100 kg K ha-1 to maintain the soil test K level very high. Because the soil is naturally high in P, none was applied. Corn was harvested by hand from the two center rows of each sub-subplot for a total harvested area of =0.001 ha. Grain yields were corrected to a water content of 155 g kg-1. Rye seed (Secale cereale L.) was broadcast on all plots in mid- September each year (~2 wk before corn harvest) at a seeding rate of 188 kg ha-1. The rye provided a winter cover crop, green manure for CT, and additional mulch for NT. Corn stalks were shredded and left on the soil surface following corn harvest.

column33: N + 60kg P2O5 ha-1 + 60 kg K2O ha-1
column38: An aromatic rice (Jasmine) with a maturity period of 114 days and extensively cultivated in Ghana was planted at the Central Agricultural Station (6o40’25.6” N, 1o40’40.3” W) located at Kwadaso in the Ashanti region of Ghana. The study was conducted on an experimental field established five years ago. Intermittent irrigation was carried out when necessary. Mineral fertilizer was also applied at the rate of 90 kg N ha-1, 60 kg_P2O5 ha-1 and 60 kg K2O ha-1 to all treatment plots. All P and K and 50% N were applied three weeks after seeding on the ZTDS plots and immediately after transplanting on the ZTTS, RTTS and the CT plots. The remaining 50% N was applied at panicle initiation stage for all treatments. Direct seeding and transplanting were all done manually by hand. Crop protection (weed and disease control) was carried out when necessary with the use of glyphosate (Isopropylamine salt). ZTDS plots were sprayed with non-selective weedicide (Gylphosate). The high nutrients levels among the conservation tillage methods at the soil depth of 0–20 cm could be as a result of the additional nutrients realized from the mineralization of rice straw coupled with the application of inorganic fertilizer. Five treatments made up of four conservation tillage methods and one CT method were used for the study. The experimental plots had been under cultivation for the previous five years. The treatment descriptions are: zero tillage direct seeding (ZTDS); zero tillage transplanting (ZTTS); reduced tillage direct seeding (RTDS); reduced tillage transplanting (RTTS) and CT.

column24: residue, legume roots and stalks retained
column33: residue + legume roots + symbiotic N fixation
column38: Crop-rotation components were present every year. The herbicide program on CT and ZT used pre- and postemergence applications. Glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] at a rate of 783 g a.i. ha-1 was applied preplant in either fall or spring for perennial weed control. Postemergence applications of cyanazine + MCPA{2 -[[4-chloro-6-(ethylamino)-l, 3,5-triazin-2-yl]amino]-2-methylpropanenitrile + (4-chloro- 2-methylphenoxy)acetiacc id} at a rate of 281 g a.i. ha-~, thifensulfuron methyl {methyl 3-[[[[[4-methoxy-6-methyl-l,3,5-triazin- 2yl]amino]carbonyl]amino] sulfonyl]-2-thiophenecarboxylate} at 20 g a.i. ha-~ or diclofop-methyl + bromoxynil {methyl ester of (+-)-2-[4-(2,4-dichlorophenoxy)phenoxy]propanoic acid 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxybenzonitrile} at a rate of 805 + 280 g a.i. ha-1 were applied to barley crops in these treatments. Barley-field pea plots received postemergence applications of MCPB + MCPA, a 15:1 mixture of the sodium salts of MCPB [(4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy)butanoic acid] and MCPAa,t a rate of 563 + 38 g a.i. ha-1. Fababean plots received postemergence applications of bentazon[ 3 -(1-methylethyl)-(1H) -2,1,3 -benzothiadiazin- 4(3H)-one 2,2-dioxide] at a rate of 720 g a.i. -1. At Breton, continuous cropping treatments received pre- and postemergence herbicides as at Ellerslie. Low-input treatments at both sites and the DT treatment at Breton were hand-weeded once in 1990 and 1991 to ensure harvestable biomass. Harvest each year was between the last week of August and the first week of Septembe.

column33: N + 30 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 80 kg K2O ha-1
column38: In the non-tilled plots, the soil was undisturbed except for making planting holes and surface scraping for weeding. From June to November, 1999, soybean was cultivated under the condition described below for both treatments. All the fertilizers were broadcasted on the soil surface. The prefectural guidelines for fertilization regarding the amount and timing were as follows. For wheat, 6 g/m2 each of N, P2O5 and K2O were applied as a basal dressing using compound synthetic fertilizer (0.14 g g -1, N; 0.14 g g -1, P2O5; 0.14 g g -1, K2O). An additional application was conducted by three-time split dressing to supply 7 g/m2 each of N and K2O using ammonium sulfate and potassium chloride, respectively. When the soybean was sown, 2, 6 and 8 g/m2 of three major elements were applied using a compound synthetic fertilizer (0.05 g g -1, N; 0.15 g g -1, P2O5; 0.2 g g -1, K2O), and without additional application. Pest management was conducted for soybean on demand, but was not conducted for wheat. During the soybean growth period in 2000 and 2002, the plots were irrigated when a severe drought symptom was observed. All the plant residuals (leaf, stem and pod) were removed from the fi eld during harvest for both treatments. The no-tillage practice was started from May 1999, and continued for three successive years. The top soil in the fi eld was light clay, and its chemical property was as follows: pH (H2O), 7.02; total N, 1.75 g kg -1; total C, 20.9 g kg -1; CEC, 15.15 cmol kg -1.

column24: 50% rice residue retained in maize cycle
column33: N+ 35 kg P ha-1 + 26 kg K ha-1 + 10 kg Zn ha-1 (di-ammonium phosphate + murate of potash zinc sulphate)
column38: A long-term (10-year) field experiment was conducted from 2007 to 2017 with a set of tillage and crop establishment (TCE) and residue management treatments in irrigated RM cropping system at the research farm of Dr. Rajendra Prasad Central Agricultural University, Samastipur, Bihar, India (25.58, 51 °N, 85.4°, 313E). The climate of the site is characterized by hot and humid summers and cold winters with an average yearly rainfall of 1344 mm, 70% of which is received between July to September. Rice crop was sown with seed rate of 12 kg/ha, 20 kg seed/ha and 25 kg/ha under transplanted, PBDSR and ZTDSR treatments, respectively. Winter maize was sown with a uniform seed rate of 25 kg seed/ ha in all the treatments. Irrespective of the treatments, rice hybrid Arize 6444 was planted in 2013 and 2014, and long duration variety (Rajendra Mashuri) was used in the other years of study. The maize variety 30V92 (2007-08), Proagro Sampann (2008-09 and 2009-10), NK 6607 (2010-11), 900M Gold (2011-12 and 2012-13), DKC 9120 (2013-14) and DKC 9081 (2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17), were grown. During all the study years, the rice and maize crops were sown in mid-June and mid-November and were harvested in the first fortnight of November and second fortnight of May, respectively. Monsoon rice received a common fertilizer dose of 150 kg N+26 kg P+17.5 kg K/ha and winter maize was fertilized with 200 kg N+35 kg P+26 kg K/ha. In both the seasons, 11% N and whole P, K and 10 kg Zn /ha were applied as basal using di-ammonium phosphate, murate of potash and zinc sulphate hepta hydrate with seedcum- fertilizer drill, while remaining N was top dressed as urea in two equal splits at tillering and panicle initiation in rice and at V5 and VT growth phases in maize. Application of Zn fertilizer was made in alternate years. For managing weeds, in permanent beds and zero-till plots, prior to seeding of rice and maize weeds were killed using pre-plant application of glyphosate 1.25 L a.i. per hectare but no herbicides were applied in conventionally tilled plots before seeding. The weed in the experimental plots were controlled by using pre-emergence as well as postemergence herbicides as and when required but when applied, it was applied in all the treatments. The herbicides used for weed control in rice were: pendimethalin (1.0 L a.i./ha) as pre-emergence, ethoxysulfuron (18 g a.i./ha) and bispyribac sodium (25 g a.i./ha) as postemergence. In maize, combinations of 2, 4-D (500 g a.i./ha) and Atrazine (1000 g a.i./ha) was used as post-emergence as per the need depending on the intensity and diversity of weed species. In the subsequent years, about 3.1–4.8 and 2.8–5.0 Mg/ha, of rice residues were retained in ZTM and PBM treatments on soil surface in maize plots and maize residue of 2.2–5.0 and 2.6–5.0 Mg/ha were retained in ZTDSR and PBDSR plots of rice, respectively, and the remaining amounts of residues were removed for use as fodder for cattle. The experimental site was under rice-wheat cropping system for more than twenty years before the initiation of experiment in 2007. The experiment was conducted in large plots, each measuring 600m^2 and replicated 4 times.

column33: N + 26 kg P ha-1 + 50 kg K ha-1 + 8.75 kg Zn ha-1
column38: The experimental soil (0–15 cm) was a typic Ustochrept (Sobhapur sandy loam), with 165 g clay, 205 g silt and 620 g sand kg-1 that retained 18% and 7% water (mass basis) at 30 and 1500 kPa water potential. Other soil characteristics include bulk density (0–15 cm) of 1.59 Mg m_3; weighted mean diameter of soil aggregates, 1.54 mm; pH, 8.2; organic C, 5.4 g kg-1; Olsen P, 10.5 mg kg_1; NH4OAc–extractable-K, 0.20 C mol kg_1; and diethylene triamine pentaacetic acid (DTPA)–extractable Zn, 0.60 mg kg_1. The second irrigation was applied 5 days after the first irrigation and subsequent irrigations (5-cm depth each) were applied at the appearance of hairline cracks at the soil surface. All plots received 150 kg N, 26 kg P, 50 kg K and 8.75 kg Zn ha-1 in rice and 120 kg N, 26 kg P and 50 kg K ha-1 in wheat. Both rice and wheat received 23 kg N and full doses of P and K placed at 10- cm depth using a no-till seed-cum-fertilizer drill at the time of seeding except in puddled transplanting (TCE 1), where fertilizers were placed at 10-cm depth manually at the centre of each cluster of four hills using NPK complex fertilizer (10:26:26, N:P2O5:K2O). Zinc fertilizer was broadcast in rice at the time of the last puddling operation. Weeds that germinated before the seeding of rice and wheat in no-till and permanent-bed plots were killed by spraying glyphosate at 900 g a.i. ha-1. Butachlor (1300 g a.i. ha-1) at 2 days after transplanting (DAT) in transplanted rice and pendimethalin (1000 g a.i. ha-1) at 2 days after seeding (DAS) in direct-seeded rice were applied for controlling grassy weeds, followed by a spray application of 2,4-D ester (400 g a.i. ha_1) at 25–30 DAS for broadleaf weeds. Additionally, one hand weeding was done to keep the plots weed-free. For wheat, grassy and broadleaf weeds were controlled by spraying sulfosulfuron (25 g a.i. ha-1) at 25 DAS. Grain and straw yields were determined from an area of 70.2 m2 in flat beds and 69.7 m2 in raised beds located in the center of each plot. The crops were harvested manually and the crop residues were removed keeping only stubbles of 3 in. height from ground level under all the tillage and crop establishment techniques. In conventional-tillage practices, the stubbles were incorporated whereas under no-till practices, the stubbles were kept on surface.  Rice (hybrid) variety PHB-71 was seeded on June 2 and June 5 in direct-seeded plots, whereas transplanting was done on June 25 and June 27 in 2005 and 2006, respectively. Wheat variety ‘PBW 343’ was seeded on 5 November and 15 November in year 1 and year 2, respectively, at 100 kg ha-1.

column33: Urea + calcium ammonium nitrate + 140 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 150 kg K2O ha-1P+K
column38: A long-term stationary field experiment was conducted since 2009 at two experimental fields on two different soil types, Stagnosol at the site Cacinci, and Gleysol at the site Magadenovac (WRB, 2015) in the Central Pannonian agricultural subregion of Croatia. The experimental fields were located in the lowlands area with a 0–1% slope (the site Cacinci, Long. 17.86336 E, Lat. 45.61316 N, Alt. 111m and the experimental field Magadenovac, Long. 18.17254 E, Lat. 45.67046 N, Alt. 92 m), which belongs to the most crop productive agricultural region of Croatia. The data presented in this manuscript (soil and plant samples) was collected from the part of the second rotation of usual crop rotation in this region, in the years 2013–2014. Crop rotation includes crops in the following sequence: 2009-maize, 2010-winter wheat, 2011-oilseed rape, 2012-soybean. Maize (Zea mays L.) was sown in spring of 2013 (after soybean) and winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) in autumn of the same year (after maize). The experiment was set up as split-plot design (RCBD - randomized complete block design) with four repetitions. The size of the basic experimental plot for each individual tillage treatment was 600m2 and 195m2 for each individual fertilization treatment. Except for the soil tillage and nitrogen fertilization, all the other crop growing practices sequences: sowing, P and K fertilizing, pests' control, machinery and equipment used were identical in all the treatments. The rates of N, P and K fertilization in amount 50% of total were added prior to basic soil tillage in autumn. On NT treatment fertilizers were applied on the soil surface and without any further tillage treatment. The rest of fertilizers to total amount was applied in spring simultaneously with sowing. Nitrogen fertilizer was applied 50% in the form of urea (46% N) in autumn and 50% as CAN (27% N, calcium ammonium nitrate) in spring. Weeds were controlled with selective herbicides (according IUPAC: N2-tert-butyl-6-chloro-N4-ethyl-1,3,5-triazine-2,4-diamine) in post sowing pre-emergent treatment (PSPE) to the seedbed on April 28 on both fields. NT treatment was additionaly treated with non-selective herbicides three weeks before seeding in the beginning of April. Weeds were controlled with selective herbicides (chlortoluron 79.00% + triasulfuron 0.75%) in post emergent treatment (PE) on February 16 on both fields. Fungicide (epoxiconazol 125 g l−1 + kresoxim-methyl 125 g l−1) was applied on both fields for prevention and curative treatment on April 29. On April 28, 2013, after maize sowing and on October 29, 2013, after winter wheat sowing, soil crop residues cover were measured using the Line-transect method. CT~3-5%, NT ~ 42~46%

column2: Advances in Integrated Soil Fertility Management, Challenges and Opportunities
column38: The research work was conducted at Hombolo Agricultural Research Institute (ARI) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, in Dodoma, Tanzania. Hombolo is located about 58 km North-East of Dodoma Municipality at 05◦45’S latitude, 35◦57’E longitude and 1020 m above sea level. The soil of experimental site is fairly uniform, based on colour and texture (Hatibu et al., 1995) and has been classified by Mahoo and Kaaya (1993) as Typic Ustorthent. The mean annual precipitation in Hombolo is 589 mm. Overall mean annual rainfall for 18 years (1982–2000) was 658 mm. Experimental plots were established in 1996/97 cropping season; the plots had been under intensive sorghum cultivation for the past five years. The 2001/02 cropping season was a continuation of the previous studies on the site. Seven treatments comprising different water conservation techniques (tillage practices) and FYM were arranged in Randomised Complete Block Design with three replications. Treatment 5 was similar to treatment 3 except that 30 t ha−1 of FYM was applied before making the ridges. Treatment 6 consisted of making one deep tillage at the beginning of the experiment, application of FYM at 30 t ha−1 followed by formation of ridges. Planting was done on 6 December, 2001.  The crop was weeded three times, 17 days after planting (DAP), 50 DAP and 85 DAP. As in the previous years, weeding was done using a hand hoe. The study was on residual tied ridges, so no inorganic fertilizer or manure was applied during the 2001/02 cropping season. This was done purposely to reflect farmers practice in the study area as most of them do not apply inorganic fertilizer or manure. Land preparation consisted of the collection, removal of previous crop residues, grasses and weeds from the field which previously had tied ridges grown with sorghum variety Tegemeo since 1996/97 season and these were burned in between plots. The previous tied ridges (residual tied ridges) both shallow and deep ones were maintained to their original shape without altering their dimensions. The absolute control plots (no-till) which are analogy of the local practice (kuberega) were prepared in the same way as what farmers normally do every year.

This field study was conducted on two sites at the USDA-ARS Grazinglands Research Laboratory near El Reno, Oklahoma that were part of a long-term (multi-decade) experiment (initiated in 2011) to examine responses at the soil–plant interface to forms and amounts of applied N and tillage systems in continuous systems of wheat production. The predominant soil series of the upland site (35°32′45′′ N, 98°00′44′′ W; 421 m elevation) is a Norge silt loam (fine-silty, mixed, thermic, Udic Paleustolls) moderately drained with 1−3% slope. Soils (0−15 cm) of the upland site had average total organic carbon of 1.39%, and total N content of 0.11% (unpublished results, B.K. Northup). The predominant soil series of the bottomland site (35°34′21′′ N, 98°02′ 12′′ W; 411 m elevation) was a Dale silt loam (fine-silty, mixed, thermic, Pachic Haplusttols) with 0−1% slope. Soils of the bottomland site had average total organic carbon of 1.31% and total N content of 0.10%. The current study on radiation interception was conducted during the 2016−2017 growing season (October–May) of winter wheat. At each site, four N treatments were identified for the study. Included were two levels of inorganic N fertilizer (45 and 90 kg N ha−1), an annual legume (cowpea; Vigna unguiculata L.) as a source of green N, and an unfertilized control. These treatments were randomly assigned to three replicated plots (8 × 10 m) within each site. Each of these whole-plots was subdivided into two subplots (4 × 10 m) that were randomly assigned one of two tillage systems; NT and CT. Thus, the experimental design was a split-plot in a completely randomized design with four N treatments, two tillage systems and three replications in each N-treatment/ tillage-system combination. For the current study during 2016–2017, winter wheat was harvested on 10 June 2016. All NT plots were sprayed with Roundup® herbicide as a 1% glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] solution to control weeds on 16 June. Additional applications were undertaken as required to control weeds on plots that were summer fallowed (post-grain harvest through September). The cowpea plots were terminated on 17 August by shredding all plots, spraying the stubble in NT plots, and tilling CT plots (disked once, roto-tilled once) on 19 August. At termination, cowpea produced 1.9 Mg ha−1 aboveground DM and containing 62 kg N ha−1. The 45-N and 90-N plots were fertilized on 21 September and winter wheat was sown in all plots on the next day. Winter wheat was harvested on 31 May 2017. Crop management applied during the period of this study was similar to the timing and application rates as was used during all other years of the study (2011 to present). The two applied tillage systems represented points along a continuum from tillage only for planting and weed control with no applied herbicides, to NT combined with use of only chemicals to control weeds. Within the overall study, the effects of NT (chemical control only of weeds and no mechanical disturbance of soil) were compared to effects of CT that was undertaken with use of two best management practices: 1) fewest operations possible to incorporate winter wheat residues and cowpea biomass and prepare seedbeds; 2) leave roughness and residues at the soil surfaces after tillage to reduce erosion during fallow periods and times prior to adequate growth by wheat and legumes. Weed control on CT plots during the summer was largely conducted with herbicide; tillage was used for weed control in cases where weed populations were large.

It should be noted that because of the longevity of this study, many subtle management changes were made as equipment and herbicide technologies improved. Prior to the mid- 1990s, it was common for many no-till studies in central Iowa to be cultivated at least once for improved weed control. In some years it was also necessary to hand-weed the soybean plots for late-season weed control.
