column33: manure
column38: The soils, classified as chromic cambisols (Warren et al. 1997), had 65% sand, 22% clay and 13% silt. Chemical analysis was done at the main plot level because the field was observed to exhibit some variability. The Analysis showed that SOC content was 0.61 (±0.07)%, total N 0.05 (±0.01)%, pH water 6.5 (±0.46), extractable phosphorus 6.3 (±7.74) mg P kg-1, exchangeable potassium 0.56 (±0.14) me 100 g-1 of soil, exchangeable magnesium 0.78 (±0.077) me 100 g-1 of soil, and exchangeable calcium 2.29 (±1.04) me 100 g-1 of soil. The experiment, initiated in the short rainy season of 2005, was a split plot design with seven (7) tillageorganic resource treatments in main plots as follows: (1) Conventional tillage without organic residue (control) (2) Conventional tillage + crop residue (1 t ha-1) + manure (1 t ha-1) (3) Conventional tillage + manure (2 t ha-1) (4) No-Tillage + crop residue (1 t ha-1) + manure (1 t ha-1) (5) No-Tillage + manure (2 t ha-1) (6) Tied-Ridges + crop residue (1 t ha-1) + manure (1 t ha-1) (7) Tied-Ridges + manure (2 t ha-1). Split plots comprised 0 and 60 kg N ha-1 as chemical nitrogen fertilizer. Weeding in no-till system was done by hand pulling. Organic resources applied were goat manure (on average 2.67, 0.52 and 4.17% of N, P and K, respectively) broadcast at planting at 1 and 2 t ha-1 and maize stover (0.65, 0.08 and 1.78% of N, P and K, respectively) applied at 1 t ha-1. The manure was imported from one farmer at all times while maize stover was from the harvested crop, except in the first season when it was sourced from an immediate farm. The stover was spread over the plots prior to land preparation. Each of the treatments was split into two subplots that received 0 and 60 kg N ha-1, respectively. The chemical nitrogen fertilizer was split applied with 1/3 at planting and 2/3 at 4 weeks after planting.  The seeds were planted at 90 and 60 cm inter and intra-row spacing, respectively and thinned to two plants per hole after germination. Harvesting was done leaving one border row and end plants making a harvest net plot area of 4.5 m by 1.8 m from the initial subplot plot of 6 m by 3 m.

column38: Ploughing up and down the slope at a depth of 30 cm (PUDS). Seedbed preparation with a harrow and sowing were performed in the same direction. Field experiments were conducted at the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation Research Station at Embu, 0.515°S and 37.273°E, 1425m above sea level. The site is sub-humid with mean temperature of 22 °C. Soils are deep (> 2.5 m) highly weathered humic nitisols with low exchangeable bases, relatively high P-sorption, and with medium to low fertility. Two tillage systems (conventional tillage, CT and no-till, NT), three amounts of stubble (0, 3 and 5 t ha−1) and three fertilizer N rates (0, 80 and 120 kg N ha−1) were evaluated under continuous maize cropping for three consecutive seasons. Experiment 1: The experiment was laid out in a splitsplit- plot design with three replications. Tillage system was allocated to the main plots, stubble amount was assigned to the sub-plots while N rate formed the sub-sub plots. Main plot size was 31m×12.25 m, the sub-plots were 28m×3.75m and sub-sub plot size was 7m×3.75 m. Nitrogen was supplied as urea and provided as ⅓ at sowing and ⅔ at six leaf stage (V6), for both 80 and 120 kg N ha−1. Top dressing fractions were banded around plants, prior to sufficient amounts of rainfall to promote movement of urea into soil. Experiment 2: Treatments were control (no fertilizer; N0), and 80 kg N ha−1 applied at sowing (N1) or applied as ⅓ at sowing and ⅔ at six-leaf stage (N2), ⅓ at sowing, ⅓ at six-leaf and ⅓ at 12-leaf stage (N3), and ½ at six-leaf and ½ at 12-leaf stage (N4). These treatments were evaluated under both CT and NT with the application of 5 t ha−1 of stubble. The experiment was laid out in a split-plot design with three replications. Tillage system was allocated to the main plots while N supply formed the sub-plots. Main plots measured 31m×12.25m while the sub-plots were 7m×3.75 m. Crops were sown at the onset of rains: on 25th March for 2015 long rains season, 19th October for 2015/2016 short rains season and 3rd April for 2016 long rains season. Weeds were controlled with 1.5 L ha−1 of Roundup® (glyphosate) before sowing and 1.5 L ha−1 Dual Gold® (960 g L−1 S-metolachlor) after sowing in both tillage systems. In-crop weeds were removed by hoe-weeding in CT plots but with Twiga 2, 4-D® (Dimethylamine salt and 2, 4-diclorophenoxy acetic acid) in NT plots. The reason was to minimise soil disturbance in NT and to increase tillage in CT treatments. Insect pests were controlled with Thunder® (100 g L−1 imidacloprid) at 300 mL ha−1.

column5: Indiana, Southeast Purdue Agricultural Research Center
column38: Long-term tillage studies were conducted on 5 soil series throughout the state of Indiana from 1967 to 1973, and two newer studies were begun in 1975 and 1980, respectively. The objectives of the studies were to measure crop growth and yield under a range of different tillage systems, soil types and locations (latitudes) within the state.  A corn/soya bean rotation is better adapted to no-till than is continuous corn. Cover values with any given tillage system may vary widely due to amount of residue produced, distribution by the harvester, condition of residue at tillage or planting and depth of tillage. Cover rate of moldboard plow 1%, for no tillage 76%. In the 1967--1973 study, annual corn residue production on these plots ranged from 4.9--8.6 Mg /ha. Crop rotations studied on this soil were continuous corn and a corn/soya bean rotation. For no-till planting, the planter is equipped with 3--5- cm-wide non-powered fluted coulters to open a slot for the seed. The same rates of fertilizer, herbicide and insecticide were used in all tillage systems at a given site. Rates were adjusted to try to remove any limitations to crop growth and yields caused by pest problems or nutrient deficiencies.

column33: N + 25 kg P ha-1 + 43 kg K ha-1 + crop residue
column38: A 3-year field experiment was initiated in 1980 near the Delta Agricultural Project, Delta Junction, Alaska. Soils at the study site are in the Nenana series (Typic Cryochrepts; coarse-silty, mixed, acid) averaging 31 cm in depth overlaying coarse sand and gravel. The site had been farmed for approximately 15 years. During the three years of this study, neither ammonium nitrate nor urea was found to be a superior N-source for subarctic crop production. No significant differences in grain yield, crop residue production, available soil N, soil moisture or soil temperature could be attributed to N-source. Each year, all plots except those being fallowed were fertilized with N as ammonium nitrate or urea, phosphorus (P) as triple superphosphate and potassium (K) as potassium sulfate, at a rate of 84, 25 and 42 kg ha -1 N, P and K, respectively. Continuous barley plots received an additional increment of 28 kg ha -1 N for each 2200 kg ha -1 of crop residue present at the time of fertilization. All N and K fertilizers were broadcast prior to spring tillage and all P was banded in the row with the seed. Fallow in maximum-tillage plots was accomplished by chisel plowing once in autumn to a 20-cm depth with 5-cm wide twisted points, then disking the following summer as needed for weed control. Minimum-tillage fallow consisted of one tandem disking operation in the spring, followed by shallow (8-cm depth) chiseling as needed with 45-cm wide sweeps. Zero-tillage fallow was accomplished entirely with the herbicides paraquat (1,1'-limethyl-4,4'-biypridinium ion) and glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] applied as needed. one of which was continuously cropped to 'Galt' barley (Hordeum vulgare L.), the other three were alternately fallowed or cropped to 'Candle' rapeseed (Brassica campestris L.) or barley in a rapeseed--barley--fallow rotation. Each subplot was randomly split and one-half received all nitrogen (N) fertilizer in the form of urea, the other half received ammonium nitrate. Each subsubplot was 0.14 ha in size. The spring crop residues in that year are from the crop seeded in the preceding year. For example, in 1981, barley was seeded in rapeseed residue of 412 kg/ha.

column38: The soil of the University campus, characterized as Banaras Type III by Agarwal and Mehrotra (1952), is an Inceptisol with a flat topography, pale brown colour and sandy loam texture (clay 23%, silt 21%, sand 56 %). No irrigation was applied to either crop. The six treatments were: (1) conventional tillage (disked twice, cultivated once to 0.20 m depth), and residue removed (CT−R); (2) conventional tillage (as above), and residue retained (CT +R); (3) minimum tillage (disked once, cultivated once to 0.10 m depth), and residue removed (MT−R); (4) minimum tillage (as above), and residue retained (MT +R); (5) zero tillage (no cultivation other than the disturbance caused by the planting tines), and residues removed (ZT−R); (6) zero tillage (as above), and crop residues retained (ZT +R). In the residueremoved treatments, the rice was harvested at ground level, leaving no standing aboveground crop residue (stubble). However, in the residue-retained treatments, rice was harvested 0.2 mabove-ground level.The rice residue retained in the different plotswas incorporated into the soil during subsequent tillage operations. In all tillage combinations, residue retention significantly increased grain yield compared with when the residue was removed. The recommended dosages of fertilizers (80 kg N ha−1, 40 kg P ha−1 and 30 kg K ha−1for rice and 60 kg N ha−1, 40 kg P ha−1 and 30 kg K ha−1 for barley) were applied in all treatments at the time of crop sowing. The rainy and winter seasons are the major cropping periods in this region where a rice-based crop rotation is most common. Rice (Oryza sativa var. NDR 118) was selected as the rainy season test crop and barley (Hordeum vulgare var. Joyti) as the winter season crop.

The rotations used included increasing proportions of broadleaf crops: Rotation 1: canola (Brassica napus L.)-wheat-barley (Hordeum vulgare L.)-barley (cereal intensive); Rotation 2: canola-barley-pea (Pisum sativum L.)-wheat (balanced cereals to broadleaf crops); and Rotation 3: canola-peaflax (Linum usitatissimum L.)-barley (broadleaf intensive). Crop cultivars and seeding rates were cv. AC Oxbow barley (108 kg ha−1), cv. AC Barrie spring wheat (134 kg ha−1), cv. Exceed canola (7 kg ha−1) with 7 kg ha−1 of 5% granular terbufos (Counter 5G®) applied in furrow for flea beetle control, cv. Swing pea (164 kg ha−1), and cv. Normandy flax (56 kg ha−1). The N fertilizer urea was side-banded with target rates of 80 kgNha−1 for barley and wheat, 90 kgNha−1 for canola, 60 kgNha−1 for flax and no N for pea. All plots received 100 kg ha−1 of 14-20-10-10 as a blanket fertilizer application to ensure adequate amounts of P, K and S. no  fungicide or water. Propiconazole (Tilt®; 250gai L−1) was applied at 125 g ai ha−1 to wheat and barley when the flag leaf was fully emerged to control leaf spot diseases [net blotch (Pyrenophora teres Drechsler) and spot blotch (Cochliobolus sativus (Ito & Kuribayashi) Drechs. ex Dastur) in barley; Septoria leaf blotch complex (Septoria tritici Roberge in Desmaz., Stagonospora nodorum (Berk.) Castellani & E.G. Germano) and spot blotch in wheat]. Azoxystrobin (Quadris®; 250gai L−1) was applied at 175 g ai ha−1 to pea at early flower to mitigate mycosphaerella blight (Mycosphaerella pinodes (Berk. & Blox.)) Vestergr. and ascochyta foot rot (Phoma medicaginis Malbr. & Roun. in Roun. var. pinodella (L.K. Jones) Boerema). Canola was sprayed with azoxystrobin (250 g ai L−1) at 125gaiha−1 at the 2–3 leaf stage to reduce the impact of blackleg (Leptosphaeria maculans (Desmaz.) Ces. & De Not.) and with vinclozolin (Ronilan EG®; 1.0 kg ai ha−1) at 20–30% bloom to control sclerotinia stem rot (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (Lib.) de Bary). Rotation did not have an impact on leaf spot severity in 1998, but in all other years leaf spot severity was higher in the second barley phase of Rotation 1 (barley grown on barley stubble) than the first (barley grown on wheat stubble), or barley in other rotations (barley grown on canola or flax stubble). Fungicide effectively reduced leaf spot severity in 1998, 2000 and 2001. In 1999, there was a rotation×fungicide treatment interaction, which indicated that fungicide reduced leaf spots in all rotations, but the magnitude of the reduction was greater in the first phase of barley in Rotation 1 than the second phase or than in Rotations 2 and 3. Previously in northeastern Saskatchewan it was reported that continuous wheat yielded 34% less than stubble wheat grown in a fallow–wheat–wheat rotation, a reflection of the increased perennial weed and leaf disease pressure in the monoculture wheat system.

column33: N + 30 kg P ha-1 + 30 kg K ha-1
column38: The soil of the experimental site belongs to the Ibadan series and is classified as clayey, skeletal, isohyperthermic, kaolinitic Oxic Paleustalf. The soil is sandy near the surface and contains a gravelly horizon between 25 and 75 cm below the soil surface. The typical Ibadan soil profile is characterized by the following properties of the top two horizons (Moormann et al., 1975). The surface (O-25-cm) horizon contains 71.0% sand, 11.7% silt, and 17.3% clay, and the skeletal fraction is about 9% of the total. The sub-soil horizon (25-50 cm) contains 71.6% sand, 11 .l% silt, and 17.3% clay, and the skeletal fraction is about 44% of the total. Tillage system:  (1) notill + crop residue mulch, (2) notill + crop residue mulch and chiselling in the row zone to about 50 cm depth once a year, (3) mouldboard ploughing and two harrowings, (4) disc ploughing and rotovation, (5) notill - crop residue mulch, (6) mouldboard ploughing in the dry season and two harrowings just before seeding, and hereafter called summer ploughing, (7) mouldboard ploughing and two harrowings + mulch, and (8) mouldboard ploughing and two harrowings with contour ridging, hereafter called ridge till. Residue from the previous season crop was ploughed under in all plough-based treatments except in treatments specified as mulch. Maize variety (TZSR-white) recommended by IITA’s Cereal Improvement Program was sown every season. Sowing was done on about 15th April for the first season and on 20th August for the second season. Uniform plant population was maintained at 53 000 plants ha-‘. All treatments for each crop received uniform application of fertilizer, i.e. 100 kg N, 30 kg P, and 30 kg K ha-‘. Nitrogen fertilizer was applied in two split applications of 40 kg ha-1 at seeding and 60 kg ha-1 4 weeks later. All plots were weeded manually (slashing at the ground level with a machete) once at 4-6 weeks after seeding. Weed infestation was not a serious factor, because weeds were effectively controlled with paraquat and manual weeding. Buildup of insects and pathogens may be a factor that needs to be assessed. Some crop damage in the second season was observed due to stalk borers and termites.

column33: N + 26 kg P ha-1 + 30 kg K ha-1

No-till plots were sprayed with paraquat (1,1'-dimethyl-4-4'-bipyridiliumion) at 0.5 kg ha-1 active ingredients, and dead weeds and the residue from the previous crop were left on the surface. Post-emergence weeding was done manually as and when required. Grain and stover yields were measured at maturity. The harvest index (HI) was computed as the ratio of grain: grain . stover yield expressed in per cent. A uniform crop rotation of maize (Zea mays)/cowpeas (Vigna unguiculata) was adopted for all four years.

Experiment lasts from 1975 to 1987.Soil at the experimental site belongs to the Hoytville series. It is a member of the fine, illitic, mesic family of Mollic Ochraqualfs. This soil is derived from a fine-textured, calcareous, glacial till. It is characterized by a dark-colored surface horizon of about 20-cm depth, very dark-grey firm clay from 20 to 60 cm depth, and dark grayish-brown but very firm clay and mottled horizon from 60 to 100 cm depth. Mechanical analysis of the top 0-10-cm layer conducted in 1975 revealed the following composition: 18.7% sand, 42.4% silt and 38.9% clay. The clay fraction is composed of 28.5% (11.1%) of fine clay and 71.5 % (27.8%) of coarse clay. Corn or soybean were grown in an annual cycle except for 1984 and 1985 when winter wheat was grown Corn was sown in rows 75-cm apart with plant population of 75 000 plants ha-1. Soybean was sown in rows 37.5-cm apart with plant population of 450 000 plants ha- 1. Chemical weed control was achieved by applications of atrazine, lasso and roundup in corn and by amiben, dual and roundup in soybean. These herbicides ensured an adequate weed control in all crops. In general, relatively large pores and earthworm activity were visibly more in the soil layer where the crop residue had been incorporated. The fewer macropores in the RZ may be due to the reduction in activity of earthworms owing to the use of banded starter fertilizers.

column33: N + 50 kg P ha-1 as superphosphate + 50 kg K ha-1 as potassium chloride
column38: The shallow soil (Soil B) was a loamy, mixed, calcareous, mesic, shallow Lithic Xeric Torriorthent of 30 cm depth, with a water-holding capacity of 56 mm. No-tillage (NT) consisted of direct-drill sowing after spraying with herbicide (2 l 36% glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl)- glycine] per hectare). Before sowing, fertiliser was broadcast at a rate of 50 kg P (18% superphosphate) ha ÿ1 and 50 kg K (60% potassium chloride) ha ÿ1. Nitrogen fertilisation was done in February at a rate of 50 kg N (33.5% ammonium nitrate) ha ÿ1. On Soil A, barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) cv. Dobla was sown in late October or early November in 1992, 1993, 1995 and 1996. In 1994 heavy rainfall in September and October waterlogged the experimental field so sowing was delayed until the beginning of February with another barley cultivar, cv. Garbo. In 1996 heavy winter rainfall waterlogged the field, the crop failed, and was resowed in February with cv. Trait d'Union. Dry spring conditions, however, prevented good establishment and the crop was never harvested. On Soil B, cv. Dobla was sown in late October or early November in 1994, 1995 and 1996. The sowing rate was 160 kg ha ÿ1 (_450 seeds/m2) in rows spaced 17 cm apart. After emergence, herbicide was applied as 25 g 75% tribenuron-methyl [Methyl 2-1 ((((n-3-(4- methoxi-6-methyl-1, 3, 5-triazin-2-il)methylamino)- carbonyl)amino)sulfonyl)benzoate] per hectare to control broadleaf weeds and with 2.5 l 50% clortoluron [N-(3-chloro-4-methylphenyl)-N-N-dimethylurea] per hectare to control Lolium rigidum L. In some years an application of 2.5 l 30% imazametabenz-methyl [2-(4,5-dihydro-4-methyl-4-(1-methylethyl)-5-oxo- 1H-imidazol-2-yl)-4 (and 5)-methylbenzoic acid (3:2)] per hectare was necessary to control Avena sterilis L. in Soil A, and of 2% lindane [Gamma 1,2,3,4,5,6- hexaclorociclohexane] to control Zabrus tenebrioides L. in Soil B. Harvest was done with a microcombine. After harvest, the cut straw was removed from all plots.

column33: N + 55 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 169 kg K2O ha-1 + 29 kg MgO ha-1
column38: The experiment was established in the sandy loam soil in Bottelare (50.96N, 3.75 E, Belgium) in 2007 and lasted until 2015. The soil properties were: pH 6.4, soil organic carbon content 11 g kg–1, 28 mg P 100 g–1 soil, 16 mg K 100 g–1 soil, 10 mg Mg 100 g–1 soil, 104 mg Ca 100 g–1 soil, 2.1 mg Na 100 g–1 soil. The subplot treatments were three nitrogen fertilizer levels: (1) 30% lower than the recommendations, (2) according to the recommendations, and (3) 30% higher than the recommendations. Based on the N-index method (Vandendriessche et al., 1996) a field-specific fertilization recommendation was formulated. Also phosphate (P2O5) and potassium (K2O) fertilizers were applied according to the advice based on the soil sample analyses. Based on the analysis of the cattle manure injected in the field, the necessary amounts of additional mineral fertilizers, according to the local agronomic practices, were calculated. Depending on the growing season, in average, 45 Mg ha–1 cattle manure were injected. The exact composition of the cattle manure differed each year, the average composition was: 75 kg ha–1 N active, 55 kg ha–1 P2O5, 169 kg ha–1 K2O, 29 kg ha–1 MgO. In average, it was advised to add 150 kg N ha–1, thus, approximately half of the advised N came from cattle manure and the other part came from mineral fertilizers. Maize was sown in April–May. Before maize sowing a first herbicide treatment was applied [glyphosate 1440 g ha–1 (Roundup Ultra 4 L ha–1)], a second herbicide treatment was applied in June {Calaris [1 L ha–1] [mesotrion (70 g L–1) + terbuthylazin (330 g L–1)] + Samson Extra 60OD [0.4 L ha–1] [nicosulfuron (60 g L–1) + Dual Gold (1 L ha–1) (S-metolachloor 960 g L–1)]}. Depending on the moisture content and weather conditions, the maize was harvested in September– October. At harvest, fresh yield and dry matter yield were determined.

column38: The experiment is located at the Institute of Agricultural Science of Dongping County, Dongping (35°89' N, 116°36' E), Shandong Province, China. The experiment location is a typical site of a Chinese region of corn and wheat cropping systems. Corn-wheat cropping system with notillage in the corn season and rotary tillage in the wheat season is typical in North China Plain. The annual average air temperature is 14.4 °C with an average precipitation of 609.2mm which is concentrated in April–August. During the experiment, the total precipitation from the seedling to maturity stage of wheat was 198.0 and 156.6mm during 2015–2016 and 2016–2017, respectively (Fig. 1). The soil is cumulated irrigated fluvo-aquic soil according to the classification system of the USDA . Soil organic matter, total N, available N, available phosphorus, available potassium at 0–20 cm depth were 18.6 g kg−1, 1.2 g kg−1, 104.9 mg kg−1, 40.5 mg kg−1, 108.7 mg kg−1, respectively. The multiple-year field experiment was established during the wheat growing season of 2012–2013 with three tillage practices for the wheat season i.e. strip rotary tillage (sTR), rotary tillage (R), and subsoiling with rotary tillage (SR). In subsequent the corn season of 2013, two tillage practices i.e. no-tillage (N) and sub-soiling with rotary tillage (SR) were introduced for corn planting. After harvest, wheat and corn straw was returned to the soil; During the wheat growing season, 60% of nitrogen and all phosphorus and potassium chemical fertilizers (135 kg N ha−1, 130 kg P2O5 ha−1 and 77 kg K2Oha−1) were applied as basal fertilizers; and remaining 40% of nitrogen fertilizer (90 kg N ha−1)) was top dressed at the jointing stage. Irrigation and other agronomic management were kept same in all treatments as per local recommendations for high yield.

column38: The soil type is known as a gradational calcareous earth (Gc 1.22; Northcote, 1979); Calcic xerosol (FAO-UNESCO, 1976) or Calcarosol (Isbell, 1996). Locally the soil is known as mid-Mallee sandy loam (Newell, 1961) which has a clay content increasing from 14% in the top 10 cm to 30% at 100 cm. In the zero-tilled fallow (ZTDD) weeds were controlled exclusively with ‘‘knockdown’’ herbicides such as glyphosate (540–720 g ha-1) or a mixture of diquat (113–150 g ha-1) and paraquat (188–250 g ha-1). The number of cultivations and sprayings varied from year-to-year because of the influence of seasonal conditions on the germination of weeds. Wheat (Triticum aestivum cv. Millewa 1982–1985, cv. Meering 1986–1996 and cv. Ouyen 1997–2000) was sown at 60–70 kg ha-1 and superphosphate applied with the seed at 12 kg P ha-1. No nitrogenous fertilisers were applied. A pure medic pasture (Medicago truncatula), consisting of a 3:1 mixture of cultivars Jemalong and Paraggio, was sown at a rate of 10 kg ha-1 in the pasture phase in the first cycle of the PW and PFW rotations. Medic pastures were maintained free of grass weeds with selective grass herbicides sprayed at the three to five leaf stage of medic pasture development. Pastures were slashed two to three times during the growing season to simulate the reduction of biomass that would occur from grazing and a subsequent reduction in water use. column38: The four tillage systems evaluated were no-till (NT), which consisted of slot planting directly into the previous seasons maize residue; reduced till (R,T), which included winter chisel ploughing and spring chisel ploughing to 120 mm depth; reduced till (R2T), which included winter chisel ploughing to 120 mm depth and spring discing to 150 mm depth; and conventional tillage (CT), which consisted of winter discing to 150 mm depth followed by spring mouldboard ploughing to 250 mm depth and discing to 150 mm depth. Fertiliser (2.3.4(30)+Zn) was banded at planting at a rate of 450 kg ha-1 (30 kg N, 45 kg P and 60 kg K ha1). Additional nitrogen was broadcast in the form of L A N (28) at a rate of 350 kg ha-1 (98 kg N ha1 ) five weeks after planting. Herbicides used in the trial varied from year to year, depending on weather conditions, weed pressure, and the introduction of new products.. EPTC herbicide was applied as pre-plant, and paraquat was applied as a pre-emergence herbicide to control yellow nutsedge grass. Typical pre-emergence maize herbicides used included atrazine and terbuthylazine and if weeds were present at planting, then paraquat was applied. Typical ..post-emergence herbicides were atrazine and cyanazine, as well as paraquat. Insecticides consisted of carbofuran and sodium fluosilicate for control of cutworms, and deltamethrin and monocrotophos for control of stalk borer infestations.

column33: urea & amonoammonium phosphate + 24 kg P ha-1 + 48 kg K ha-1
column38: The study site was located 8 km northwest of Sidney, MT, USA (47°46´ N, 104°16´ W; altitude 690 m). Soil at the site was mapped as a Williams loam (fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, frigid Typic Argiustolls) formed in glacial till plains and moraines, with 350 g kg–1 sand, 325 g kg–1 silt, 325 g kg–1 clay, 6.1 pH, 18 g kg–1 organic matter and 12 mg kg–1 Olsen P. Long-term mean annual precipitation at the site is 357 mm, with 76% occurring from May to October (corn growing season). Average monthly air temperature ranges from −8°C in January to 23°C in July and August. Prior to the initiation of the study, the site had been in a spring wheat–summer fallow rotation under CT for several decades. The experimental design was a randomized complete block in a splitplot arrangement with three replications. In the crop rotation, each phase of the rotation was present in every year and phase followed the order: spring wheat, forage barley, corn, and pea. Traditional and improved crop management intensities for corn included conventional and increased seed rates from 2005 to 2007. The split plot size was 12.2 × 12.2 m and the main plot size 219.6 × 12.2 m. At planting in May 2004–2010, P fertilizer as monoammonium phosphate (11% N, 23% P) at 24 kg P ha–1 and K fertilizer as muriate of potash (52% K) at 48 kg K ha–1 were banded to all crops to a depth of 5 cm below and 5 cm away from seeds. N fertilizer as urea (46% N) and monoammonium phosphate were applied at recommended N rates of 101, 67, and 78 kg N ha–1 to spring wheat, forage barley, and corn, respectively. Pea received N fertilizer at 6 kg N ha–1 from monoammonium phosphate. Nitrogen fertilization rate for each nonlegume crop was adjusted by deducting soil NO3–N content in samples to a depth of 60 cm collected after crop harvest in the autumn of the previous year from recommended N rates. This was done to avoid excessive application of N fertilizers. Corn (cv. Pioneer hybrids 39T67-RR from 2004–2008 and 39D95-RR from 2009–2010) was planted using a John Deere 1700 MaxEmergePlus planter (Deere and Company, Moline, IL) in early May at a spacing of 60 cm. Corn seeding rates differed between two crop management intensities from 2005 to 2007, but were at lower rates that were similar between intensities from 2008 to 2010. Forage barley, spring wheat, and corn seeds were treated with labeled fungicides. Damage from arthropods or foliar diseases was not observed, precluding the need for insecticide or foliar fungicide applications. Plots in NT received a preplant application of glyphosate (N-[phosphonomethyl] glycine) at 3.36 kg a.i. ha–1 to control early emerging weeds. As corn was resistant to glyphosate, the herbicide was also used at the same rate as above to control weeds at corn leaf 6 to leaf 7 growth stages.Herbicide applications for spring wheat, forage barley, and pea were done with labeled compounds and rates that were previously described . Postharvest residual weeds in spring wheat, forage barley, and pea were treated with tank-mixed glyphosate (3.36 kg a.i. ha–1) and dicamba (3, 6-dichloro-2-methoxybenzoic acid) at 0.28 kg a.i. ha–1. After measuring grain yield, the remainder of the grain was harvested with a self-propelled combine and crop residue was returned to the soil.

column19: spring maize- winter wheat- summer soybean
column33: 300 kg ha-1 Urea + 300 kg ha-1 diammonium phosphate
column38: A 7-yr tillage × residual straw mulching study was conducted in a spring maize-winter wheat-summer soybean rotation system at the Qingyang Loess Plateau Research Station of Lanzhou University (35°39′N, 107°51′E; elevation 1298m) from 2001 to 2007. The average long-term annual temperature ranges from 8 to 10 °C. The minimum and maximum temperatures are 39 °C and −22.4 °C, respectively. Mean annual accumulated heat unit is 3446 ° days. The growing season for major warm-season crops extends from March to October for about 255 days with 110 frost-free days on average. Annual precipitation is between 480–660 mm, and average annual pan evaporation is 1504 mm. The dominant soil type is sandy loam. All plots were hand-weeded periodically throughout the growing season and a one-time broadcast application of 3 kg ha−1 a.i. of Triadimefon [1-(4-Chlorophenoxy)-3,3- dimethyl-1-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)-2-butanone] was used in 2003 for an insect outbreak. Maize was harvested manually in September and the remaining stalks were removed from the field by hand (T and NT) or shredded into 15-cm long pieces using a corn stalk shredder and returned evenly back to the original plots (TS and NTS). ‘Xifeng NO.24’ winter wheat was planted in late September immediately after maize harvest using a ‘Jinniu 2BF’ no-till drill (Jinniu Manufacturing Co., Qingyang, Gansu Province, China) under no-till treatments (NT and NTS) or a Xingnong drill (Xiguan Manufacturing Co., Baoji, Shanxi Province, China) after tillage treatments (T and TS). The seeding rate was 187 kg ha−1 PLS with a row spacing of 0.15 m. Starter fertilizer (diammonium phosphate) was applied at a rate of 300 kg ha−1 below the seed using a fertilizer coulter attached to the drill. Urea fertilizer was surface-broadcasted by hand at a rate of 150 kg ha−1 at the green-up stage. Last but not the least, the entire study was conducted on a rainfed system, therefore, no irrigation was included.

The soil is a Haplic Chernozem (FAO) of about 60±90 cm depth overlaying neutral to calcareous outwash gravels and sands. The average accumulated growing degree days are approximately 1000 providing an adequate season for 100±105 maturity-day rated corn varieties. Three tillage treatments: fall moldboard plow (MB), fall chisel plow (CH), and no-till (NT) were randomly combined with two residue management schemes (corn stover residue returned or removed) forming six unique treatments. Three nitrogen (N) treatments (0, 100, and 200 kg N ha-1 applied broadcast just before planting) were randomly assigned to three split plots of each tillage-residue treatment block. Prior to year 4, the 100 kg N ha ÿ1 treatment had been 200 kg N ha ÿ1 with the N application split one-half at planting and one-half at ``lay by''. For no-residue treatments, all corn residue was removed from the plot using a silage chopper. This technique did not remove the base of the corn stalk (approximately 15 cm high), some leaves and brace roots. The residue on the residue-returned treatment plots consisted of all plant material, except grain. This material was left standing after combine harvest and was stalk chopped just prior to tillage. Phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) fertilizer was broadcast applied to the blocks in the initial year before planting at the rates of 171 kg P ha ÿ1 and 246 kg K ha ÿ1, respectively. Soil test samples of 10 composited probes at 0±15 and 15±30 cm depth were taken in the fall of each year to determine soil fertility levels. Standard soil test analyses were performed by the soil testing service at the University of Minnesota. No further P or K were applied during the course of this experiment. Nitrogen fertilizer in the form of ammonium sulfate was applied broadcast according to N treatment in the spring of each year just before, or soon after planting. Annual soil tests monitored the pH status in plots of each treatment. In 1985, half the plots receiving 200 kg N ha ÿ1 received lime to correct the falling pH. Thereafter, yields are reported only for the limed plots where pH remained at 6 or above. Herbicides were used primarily to control foxtail (Setaria fabaria Herrm.) and wild proso millet (Panicum miliaceum L.). Atrazine and oil were applied post-emergence broadcast at a rate of 2.8 kg ai ha ÿ1 in the first 2 years and was combined with alachlor at the rate of 2.8 kg ha ÿ1 in the next 4 years. Plots of all treatments had alachlor alone applied for pre-emergence broadcast at rates of 2.8±3.3 kg ai ha ÿ1 for all other years. To control wild proso millet, pendimethalin plus cyanazine was broadcast before the fourth leaf stage of the corn at rates of 1.1 and 1.7 kg ai ha ÿ1, respectively. This application was carried out for years 6±8. Corn root worm insecticide (Counter (see Footnote 1), Amaze, Thimet, Lorsban, or Force) was banded over the row at recommended rates each year at planting time. Avariety of insecticides were used in rotation to avoid resistance buildup. Plots of all treatments were planted with Pioneer1 3780, 105-day hybrid seed corn in approximately the second week of May. From 60 000 to 75 000 seeds ha ÿ1 were planted in 75 cm rows at a depth of 3±4 cm.

column33: N + 120 kg P ha-1 + 100 kg K ha-1
column38: The experimental site is located in the city of Tai'an, Shandong Province, in Northern China at 36_090N, 117_090E. This region has a temperate continental monsoon climate with an average rainfall of 845.7 mm and a temperature of 12.35_C. The soil is classified as Cambisols (Food and Agriculture Organization). This study began in 2002. Before the experiment, the land had a long history of wheat and maize cropping system under same managements. A randomized block design experiment using 15-m-long and 4-m-wide plots was conducted over 15 years with three replicates. Four tillage and two straw treatment methods were used, which included conventional tillage (CT), subsoiling (ST), rotary tillage (RT), and no-tillage (ZT) without straw incorporation, and those same four tillage treatments with straw incorporation, identified as CTS, STS, RTS, and ZTS, respectively. Winter wheat–summer maize double cropping system served as the main cultivation method in this region. A typical rotation of winter wheat (cv. Jimai-22) and summer maize (cv. Zhengdan-958) was chosen for this study. Before sowing wheat, a corresponding tillage treatment was carried out, if needed. No-tillage was carried out before the maize was sown, and pesticide was sprayed after sowing. Winter wheat was generally sown in mid-October and harvested in early June of the next year. Basal fertilizer was applied at 225 kg N ha−1 and 180 kg P ha−1 before wheat sowing and at 180 kg K ha−1 and 110 kg N ha−1 were applied at the jointing stage, with 160 mm of irrigation at both times. Summer maize was sown in mid-June and harvested in early October. For maize, a basal fertilizer was used at 120 kg N ha−1, 120 kg P ha−1, and 100 kg K ha−1, whereas 120 kg N ha−1 was applied as a topdressing at the jointing stage.

column33: N + 90 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 180 kg K20 ha-1
column38: The experimental field (29_5100N, 115_3300E) is situated in Wuxue City, Hubei Province, China.  The paddy soil, a type of sandy loam soil, is classified as Gleysol . The rice (Oryza sativa, LYP9) and oilseed rape (Brassica napus, HS3) varieties were planted. Middle-season rice was direct-seeded on June 3rd in each year, and the harvest was conducted in early October. Throughout the whole rice season, fertilizers were applied at the rates of 180 kg N ha􀀀1, 90 kg P2O5 ha􀀀1, and 180 kg K2O ha􀀀1 for N fertilizer treatments. Both P (single super-phosphate) and K (potassium chloride) fertilizers were used as basal fertilizers only at the seedling stage, and the N fertilizers were applied in four split doses: at 50% as basal fertilizer, 20% as tillering fertilizer, 12% as jointing fertilizer and 18% as earing fertilizer under IF, OFIF and SRIF treatments. Conventional urea (46%) was used as the topdressing N. For OF treatment, 3082 kg ha􀀀1 rape seed cakes (equal to 180 kg N ha􀀀1) were used in a single dose at only the seedling stage. For OFIF and SRIF treatments, 925 kg ha􀀀1 rape seed cakes (equal to 54 kg N ha􀀀1) and 616 kg ha􀀀1 slow release fertilizers (equal to 90 kg N ha􀀀1) were applied as basal fertilizer, respectively. Herbicides (36% glyphosate at 3 L ha􀀀1) and pesticides (20% chlorantraniliprole at 150 mL ha􀀀1 and 3% emamectin benzoate at 450 mL ha􀀀1) were used to control weeds and pests during rice growing seasons when needed. The contact of fertilizer particles and the soil may be reduced by the residues retained in NT soil surface, which means reduced adsorption of NH4 C from hydrolyzed fertilizer N by soil particles under NT.

Field experiments were conducted in the summer crop seasons of 2013, 2016, and 2017 at the experimental station of Universidad Autonoma Agraria Antonio Narro in Saltillo, Coahuila, Mexico. The site is located at 25Deg 23'42'' Nand 100Deg 59'57''W, at an altitude of 1743mabove sea level. The climate is semiarid with an average annual temperature of 16.9 Deg C, the mean annual rainfall 435 mm, and annual evaporation of 1956 mm. The soil is a clay loam (34.1% clay, 33.4% silt, and 32.5% sand) with 2.09% of organic matter. Average soil bulk density for the site is 1.37 g cm-3. The three tillage treatments were applied in plots of 12 m x 40 m and replicated three times. Residue retained.

column5: Ruuki Research Station of MTT Agrifood Research
column33: Artificial NPK fertilizer
column38: The soil at drilling after cereal varied by block between sandy loam (Gleyic Podzol) and mould soil (Histic Podzol) (FAO 1998), and pHw was 6.2-6.6 (0-25 cm). The soil at drilling after ley varied by block between sandy loam and mould soil in 2003-2004, but in 2005 there was only mould soil at the experimental area. Soil pHw was 5.2-6.1 (0-25 cm). Straw was chopped by combine harvester in the field before the experiment was established in autumn 2002. In 2003-2005 the straw was collected and removed from the field after harvest. Glyphosate was applied normally in autumn, but with direct drilling glyphosate could be applied before drilling in spring. Treatment D was also sprayed with glyphosate in spring 2005. Glyphosate was used to control the severe E. repens infestation that interfered with barley growth in treatment D in 2004. The trade name of glyphosate was Roundup† Max (680 g/kg) and the application rate was 1.5-2 kg/ha. For treatments A, B, D and E the artificial NPK fertiliser was chosen so that the amount of nitrogen was the same as in slurry, and phosphorus and potassium concentrations were estimated by soil analysis to approximate to the requirements of barley. Barley was fertilised with 60-70 N soluble. In treatments C and F all nutrients were supplied as beef cattle slurry.

This site was representative of the intensively cropped and irrigated alluvial sands along the Wisconsin River. The test soil has a thick, dark (molliclike) surface horizon that was developed under prairie vegetation (Seybold et al., 1994); it is excessively drained (Hart et al., 1994) and has no structurally controlled macropores. Little or no runoff occurs at this site because of level topography and high infiltration. The research site is bordered on the east by a gravel road consisting of crushed limestone rock, on the south by a red pine (Pinus resinosa Ait.) plantation, on the west by a commercial farm (center-pivot irrigated seed corn or vegetables), and on the north by indigenous lowland trees along theWisconsin River. The site had not been cultivated for at least 7 years prior to 1989 and was covered with typical prairie vegetation. The initial study consisted of three irrigation treatments each in a randomly selected block. column33: N + 79.8 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 100.5 kg K2O ha-1
column38: This on-farm experiment was conducted for six years in Shuanghe Village, Dongxi town, Jianyang City (E 104Deg 36',N 30Deg 24' ) in the Sichuan basin of southwest China. Mean annual temperature there is 17.1 ºC, with annual precipitation of 830 mm/year . The soil texture of the paddy fields is mostly clay, with a 24.0% sand and 41.5% clay fractions; with 9.4 g kg-1 of organic carbon and 1.42 g kg-1 of total nitrogen concentration. The field experiment was conducted in an organic rice-rapeseed rotation system with four respective treatments. CT—conventional tillage without plastic cover and without plant residue return NTPC—no tillage with only plastic cover in the rice season (no rice straw mulch in the rapeseed season). NTCM—no tillage with rapeseed plant residue mulch in the rice season and rice straw mulch in the rapeseed season (no plastic cover in the rice season). NTCMPC—no tillage with straw mulch and plastic cover in the rice season and straw mulch in the rapeseed season. In the rice season, each treatment received 113.7 kg N ha-1, 79.8 kg P2O5 ha-1, and 100.5 kg K2O ha-1; and in the rapeseed season, each received 93.3 kg N ha-1, 81.7 kg P2O5 ha-1, and 122.5 kg K2O ha-1. All the organic fertilizers were applied as basal fertilizer. In the NTCM and NTCMPC treatments, after the rice was harvested, all the rice straw from the plot was left in the field. After the rapeseed was harvested, rapeseed plant residues were shredded into small pieces of 20–25 cm and left in the field. In the NTCMPC treatment, the middle of the beds had a furrow 10 cm depth and 10 cm wide, and the rapeseed residue was put back into these furrows; then the raised beds’ surface was flattened and covered with plastic film. In the NTPC and NTCMPC treatments, after making the soil soft with irrigation, raised beds were constructed and the surface flattened. The plastic-covered raised-beds have furrows between them that permit furrow irrigation which  replaces flood irrigation and economizes on water.

column5: Jiangsu Province, Changshu agro-ecological experiment station
column33: Urea + 80 kg P2O5 ha-1 as calcium surphosphate + 90 kg K2O ha-1 as potassium chloride
column38: A field experiment was conducted on a rice–wheat system during 2011–2012 at the Changshu agro-ecological experimental station (31° 32′ 93″ N, 120° 41′ 88″ E), Chinese Academy of Sciences, Jiangsu province. The main crops are flooded summer rice and drained winter wheat on an annual rotation. The soil is classified as Gleyi-Stagnic Anthrosol (CRGCST 2001) developed from lacustrine sediment with a texture of silt clay. Wheat was grown from November 2011 to May 2012 (199 days duration). The experiment included two tillage practices: conventional tillage (CT) and no-tillage (NT), each with four treatments: U0 (the control, zero urea, and zero NI), U1 (urea without NI), U1 + DCD (urea with DCD), and U1 + CP (urea with CP). In total, eight treatments were established in a randomized block design with three replications in plots 6 m in width and 7 m in length. The NT treatments were initiated in place since the wheat season in 2011. The land for conventional tillage was prepared by the initial use of a moldboard plow to invert the upper soil layers. This was followed by two crossharrowings for cutting and smoothing prior to sowing. The no-tillage plots were not plowed and the sowing was performed using a no-till seed drill. Urea was applied at a rate of 200 kgNha−1 at 2, 120, and 130 days after sowing (DAS) at a ratio of 6:1:3 for the three applications. Application rates of CP and DCD were 0.24 and 3 %, respectively, of urea–N and the mixtures were obtained by physically mixing NI with urea. Phosphorus (80 kg P2O5 ha−1) as calcium surphosphate and K (90 kg K2O ha−1) as potassium chloride were incorporated into the soil in all plots at the time of sowing. Wheat (cultivar Yangmai 16, 180 kg seed ha−1) was sown on November 11, 2011 and harvested on May 28, 2012.

column38: The experiment was started in 1978 at the Central Rice Research Institute farm, Cuttack, on an alluvial soil (Aerie Haplaquept) of the Mahanadi Delta. Average annual rainfall at Cuttack is 1409 mm, most of which is received during the south-west monsoon (June-September). The rice (Oryza saliva) was established in the wet season either without tillage (NT) or after dry ploughing (DP) or puddling (P). Paraquat (2-5 1/ha) was sprayed for the NT treatment and weeds that survived or emerged subsequently were hand weeded before sowing. To distinguish tillage effects on seedling growth, no N fertilizer was applied at sowing but prilled urea was broadcast at 60 kg N/ha in three equal splits at c. 30, 45 and 60 days after sowing. The last dose was applied mainly for the studies of N movement. Superphosphate (20 kg P2O5/ha) and muriate of potash (40 kg K2O/ha) were broadcast at sowing. During a rainless period, the soil was not allowed to dry for more than 4-5 days before it was irrigated. Weeds were controlled by hand weeding once or twice. Yield of straw is recorded, but whether they are returned or not is unknown.

column33: N + 30 kg P ha-1 + 42 kg K ha-1
column38: An 8-yr (1998–2005) field experiment with two 4- yr rotations was conducted on a Gray Luvisol (Boralf) sandy clay loam soil with 7.1 pH near Star City in northeastern Saskatchewan, Canada. The experiment was a factorial combination of two tillage systems: no-tillage (NT), and conventional tillage (CT); two levels of straw management: straw retained (R), and straw not retained (NR); four levels of fertilizer N: 0, 40, 80, and 120 kg N ha-1, except that no N was applied to the pea (Pisum sativum L.) phase of the rotation. In the NR treatments straw was removed, while in the R treatments straw was returned to the plots after crop harvest in late August or early September. The NT plots were sprayed with glyphosate (RoundupTM) for weed control in spring prior to seeding. All plots received blanket annual applications of P (30 kg P ha-1), K (42 kg K ha-1) and S (17 kg S ha-1) fertilizers broadcast prior to tillage and sowing in spring. Urea N fertilizer was side-banded 2.5 cm away and 2.5 cm below seed rows at sowing. The plots were seeded to barley (Hordeum vulagare L., cv. AC Lacombe) in 2002, peas (P. sativum L.cv., Alfetta) in 2003, wheat (Triticum aestivum L., cv. AC Barrie) in 2004 and canola (Brassica napus L., cv. 45A71) in 2005. Seeding rate was 108, 202, 134, and 9 kg ha-1 and seeding depth was 3.8, 4.5, 4.4, and 1.9 cm for barley, peas, wheat, and canola, respectively. The crop was seeded in May each year with a ConservaPack drill, equipped with knives (about 2 cm wide) in 22.5 cm rows, at a speed of about 3.5 km h-1. Appropriate herbicides were used in all plots for in-crop weed control. Barley-pea-wheat-canola rotation.

column33: Urea + 60 kg P2O5 ha-1 as super phosphate
column38: The study was performed with data obtained during eight growing seasons (1998–1999 to 2006–2007) obtained from NT and CT trials located at the Antumapu Experiment Station of the University of Chile (338400S, 708380W; 608 m elevation). In the CT treatment, maize residues (equivalent to 7565 kg C ha-1) were mechanically shredded and buried with a moldboard plow to a depth of 20 cm. The soil was disked twice using a disk harrow before wheat planting. In both tillage treatments, wheat was planted on June at a density of 300 plants m-2 using a NT drill (Semeato SHM 11/13, Brazil). During the wheat rotation phase, the soil was fertilized with urea and triple super phosphate. column33: 200 kg ha-1 NPK-8-24-8 fertilizer + 200 kg ha-1 NH4NO3
column38: The soil was a Calciortidic Haploxeralf characterized by a lime horizon within a meter of the surface. It had a loamy–sandy texture in the two surface horizons (Ap, Bt), changing to sandy with depth (CCa). The soil had 5% total carbonate, 1% active limestone and an average pH of 7.8 in the upper 60 cm at the beginning of the experiment. Barley was fertilized in February with a fertilizer placement drill. Cultivator (10–15 cm) and roller on fallow plots were used when needed to control weeds in CT and MT. Barley was harvested in June. Vetch (Vicia sativa) was harvested in May and tilled according to treatment 10 days later. No tillage (NT): Herbicide was applied at the beginning of October and sown (5 cm) at the end of October with a seed drill. Herbicide was applied when needed before the middle of May. Crop rotations were continuous barley (BB), fallowbarley (FB) and vetch-barley (VB). Plots were sown with 175 kg ha-1 of winter barley (v. Tipper) and 100 kg ha-1 of vetch (v. Muza). Only barley was fertilized, independently of tillage system, with 200 kg ha-1 of an 8-24-8 fertilizer incorporated at seeding and 200 kg ha-1 of a 26-0-0 NH4NO3 fertilizer broadcast at tilling. Lack of residue mixture, poor contact with soil micro organisms, and lower aeration allowed residue to remain for a longer period in soil. Straw and grain samples were dried at 80 8C, milled and, straw samples, furnace oxidised.

column33: N + 26 kg P ja-1 + 50 kg K ha-1
column38: The experiments reported here were initiated in June 1981 with a uniformly treated maize crop at the Irrigation Research Station. The residue mangement treatments were: (1) previous crop residue left on the surface in no-tillage plots and incorporated in conventional tillage; (2) previous crop residue removed from the plots, irrespective of tillage treatment. Fertilizer was applied at 60 kg ha -1 N, 26 kg ha -1 P and 50 kg ha -1 K for each crop before planting. Four weeks after planting, a further 60 kg ha -1 N was applied as a top dressing. Wheat (cv. Slete Cerros) was planted in rows 25 cm apart in the third week of November each year. Two irrigation treatments were imposed on the dry-season wheat cultivation, namely irrigations with 45 mm water at 8-day and 16-day intervals. Maize (cv. TZB) was planted at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows in the second week of June each year. Irrigation was not provided for maize because it is a rain-fed crop. Two weeks before planting the crop, the no-tillage plots were treated with 1.4 kg ha -1 glyphosate.

Fertilizer was applied at 60 kg ha -1 N, 26 kg ha -1 P and 50 kg ha -1 K for each crop before planting. Four weeks after planting, a further 60 kg ha -1 N was applied as a top dressing. Wheat (cv. Slete Cerros) was planted in rows 25 cm apart in the third week of November each year. Two irrigation treatments were imposed on the dry-season wheat cultivation, namely irrigations with 45 mm water at 8-day and 16-day intervals. Maize (cv. TZB) was planted at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within rows in the second week of June each year. Irrigation was not provided for maize because it is a rain-fed crop. column33: Urea + 20 kg P ha-1
column38: The sites were chosen from among the Dark Brown (Alliance), Black (Wainwright and Hairy Hill), and Gray (Elk Point and Plamondon) soil zones. The soils included coarse and medium-textured Chernozemic, Luvisolic, and Gleysolic soils. All sola were free of CaCO3 and soluble salts with pH values ranging from 5.9 to 7 .5. The experimental design was a split plot with six replicates with fungicide application as the main plot treatment and tillage system as subplot treatrnents. Fungicide was applied when plants were in the flag leaf stage. The ZT treatment received no tillage operations thus herbicides were used for weed control. Each site was in standing cereal stubble in the fall of 1987 when sites were sampled for characterization. Glyphosate was applied to improve weed control at this time. In the spring of 1988, the required number of tillage operations for Cl and C2 were conducted in the spring. All plots were seeded to barley (cv. Leduc) at a rate of 78 kg ha-r using a self-propelled 8-row double disk plot seeder with offset double disks. The rate of N fertilization was calculated so that residual N plus applied fertilizer N was equal to 100 kg N ha-r in all plots. Urea (46-0-0) was applied during seeding at the prescribed rate in a mid-row band between every second seed row at a depth of 8-10 cm. Each year 2O kg P ha-r was applied as mono-calcium phosphate (0-45-0) with the seed. Herbicides were applied as required at each site to ensure complete control of the weeds identified (Table 2). Lower rates may have been adequate to control or suppress weeds. Glyphosate was used on ZT plots for weed control prior to seeding. Both glyphosate and 2,4-D were used for fall weed control on ZT and MT plots. Difenzoquat and diclofopmethyl were used to control grassy weeds, whereas, bromoxynil, MCPA and,2,4-D were used to control broadleaf weeds in the crop.

column33: N + 10 kg P ha-1 as monoammonium phosphate
column38: Two other sites were added in 1982, one on a Scepffe heavy clay (Rego Brown Chernozem) and the other on a Hatton fine sandy loam (Orthic Brown Chernozem). Cont W had two tillage systems: CT with and NT without a tillage operation immediately before seeding. F-W (CT) was omitted on the sandy loam soil to minimize chances oferosion occurring, and on the clay until 1990, to minimize highway travel of machinery. CT practices mimicked those widely used in southwestem Saskatchewan. Fall applications of 2,4-D ester (all tillage treatments) or chlorsulfuron (MT and NT fallow for 1985-1989) were used each fall to control winter annual broadleaf weeds. Nitrogen fertilizer (ammonium nitrate), based on soil nitrate levels measured in the upper 0.60 m of the soil in the fall and the regional soil test recommendations, was broadcast applied prior to seedbed preparation or seeding until 1990, aher which up to 45 kg N hrr was applied with the seed and any additional fertilizer required was broadcast applied. Sprine wheat (Canuck, Leader. or Neepawa) was sown at a rate of 67 kg ha-1 on the silt loam and clay, while durum wheat (Wakooma or Kyle) was sown at a rate of 101 kg ha-1 on the sandy loam. All tillage ffeafinents received 10 kg ha-1 P (monoammonium phosphate) placed with the seed. All crop residues were spread behind the combine with straw and chaff spreaders.

The entire study site had been cropped to spring wheat in 1988. The soils are mapped as Ardill loam, predominantly orthic Brown Chernozems with a significant proportion of calcareous Brown Chernozemic soils. The strip treatments were stubble height and deep tillage. The stubble treatments were conventional short stubble and uniform tall stubble. Average short stubble heights were 15, 12, and 14 cm for the winters of 1988–1989, 1989–1990, and 1990–1991, respectively. Corresponding tall stubble heights for those winters were 23, 26, and 24 cm, respectively. The deep tillage plots were 20 m by 174 m. Prior to seeding, fertilizer N was broadcast as ammonium nitrate at rates of 11, 28, 40 kg N ha–1 in 1989, 1990, and 1991, respectively, based on fall soil tests. The land was seeded to “Kyle” durum wheat (Triticum turgidum L.) at 87 kg ha–1 by mid May using a discer, then harrow-packed. Fertilizer P was applied with the seed at rate of 7 kg ha–1. column38: The experiment was designed as a randomised complete block with a split–splitplot arrangement and three blocks. The main plots were divided by tillage system (no tillage, NT and conventional tillage, CT). Subplots were divided by crop rotation, with four different two-year rotations [wheat–sunflower (Triticum aestivum L.–Helianthus annuus L.) (WS), wheat–faba bean (Vicia faba L.) (WFb), wheat– chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.) (WC), wheat–fallow (WF)], and a monoculture of wheat–wheat (WW); sub-subplots were divided by N-fertilisation rates (0, 50 and 150 kg N ha-1), applied to wheat only. The area of each subplot was 50 m2 (10 m x 5 m). NT plots were seeded with a no-till drill (Great Plains). Weeds were controlled with glyphosate and (4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy) acetic acid (MCPA) at a rate of 0.5 + 0.5 l a.i. ha-1 prior to seeding. The CT treatment included mouldboard ploughing and disk. Nitrogen rate 0 50 150 kg/ha, and the grain yield is a mixture of all rates. Hard red spring wheat (cv. Gazul) was planted in rows 18 cm apart in December of each year at a rate of 150 kg ha-1. Faba bean (cv. Alameda) was planted in 50 cm-wide rows in November at a seeding rate of 170 kg ha_1. Chickpea (cv. Zoco) was planted in 35 cm-wide rows in March at a seeding rate of 80 kg ha-1. Sunflower (hybrid cv. Pioneer PR63A76) was planted in 50 cmwide rows in March of each year at a rate of 5 kg ha-1. Nitrogen fertiliser was applied to wheat plots as ammonium nitrate. At all fertiliser application rates, half was applied before sowing (incorporated by disk harrowing in CT plots and surface-broadcast in NT plots). The remaining N was topdressed at the beginning of wheat tillering. Every year, wheat plots were also supplied with P fertiliser at a rate of 65 kg P ha-1. The fertiliser was incorporated in CT soil and banded with a drill in NT plots. Crop and above-ground biomass yields were determined in each plot. In the present study, higher above-ground residues yields of wheat–faba bean and wheat–wheat rotations were also found under no tilled soils than under tilled soils. Residue were cut and weighted.

column33: Urea+ 60 kg P2O5 + 40 kg K2O ha-1
column38: A 3-year (2006–2007 to 2008–2009) field study was conducted to evaluate the effect of four tillage systems {zero tillage (ZT) in rice (Oryza sativa L.) and wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), conventional tillage (CT) in rice and wheat, and two rotational tillage sequences that alternated between CT and ZT} with three weed management levels (weedy check, recommended herbicide and herbicide + 1 hand weeding) in rice–wheat cropping system on a clay-loam soil. The soil at the study site had a clay loam texture (Typic chromusterts) in the 0–15 cm surface layer and a clay texture in the 15–75 cm depth. Main plot treatments were the four tillage sequences viz., zero tillage (ZT) in rice and wheat (ZT–ZT), conventional tillage (CT) in rice and wheat (CT–CT), and two rotational tillage sequences that alternated between CT and ZT (ZT–CT and CT–ZT) and sub-plot treatments were three weed control methods (weedy check, recommended herbicide and herbicide + 1 hand weeding at 30 days after sowing (DAS) in rice and at 35 DAS in wheat. Wheat was drill sown in third week of November. Land preparation and sowing of wheat was undertaken with the same field implements as for the CT/ZT rice. With increased combine harvest of rice, large quantities of crop residues are left on soil surface and poses problem in tillage operations resulting delayed sowing of succeeding wheat crop.

column5: Uttar Banga Krishi Viswavidyalaya, West Bengal
column38: Field studies in wheat were conducted at the instructional farm (26°24'02.2''N latitude, 89°23'21.7''E longitude, and 43 m above mean sea level) of the Uttar Banga Krishi Viswavidyalaya, West Bengal, India, for two consecutive years, i.e.winter seasons of 2014–2015 (year 1) and 2015–2016 (year 2). Rice-wheat rotation was followed in the experimental field for the last 3 years prior to the inception of the current study. Experimental design was set up as split plot with three replications. The treatments involve two main plots of tillage options [Conventional tillage (CT) and Zero tillage (ZT)] and each main plot had four subplots of different nutrient management practices. No land preparation was done for zero tillage. Seeds were sown in lines 20 cm apart with a seed rate of 100 kg/ha, manually for conventional tillage, and with 9 tyne zero-till-drill for zero tillage. The fertilizers were applied as per treatment requirement. Part of the nitrogen (N) was applied as basal (25 kg/ha N) and rest in two equal splits during first and second irrigation. Full P and 50% K were applied as basal, while the rest half K is applied along with urea during second top dressing. The fertilizer consisted of NPK complex fertilizer (10:26:26 as N:P:K), urea, SSP, and MOP. The basal fertilizer, i.e. NPK complex fertilizer (10:26:26) was furrow placed in case of zero tillage, while it is broadcasted before levelling in the conventional tillage plots. In zero tillage plots, Glyphosate 41% S.L. @ 3.75 l/ha was applied 7 days prior to sowing for smothering the existing weed flora, while the broad-leaved weeds were controlled with 2,4-D Na salt 80% W.P. @ 1 kg a.i/ha at 4-5 weeks after sowing. In conventional tillage plots, thinning and weeding were done simultaneously with the help of manual labour at 3-4 weeks after sowing. Boron (B) was applied @ 0.20% with Solubor (20% B), at 35-40 DAS and at 55-60 DASin both CT and ZT plots. Zinc (Zn) was applied with B in the second spray @ 0.10% with Chelated Zn (Chelamin). Four supplemental irrigations, each of 4-5 cm were given to wheat based on soil moisture status. Harvesting of the crop was done manually and yield was estimated on net plot basis (1m × 1m) excluding the border rows. After harvesting, the produce was threshed and grains were dried to record yield.  Rice was grown in rotation with wheat in the experimental plots in the following rainy season. Puddled transplanted rice was grown in the CT plots, while wet direct seeded rice was followed in the ZT plots. Nutrients were applied at a uniform rate, 60:30:30 kg N, P2O5 and K2O/ha, in all the plots. column33: ammonium sulphate + ammonium nitrate
column38: A long-term experiment on tillage and N fertilization of winterbarley was initiated in 1996 in Agramunt. The experiment consisted of a factorial combination of three levels of N fertilization (zero, ZN; medium, 60 kg N ha-1, MN; and high, 120 kg N ha-1; HN), and three tillage systems with two conservation tillage systems (NT and MT) and one intensive tillage system (conventional tillage, CT). plot size of 50 m x 6 m. Main soil characteristics in the plough layer were the following: soil pH was 8.5; sand, silt and clay content were 465, 417 and 118 g kg-1, respectively; and soil organic carbon content (SOC) in the soil surface (0–5 cm) was around 16 g kg-1 under NT, around 13 g kg-1 under MT and around 8 g kg-1 under CT, while SOC at deeper layers (10–25 cm) was similar among tillage systems, around 7 g kg-1. In the NT treatment, no soil disturbances occurred, and sowing was done by direct drilling after spraying with herbicide. Barley cv. Hispanic was annually sown at a rate of 450 seeds m-2, in rows spaced 17 cm apart with a no-till disc drill. N fertilizer was split into two applications, with one-third being broadcast before tillage as ammonium sulphate (21% N) and twothirds at the beginning of tillering as ammonium nitrate (33.5% N). Split application between sowing and tillering, with a major portion at tillering, have shown to improve the recovery of the applied N under semiarid Mediterranean conditions. Harvesting was done by the end of June with a standard medium-sized combine. The straw was chopped and spread over the plots by the combine machine. The field was kept free of vegetation for three to four months each summer.

column38: A long-term experiment on tillage and N fertilization of winterbarley was initiated in 1996 in Agramunt. The experiment consisted of a factorial combination of three levels of N fertilization (zero, ZN; medium, 60 kg N ha-1, MN; and high, 120 kg N ha-1; HN), and three tillage systems with two conservation tillage systems (NT and MT) and one intensive tillage system (conventional tillage, CT). plot size of 50 m x 6 m. Main soil characteristics in the plough layer were the following: soil pH was 8.5; sand, silt and clay content were 465, 417 and 118 g kg-1, respectively; and soil organic carbon content (SOC) in the soil surface (0–5 cm) was around 16 g kg-1 under NT, around 13 g kg-1 under MT and around 8 g kg-1 under CT, while SOC at deeper layers (10–25 cm) was similar among tillage systems, around 7 g kg-1. In the NT treatment, no soil disturbances occurred, and sowing was done by direct drilling after spraying with herbicide. Barley cv. Hispanic was annually sown at a rate of 450 seeds m-2, in rows spaced 17 cm apart with a no-till disc drill. N fertilizer was split into two applications, with one-third being broadcast before tillage as ammonium sulphate (21% N) and twothirds at the beginning of tillering as ammonium nitrate (33.5% N). Split application between sowing and tillering, with a major portion at tillering, have shown to improve the recovery of the applied N under semiarid Mediterranean conditions. Winter barley (Hordeum vulgare L.; c.v. Albacete) was cultivated in field 1 under continuous cropping (BC), after a 5–6-month fallow period, and under the traditional cereal–fallowrotation (BF) in fields 2 (BF1) and 3 (BF2), after a long-fallow period of 16–18 months, during three cropping seasons. column33: 224 kg ha-1 Urea + 49 kg ha-1 N-P2O5-K2O 18-18-18
column38: A tillage-rotation experiment was established in 1990 at the Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa (75o43’ W 45o 22’N), with the original purpose of evaluating the effect of tillage and crop rotation on fusarium (Fusarium graminearum Schwabe) head blight in spring wheat. Corn plots received 224 kg ha-1 urea ha-1 pre-plant broadcast and 40 kg ha-1 18-18-18, N-P2O5- K2O with the seed. Wheat plots received 100 kg N (urea) ha-1 pre-plant broadcast while no fertilizer was applied to the soybean plots. Glyphosate was used to control weeds in commercial herbicide resistant varieties of corn and soybean from 1996 to 2015. Within each crop, single degree of freedom contrasts were used to evaluate the effects of CT versus NT, crop rotations versus monoculture, and differences between the two rotation sequences (corn-soybean-wheat or corn-wheat-soybean.

column33: N + P + K
column38: The soil is a Fort Collins clay loam classified as fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, mesic Aridic Haplustalfs. The field was in CT continuous corn for 6 yr before the experiment. A randomized factorial experimental block with three replicates was established, with two tillage systems (CT-CC, conventional-till continuous corn; NT-CC, no-till continuous corn; and NT-CB, no-till corn–soybean rotation) and three N rates: 0, 134, and 202 kg N ha-1 in 2002 and 0, 67, 134, and 224 kg N ha-1 in 2003 and 2004. Mechanical tillage was used in the CT-CC plots (stalk shredder, disk, moldboard plow, rollermulcher [two passes], land leveler [two passes]) for seed bed preparation. The residue was left on the soil surface of the NTCC and NT-CB plots after harvest without mechanical tillage. Fertilizer N as urea ammonium nitrate (UAN) solution (containing 32% N) was injected to about 5 cm below the soil surface in bands spaced 33 cm apart just before planting corn in late April each year. Besides basal N application, a subsurface band application of phosphorus (0–46–0) was applied at a rate of 56 kg P ha-1 before planting in 1999 and 28 kg P ha-1 in 2004 for both CT and NT systems. Liquid starter fertilizer containing P, K, and S was applied to the seed row at planting in 2000, 2002, 2003, and 2004. A lateral move sprinkler irrigation system was used to apply water. Herbicides were used for weed control in all treatments, resulting in the plots being essentially weed-free.

column33: 75 kg ha-1 Ammonium nitrate + 100 kg ha-1 triple superphosphate + 50 kg ha-1 urea
column38: The soil is a classified as entic Chromoxeret with little or no slope, and represents a large portion of flat lands in semiarid Morocco. The experiment was designed as a randomized complete block with four replicates. Plots were 4 mx15 m, each occupied by one of seven tillageresidue cover treatments (TRC). Sand Silt Clay 25 24 51 g/kg; This newly developed drill permitted P fertilizer placement beneath the seeds. Wheat (Triticum aestivum L. cv achtar or tilila) was drilled at a rate of 120 kg ha -1 (or 280 seeds m -2) in mid- November of each year. Soil fertility was maintained using the dryland center's soil testing laboratory indexes to determine the total amount of N, P and K needed for the experiment. No K fertilizer was necessary. Ammonium nitrate, at a rate of 75 kg ha -1, and triple superphosphate, at 100 kg ha -1, were placed in the seed row as starter fertilizers. Additional urea fertilizer was surface broadcasted at mid-tillering stage (50 kg ha -1). As needed, glyphosate at a rate of 2 l ha -1 was applied to control any standing vegetation prior to planting on the no-till plots. All plots were also sprayed with cholorosulfuron at a rate of 10 g ha -1 before seeding. The use of chlorosulfuron provided residual weed control. Carbofuran was used to avoid insect damage (25 kg ha -1). Foliar diseases were prevented using a fungicide. Fertilizer, insecticide, and herbicide applications and seeding rate were the same for all plots (except TFT which had higher seeding rate 200 kg ha -1) in order to associate plant response differences with tillage practices and soil moisture differences. Residue cover (%) NT: 70%, CT: 10 -25%.

The field trial was established in 2012/13 at the University of Fort Hare research farm (UFH) in the Eastern Cape, South Africa. The UFH site (32°47′ S and 27°50′ E) is at an altitude of 508 metres above sea level. The site is in a semi-arid area and receives an average of 575 mm annual rainfall. About 30% of the annual rainfall is received in winter and the rest in summer (Palmer and Ainslie, 2006). The site has surface layer soils of the Oakleaf form (Soil Classification Working Group, 1991). Prior to the establishment of the trial, the land was under lucerne (Medicago sativa) production.  The field trial was a split-split plot design with 16 treatments and 3 replicates. Main plots were allocated to no-till and conventional tillage (CT). The main plots were split into four crop rotations; maize-fallow-maize (MFM), maize-fallow-soybean (MFS), maize-winter wheat-maize (MWM) and maize-winter wheat-soybean (MWS). The sub sub-plots were allocated to residue management at two levels; residue removal (R-) and residue retention (R+). The main plot sizes were 32.5 × 10 m, sub plots were 7 × 10 m and sub-sub plots were 5 × 7 m. The net plot were measuring 3 × 4 m. However, for the purpose of this study, only tillage and crop rotations under residue retention were considered to give a 2 × 4 factorial experiment laid out in a randomized complete design. A short season and prolific maize cultivar (BG 5785BR) was planted in summer (October-February) targeting a population of 25,000 plants/ha, recommended for dryland conditions in the central Eastern Cape Province of South Africa. An early maturing, dryland spring wheat cultivar (SST015) was planted in winter (May-August) at a seeding rate of 100 kg/ha. Residue retention was implemented soon after harvesting each crop, whereas tillage treatments were implemented just before planting of each cropping cycle. Fertilizer was only applied to the summer maize crop at a rate of 90 kg N, 45 kg P and 60 kg K per ha in all plots for a target yield of 5 tons/ha. All the P, K and a third of the N fertilizer was applied at planting as a compound (6.7% N; 10% P; 13.3% K + 0.5% Zn) and the rest (60 kg) as limestone ammonium nitrate (LAN) at 6 weeks after planting by banding. Soybean was inoculated with Rhizobium leguminosarium before sowing. No irrigation was applied. In addition, a longer rotation including wheat often aids in weed management by suppressing the common winter weeds.

column33: 300 kg ha-1 ammonium nitrate
column38: Field experiments were conducted from 1992 through 1995 at the University of Wisconsin Arlington Agricultural Research Station on Plano silt loam soil (fine silty, mixed mesic Typic Argiduolls) with pH 5.8 and 4.1 % organic matter. A randomized complete block design with a split-block arrangement and three replications was utilized. The main plots were factorial combinations of tillage treatments and crop rotation treatments. Two crop rotation treatments traversed each tillage system in a 40-m long and 27-m wide strip; a 15-m wide grass strip was maintained between each tillage strip. This layout prevented weed seed dispersal among main plot treatments and permitted use of standard equipment for field operations. Each subplot was 6 by 12 m; four 1- by I-m and two 0.5- by 0.5-m quadrats were established within a 3- by 10-m area centrally located in each subplot. Main plots and subplots were maintained in the same location and received the same tillage, crop rotation, and weed management treatment over years. Moldboard plow, chisel plow, and no-tillage systems were established at the site in 1984, and since that time weeds had been managed primarily with soil-applied herbicides in either corn or soybean. In the NT system, crops were planted directly into the crop residue from the previous year. Continuous corn and corn-soybean rotation were compared in this experiment. Pioneer 3417 corn was planted in all subplots in 1992 and 1994, and to the CC subplots in 1993 and 1995. Kaltenberg 142 soybean was planted as a component of CS in 1993 and 1995. Corn was planted 5 em deep at 79,300 seeds ha 1, and soybean was planted 4 em deep at 392,000 seeds ha -1 in rows spaced 76 cm apart on May 14, 16, 20, and 19 in 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995, respectively. Ammonium nitrate (300 kg ha 1) was surface applied prior to corn planting. Terbufos was applied at 7.8 kg ai ha- 1 in a 38-cm wide band over the corn row at planting to control soilborne insects. Weed management treatments in corn were (1) cyanazine (2.8 kg ai ha- 1) and metolachlor (2.5 kg ai ha 1) applied preemergence broadcast (full-rate broadcast), (2) cyanazine (1.4 kg ai ha - 1) and metolachor (1.3 kg ai ha 1) applied preemergence broadcast, plus cultivation 4 to 5 wk after planting (WAP) (half-rate broadcast), (3) cyanazine (2.8 kg ai ha 1) and metolachlor (2.5 kg ai ha 1) applied preemergence over the corn row in a 38-cm band, plus cultivation 4 to 5 WAP (full-rate band), and (4) nontreated check. Weed management treatments in soybean were (1) imazethapyr (70 g ai ha 1) and metolachlor (2.3 kg ai ha 1) applied preemergence broadcast (full-rate broadcast), (2) imazethapyr (35 g ai ha 1) and metolachlor (1.1 kg ai ha 1) applied preemergence broadcast, plus cultivation 4 to 5 WAP (halfrate broadcast), (3) imazethapyr (70 g ae ha 1) and metolachor (2.3 kg ai ha- l ) applied preemergence over the row in a 38-cm band, plus cultivation 4 to 5 WAP (full-rate band), and (4) nontreated check. All herbicide treatments were applied within 3 dafter crop planting and prior to weed emergence. In 1992 and 1993, herbicides were applied with a tractor-mounted compressed- air sprayer with 8002 flat-fan or 8002 even nozzles for broadcast or band application, respectively, in a spray volume of 187 L ha - 1. In 1994 and 1995, herbicides were applied with a CO2-pressurized backpack sprayer in a spray volume of 187 L ha 1. Nozzles were spaced 38 and 76 em apart for broadcast and band application, respectively, and held about 40 em above the soil surface. In the NT system, glyphosate was applied at 1.1 kg ae ha 1 as a burndown treatment 1 to 7 d prior to crop planting with a leveroperated backpack sprayer in a spray volume of 187 L ha 1 using 8002 flat-fan nozzles.

column38: Murehwa lies in agro-ecological region II receiving annual rainfall range of 750−1000mm from November-April. The soils are dominated by low fertile inherent granitic sandy soil (Lixisols: FAO, 2014). The soil pH (CaCl2) prior to establishment of the experiment averaged pH 4 (Table 1). Major food crops grown are maize, groundnuts, cowpeas and sweet potatoes (Ipomea batatas L.) whilst major livestock include cattle (Bos indicus L.) and goats (Capra hircus L.). Each farmer was treated as a replicate with a set of six treatments testing five cropping systems where one system was CT and the other four systems were under CA. The six treatments were: i CT+sole maize continuous ii CA+sole maize continuous iii CA+maize+cowpea intercropping iv CA+maize+mucuna intercropping v CA+maize+soybean/groundnut rotation (maize phase) vi CA+soybean/groundnut+maize rotation (legume phase) An animal drawn Fitarelli direct seeder (Brazilian made) was used for opening planting furrows, seeding and basal fertilizer application at once in CA plots. In CT treatment, an ox-drawn mouldboard plough was used for land preparation (tilling the soil and opening planting furrows) while seed dropping, fertilizer application and covering of the seed were done manually by hand. Mucuna and cowpea were planted between the maize rows using hand hoes. Crop residues were fed to livestock as they freely graze during the dry season whilst some farmers stored the residues on raised platforms and fed them to their livestock as supplement feed during the dry seasons. Hypharennia grass was applied as mulch at 2.5 t ha-1 in CA treatments at the beginning of each rainy season. Maize seed was planted at 90 cm inter-row and 25 cm in row spacing with one plant per station giving a plant population of approximately 44 000 plants ha-1. Soybean seed was inoculated with rhizobia just before planting. Gypsum (20 % Ca, 17.5 % S), was applied to groundnuts four weeks after planting. Manure was banded in furrows in CT plots and on maize rip line soon after planting in CA plots at 5 t ha-1 on dry weight basis. Cattle manure from communal areas of Murehwa contains an average of 0.74 % N, 0.12 % P and 0.69 % K. Basal compound D (7N:14P2O5: 7K2O) was applied at a rate of 240 kg ha-1 at planting whilst top dressing of ammonium nitrate (34.5 % N) was applied at 200 kg ha-1. Initial weed control in CA plots was done by applying Glyphosate (480 g l-1 active ingredient) at 2.5 l ha-1 soon after planting and thereafter weeding was done manually using hand hoes. In CT treatment, all weeding operations were done manually using a hand hoe.
