column33: 200 kg ha-1 urea + 300 kg phonska + 10 t ha-1 manure
column38: The study was conducted in Alue Mudem Lhoksukon village, North Aceh District, Nanggoe Aceh Darussalam Province, Indonesia from January 2015 to May 2015. The experiment in the field using split split plot design consists of three factors: The first factor as the main plot is mycorrhizas and no mycorrhizas. The second factor as a subplot is land cultivation consisting of no tillage and tillage (one round cultivation). The third factor as sub-subplot is rice varieties consisting of three groups of varieties, namely tolerant varieties (Ciapus, Inpago 4 and Inpago 8), moderate varieties (Inpago-5, Situbagendit, Inpago-7 and towuti) and sensitive (Inpari-6 jete , inpari-33 and Sintanur). On soil tillage treatment, the soil was cultivated one week before planting whereas for no soil tillage the land was conducted by scrapping soil surface using small hoe. There were 120 plots with the size of 1 m x 2.5 m. Manure at 10 ton ha-1was applied two weeks before rice planted. Fertilizer of Phonska at the dose of 300 kg.ha-1and urea 200 kg.ha-1were applied at the day of rice planted. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, 10 g. planting hole-1wasinoculated before the rice seeds were planted. Prevention of pests and diseases is done intensively from seed treatment to harvest. Fungicides in use are Oksiklorida 50 % and insecticides used are BPMC 480, MIPC Carbaryl 85% and Diazinon.

column38: Experiments were conducted in two locations: Bugesera in Rwanda and Meki in Ethiopia. Both are classified as semi-arid in the national systems with a Köppen-Geiger classification “equatorial savannah with a dry winter”. Bugesera is located at 2° 21′ S, 30° 15′E, at an elevation of about 1400m above sea level (a.s.l). The climate is characterized by a bimodal rainfall pattern with primary and secondary peaks in April and November, respectively. The first harvest is in January/February, after the “short rains” from September to January (season A), and the second harvest is in August, after the “long rains” (season B) from mid-February to mid-July. Annual rainfall varies between 850 and 1000mm per year with an average annual temperature of about 21 °C. Soils are humic Ferralsols at lower and haplic Ferralsols at higher landscape positions with soil depths of about 100–200 cm. The selected plots were cropped with maize or sorghum in rotation with bush beans in previous seasons. In Ethiopia, experiments were carried out in Meki, in the lowlands of the Central Rift Valley located at 8°11′N, 38°51′E and an elevation of about 1500m a.s.l. The average annual temperature is about 19.3 °C. Soils are predominantly deep Andosols. The selected plots were previously cropped with maize. Experiments compared maize crops under CT, CA, CTWT and CAWT during the 2015 A, 2015 B, 2016 A and 2016 B seasons in Rwanda and during the 2014 and 2015 seasons in Ethiopia. Mature G. robusta and S. spectabilis trees were selected in Rwanda and mature A. tortilis trees in Ethiopia. In Rwanda, for each farm included in the experiment, one plot with a tree in the centre and one plot in an adjacent open field were selected. The plot size was 10×10 m, and each plot was split into two subplots of 5×10 m; one managed under CT and the other under CA Plots and planting lines were oriented from East to West to allow similar shading effect on the CAWT and CTWT subplots. In Ethiopia, there were four plots per selected farm: two plots were located under almost identical trees and two control plots in an open field. One plot with tree and one control plot in open field were managed under CA while the other plot with tree and the other control plot in open field were managed under CT. The plot size was 10×10 m, but here plots were split into four subplots to accommodate four open pollinated maize varieties (OPVs) Unfortunately, one replicate in the Ethiopian experiment was damaged by livestock and was excluded from the analysis. In the CA and CAWT treatments, seeds were sown after slashing weeds with a sickle, without prior land preparation. No crop residues were left in the plots during the first season since farmers had harvested before the sites were selected. For other seasons, crop residues were kept in situ in the CA and the CAWT plots but amounts produced and maintained were too small to cover the soil and were rapidly consumed by termites within one month after each harvest. In CT and CTWT treatments, crop residues were removed as commonly practiced in the area. Planting stations were opened with a hand-hoe to a depth of about 10 cm at the onset of the rainy season. Fertilization included the application of 18 kg of N ha−1 and 20 kg of P ha−1 as di-ammonium phosphate at sowing and 46 kg of N ha−1 as urea at top-dressing six weeks after plant emergence, following general recommendations for the area. Fertilizers mixed with soils were placed in the planting station before sowing seeds and covered by 2–3 cm of soil. Glyphosate was applied to control weeds in Ethiopia, but not in Rwanda. Weeding was done manually twice a month in all treatments.

column38: This study was conducted for three years from 2014–2015 to 2016–2017 cropping seasons, in Ntiya and Mthirammanja Extension Planning Areas (EPA) in Mangochi district, Chinguluwe and Tembwe EPAs in Salima district and Manyamula and Zombwe EPAs in Mzimba district . column19: maize intercropped with legumes - lablab, mucuna and pigeonpea
column33: 100 kg ha-1 NPK 21:21:0+4S + 100 kg urea ha-1
column38: Soil samples were taken from on farm trial sites on plot by plot basis. Sand content in Balaka market and Ntonda sections was 82% and 75% respectively. Soils with more than 85% sand content tend to be excessively drained, low in organic carbon (C) and very low in nutrient content. Balaka market had lower soil organic C on average 0.64%. Soil organic C values of Ntonda were higher, about 0.93%. Balaka market 0-20cm depth soil: sand 82%, clay 10%; Ntonda, sand 75%, clay 16%. Hybrid maize SC627 was planted at both sites for all the three cropping seasons. All plots were seeded on the same day after the first effective rains in each year, defined as a rainfall greater than 30 mm after 15th November.  Intercropped legumes were seeded in between every two maize rows planting two seeds spaced at 40 cm, 10 cm and 60 cm for lablab, mucuna and pigeonpea respectively. All treatments received uniform fertilizer rate of 69 kg N ha−1 that was supplied as 100 kg of N:P:K ha−1 (23:21:0 + 4S) at seeding and 100 kg urea ha−1 (46% N) approximately three weeks after planting. Weed control in CP plots was done by manual weeding as necessary. In CAM, a tank mix of 2.5 l ha−1 glyphosate (N-phosphonomethyl) and 6 l ha−1 bullet (which contains 22.5% altrazine) was applied as post-planting and pre-emergence herbicide respectively. In CA plots with maize intercropped with legumes, only 2.5 l ha−1 post-planting herbicide, glyphosate was used followed by manual weeding when weeds were 10 cm tall or 10 cm in circumference. All maize stalks and leaves without cobs were weighed at harvest; The remaining biomass was returned as surface mulch in CA plots and incorporated later into the soil during ridging in CP plots.

column38: In 1990, several rotations  were established to investigate the possibility of frequently than every other year, as done with the traditional  winter wheat–fallow system. All phases of each rotation were present every year.  Details of the weed control practices used for the CT and NT systems are given in Anderson et al. (1999). Briefly, the CT system employed four to eight sweep plow operations as needed for weed control during fallow. The NT system relied on contact and residual herbicides for all weed control. Wheat planting occurred between 18 and 28 September in any given year. Seeding density was approximately 2.125 million seeds ha-1 in all years. Fertilizer N as ammonium nitrate (34–0–0) was surface broadcast to each plot before planting during the falls of 1992 to 1995, and banded at planting in 1996 to 2000. Application rateswere determined according to annual soil tests and a yield goal of 2688 kg ha-1. Actual fertilizer rates varied between 34 and 67 kg N ha_1 depending on the plot and the year. Phosphorus (11–23–0, N–P–K) was banded with the seed at planting at a rate of 17 kg ha-1 P2O5.

The experiment was established in 1994 in a field infested with a population of H. glycines classified as a race 3 and for which female indices were 3, 0, <1, and 0, respectively, for ‘Pickett 71’, ‘Peking’, Plant Introduction (PI) 88.788, and PI 90.763 (Riggs and Schmitt, 1988). The soil was a Drummer siltyclayloam (Typic Haplaquolls; fine silty, mixed, mesic) with 61.1% silt, 28.8% clay, and 10.1% sand, pH 6.6, and 6.0% OM. Phosphorous and potassium levels were 118 and 345 kg/ha, respectively. The experimental design was a split-plot with no-tillage (NT) and conventional tillage (CT) (chisel plow in the fall and a field cultivator and finishing implement in the spring) as main plots and H. glycines-resistant ‘Fayette’ (1994) or ‘Linford’ (1996, 1998, 1999, and 2000), and susceptible ‘Williams 82’ soybean as subplots arranged in randomized complete blocks with six replications. Each experimental unit was a 3-m × 12-m plot with four rows on 76-cm centers. Each plot was divided equallylengthwise into two subsubplots to obtain subsamples for both yield and numbers of nematodes. Soybean was planted in 1994, 1996, 1998, 1999, and 2000, and corn was planted in 1995 and 1997. Plots that were planted to either the H. glycinesresistant or H. glycines-susceptible soybean in 1994 were planted in a resistant or susceptible monoculture when soybean was planted. When corn was planted, plots were labeled with the soybean cultivar planted the previous year to maintain continuity for comparisons among years. Instead of following the rotation with corn in 1999, soybean was planted in 1999 and 2000 in an attempt to exert selection pressure on the H. glycines population to overcome the resistance of Linford. Soil samples collected at planting (for estimation of initial nematode population density[Pi]) and at harvest final nematode population density[Pf]; consisted of 12 cores taken in a zig-zag pattern 5 to 10 cm from the center two rows of each sub-subplot. Cysts were extracted bygravitysieving with nested screens of 850- and 250-μm-pore openings (Cobb, 1918). Cysts were selected, crushed individually, and the number of eggs per 250 cm3 soil was determined. Even though soybean and corn yields were obtained from the center two rows of each sub-subplot, only soybean yield is reported. Weed control in soybean consisted of preplant applications of glyphosate and 2,4-D and postemergence applications of acifluorfen + bentazon and sethoxydim. Weed control in corn consisted of preplant applications of glyphosate and 2,4-D and a preemergence application of metolachlor + atrazine.

The WF and SF systems have 15- and 19-mo fallow periods, respectively, between crops. The WSF system has 11-mo fallow periods between wheat and sorghum and sorghum and wheat. The SS system has ~ 7 mo between crops. Wheat was planted in mid-September of each year and harvested in late June of the following year. Grain sorghum was planted in the late May to mid-June period of each year and harvested in mid-October. October.Hard red winter wheat cultivars were ’Larned’, planted from1 986 through 1988, and ’TA1M07’ planted from 1988 through 1991. Grain sorghum hybrids were ’DeKalb DK42, planted in 1987 and 1988, and Warner 744BR(bird resistant), planted from 1989 through 1992. The 1988 sorghum was not harvested because of bird damage. Wheat was planted with a John Deere HZ no-till drill in 0.40-m rows at a rate of 50 kg ha-1. Grain sorghum was planted with a Buffalo slot planter in 0.75-m rows at a rate of 87 500 seeds ha-1. About 62 500 plants ha-1 typically emerged. Ammonium nitrate was broadcast preplant to give 45 kg ha-1 and 67 kg ha-1 N for wheat and grain sorghum, respectively. The research was conducted on a continuous soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] field experiment located at the University of Tennessee’s West Tennessee Research and Education Center, Jackson, TN (35o 37'22” N, 88o 50'47” W). According to the Köppen classification, the study region is under humid subtropical (Cfa) climate, with a mean annual temperature of 15.6 oC and a mean annual rainfall of 1350 mm. The field experiment was established in 1979 on a one-hectare area to study six tillage systems on a uniform Lexington silt loam soil (fine-silty, mixed thermic Ultic Hapludalfs). Each plot is sized 18 m _ 6 m, including four rows of soybean with 1.5 m of row spacing and 4 field replications. Each year since 1979, following the chemical suppression of the wheat cover crop by applying 0.71 kg ha-1 paraquat (1-methyl-4-(1-methylpyridin-1-ium-4-yl) pyridin-1-ium), tillage plots were tilled in late May and soybean was seeded. Two middle rows of soybean were harvested in October and yield was adjusted to 13% moisture content. The winter wheat cover crop was reseeded in NTW plots in October–November following the soybean harvest.

column33: N+P+K
column38: Two experimental sites were chosen, with Site 1 at Breton, Alberta (53”07’N, 114”28’W), on a Gray Luvisolic soil of the Breton loam series and with Site 2 at Ellerslie, Alberta (53”25’N, 113”33’W), on a Black Chemozemic soil of the Malmo silty clay loam series. Slope gradients at Sites 1 and 2 were 3% and l%, respectively. Normal annual precipitation at Sites I and 2 is 547 mm and 452 mm, respectively. The experimental area at both sites was square with sides of 28 m. The experimental design was randomized complete block with four replicates. Plots were of 6.9 m length by 2.8 m width. The experiment was initiated in autumn 1979 to investigate the effect of tillage (zero and conventional), straw handling (removed and retained) and N fertilization (0 and 56 kg ha-1 year-1) on barley yields and N uptake. The N fertilizer was surface-applied urea, but for the CT plots, it was also incorporated within the 0-0.12 m soil depth. A blanket application of P, K and S was applied to each plot each year. A hoe-opener drill with a 0.23 m spacing between rows was used to sow spring barley at the rate of 100 kg ha-1. The remaining plant biomass was then removed from all plots and straw returned to plots as per experimental plan and in amounts equivalent to straw yield determinations. Weeds were controlled with herbicides and, if needed, by hand. Nitrogen in straw and grain was determined either by Kjeldahl method or by calorimetric analysis.

The meteorological data for Akure have been reported (Ojeniyi, 1990). The surface (0-15 cm ) soil at the site of experiment had the following properties at the start of study: sand 71.6%; silt 9.1%; clay 19.3%; bulk density 1.42 Mg m-3; porosity 0.25; C 1.9%; N 0.09%; Bray 1 P 9.0 ppm. The values at a depth of 15-40 cm were: sand 58.4%; silt 10.2%; clay 31.4%; bulk density 1.57 Mg m-3; porosity 0.14; C 0.8%; N 0.07%; Bray 1 P 4.2 ppm. The site was dominated by elephant grass (Pennisetum purpurem ) and had not been cropped in the previous 3 years. Manual clearing with a cutlass was done. preplanting zero tillage in which only herbicide treatment was performed. Maize was manually planted as this is the traditional practice. Rows were spaced 60 cm apart and plants were spaced at 30 cm intervals within the row and then thinned to one plant per stand in each 52 m2 plot. A maize variety TZPB which produces mature cobs within 90 days was used. It was not necessary to impose any other weed control methods on the treatments: no fertilizer treatment was applied.

Starting with corn in 1989, corn and soybean were grown in alternate years. In the spring of each year the MP and CP plots were moldboard and chisel plowed followed by 2 disking and planting.  In odd years corn was planted at the seeding rate of 64,000 seeds ha−1 with fertilizers of 218 kg ha−1 N, 55 kg ha−1 P, and 232 kg ha−1 K. The percentage surface residue was determined after planting by the line-transect method.

column5: Tel Hadya, Center for Ag Research (ICARDA)
column38: The soil, classified as a fine, thermic vertic Calcixerollic Xerochrept merging to a Chromic Calcixerert (Ryan et al., 1997), swells when wet, cracks deeply when dry and has a pH of 8.0±8.5, organic matter 0.9±1.0%, and EC (electrical conductivity) 0.62±1.48 dS m-1. Winter crops (wheat, chickpea (Cicer arietinum) and lentil (Lens culinaris)) were sown after the first major autumn rains, but the frost-sensitive watermelon (Citrullus lanatus) followed a short winter fallow. It was sown at a wide spacing (263 m grid) in April, to grow on profile-stored water, if there was at least 1 m depth of wet soil; otherwise, the fallow was continued. Wheat was combine-harvested, the straw baled, and the stubble grazed by sheep at a stocking rate representing local practice. Chickpea was also combine-harvested and the residues were retained; lentil was hand-harvested and the above-ground biomass was removed. The stubble-burning subtreatment was imposed on one- fourth of the plots in the wheat phase to answer the question raised by farmers concerning ease of seedbed preparation, as well as to measure the long-term effects on crop yields and moisture conservation. Each primary application was followed after the first rain by secondary tillage as described below for seedbed preparation, while zero-till plots were sprayed with a systemic herbicide for pre-sowing weed control. The three- course rotations were (1) bread wheat-chickpea-watermelon; and (2) durum wheat-lentil-watermelon. This trial, involving four tillage systems across three-course rotations, was established in 1986 to test the hypothesis that on swelling clay soils, tillage, production costs and energy use can be reduced without lowering crop yields. Tillage treatments were retained, while weed control and fertilization treatments were replaced by uniform applications, and phased entry was introduced by splitting the plots (15650 m for each crop) across the previous treatments.

The study was performed in Agramunt, NE Spain (41°48′ N, 1°07′ E, 330m asl). A rainfed long-term field experiment (LTE) was established in 1996 to compare three tillage systems (conventional tillage, CT; reduced tillage, RT; no-tillage, NT) and three increasing rates of mineral N (0, 60 and 120 kg N ha−1) under barley monocropping. In 2015 the LTE was transformed to irrigation with solid set sprinklers and 3 years of maize (Zea mays L.) monocrop as the main cropping system in the area. After the transformation to irrigation, the same tillage intensity treatments (CT, RT and NT) and three mineral N fertilization rates adapted to maize cultivation (0, 200, 400 kg N ha−1) were compared in LTE maintaining the same experimental layout as the previous rainfed experiment. At the same time, in 2015, a new experiment was created adjacent to the LTE (separated by a 15m corridor). The layout of this new experiment (so called short-term experiment, STE) was exactly the same as the LTE (same tillage and N fertilization treatments, spatial arrangement and cropping system) but with different historical tillage management. For the previous 21 years, the entire surface occupied by the STE consisted of a rainfed NT winter cereal-based cropping system and the new experiment was implemented directly in notillage soil. The experimental design in LTE and STE consisted of a randomized block design with three replications and plot size of 50 x 6 m. Soil was classified as Typic Xerofluvent with a silt loam texture (sand, 308 g kg-1; silt, 573 g kg-1; clay, 119 g kg-1) in the upper (0–28 cm) horizon. The main physico-chemical properties at the beginning of the experiment (2015) were as follows: pH (H2O, 1:2.5) 8.5; electrical conductivity (1:5) 0.15 dSm-1; soil organic carbon (SOC) concentration (0–30 cm) 7, 9 and 9 g kg-1 under CT, RT and NT, respectively in LTE and 10, 9 and 10 g kg-1 under CT, RT and NT, respectively in STE; Olsen P, 35 mg kg-1; K (neutral ammonium acetate), 194 mg kg-1; water retention (−33 kPa), 16 kg kg-1; water retention (−1500 kPa), 5 kg kg-1. The experiment was implemented in three successive maize growing seasons (2015, 2016 and 2017). In LTE and STE, tillage operations were carried out at the end of March to the beginning of April in the three growing seasons. The CT treatment consisted of one pass of rototiller (15 cm depth) followed by subsoiler (35 cm depth), finished by one pass of a disk plough (20 cm depth) with almost 100% of the crop residues incorporated into the soil before planting. The RT treatment consisted of a pass of strip-till to a depth of 20–25 cm, implemented on the maize planting row reducing the surface tilled to ca. 20%. In the RT treatment no pre-planting chemical weeding was used. Finally, the NT treatment consisted of weed control with a non-selective herbicide (i.e. glyphosate) at 1.5 L ha−1. Planting was carried out with a pneumatic row direct drilling machine equipped with double disc furrow openers (model Prosem K, Solà, Calaf, Spain) in the three tillage systems (CT, RT, and NT). Rotary residue row cleaners were installed to clear the path for the row unit openers (both in RT and NT treatments). The planting depth was adapted to each tillage treatment to reach a constant value (ca. 4 cm). Mineral P and K fertilization was applied prior to maize planting based on soil analysis at rates of 154 kg P2O5 ha−1 and 322 kg K2O ha−1, respectively, in the first two years. One to two postplanting treatments for grass and broad leaves, with authorized herbicides, were applied after planting and at V5 in all treatments. In the third year the levels of available P and K in the soil were appropriate for the crop, therefore P and K were not applied in 2017. The N fertilizer rates compared were split in one pre-planting application with urea (46% N) on April, and two top-dressing applications on May and July (V5 and V10 stages, respectively) with calcium ammonium nitrate (27% N) with 50, 75 and 75 kg N ha−1 applied, respectively, in the three splits in the 200 kg N ha−1 rate, being doubled in the 400 kg N ha−1 rate. For the three years, maize (cv. Kopias) was planted in late April at a rate of 90,000 seeds ha−1 with a 73-cm width between rows. Irrigation was supplied to meet the estimated evapotranspiration (ET) of the crop minus the effective precipitation, which was estimated as 75% of precipitation when precipitation>5 mm.  Weekly maize evapotranspiration (ETc) was calculated from the corresponding weekly values of ET and Kc. Reference ET was computed with the FAO Penman–Monteith method from meteorological data obtained from an automated weather station located near the experimental site. Crop coefficients (Kc) were estimated in function of crop development. The experiment received a total of 631, 672 and 696mm of irrigation water in 2015, 2016 and 2017, respectively, during the maize growing period. Harvesting was carried out at the beginning of November with a commercial combine. The crop residues were chopped and spread over the soil. During the winter periods between crops the soil was maintained free of weeds with an application of 1.5 L ha-1 of commercial product which contains a 36% glyphosate [(N- (phosphonomethyl)-glycine].

A long-term field experiment was established in 2008 at the research farm of Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)-Indian Institute of Maize Research (IIMR) (at 28° 40′ N, 77° 12′ E and 228.6m elevation) New Delhi, India. The experimental site has alluvial origin, flat and well drained sandy loam soil (Typic Haplustept). The soil had pH of 7.8 and was non-saline with EC of 0.32 dSm−1. Imposed treatments with crop management practices were similar in all the study years (2008–2013). The experiment was laid out in a split-plot design with 3-tillage and crop establishment practices [ZT, zero tillage; PB, permanent raised bed and CT, conventional tillage] as main plot treatments and 4-cropping systems [MWMb, maize (Zea mays L.)-wheat (Triticum aestivum)- mungbean (Vigna radiata L.); MCS, maize-chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.)- Sesbania (Sesbania aculeata); MMuMb, maize-mustard (Brassica juncea)- mungbean and MMS, maize-maize-Sesbania] as sub- plot treatments. The 12 combinations of different treatments with a harvestable sub-plot size of 16.5mx 4.0m were replicated thrice. In the entire treatments maize hybrid was sown with the seed rate of 20 kg ha−1 during the first fortnight of July and was harvested in the last week of October. Approximately 30% of the preceding crops residue was retained on the CA plots (PB and ZT) and incorporated in the CT plots during the study period.

column38: A field experiment was conducted during monsoon and winter seasons of 2012-13 and 2013-14 under six tillage and crop establishment (TCE) and residue management practices under maize-wheat and maize-chickpea crop rotations at the research farm (28o40’ N, 77o12’ E and 228.6 m elevation) of the Directorate of Maize Research (DMR), New Delhi, India. The treatments consisted a set of six TCE and residue management practices, i.e. permanent raised beds with residue (PB+R) and without residue (PB-R); zero tilled flat with residue (ZT+R) and without residue (ZT-R) and conventional tilled flat with residue (CT+R) and without residue (CT-R). In the first monsoon season, Quality protein maize hybrid HQPM-1 was sown with 20 kg/ha seed rate and in winter season wheat (cultivar HD 2967) and chickpea (cultivar Pusa 547) crops were sown with 100 and 80 kg/ ha seed rate, respectively. Crop based fertilizers doses (N: P2O5: K2O) were applied in different crops @ 150:60:40, 30:40 and 120:60:40 kg/ha for maize, chickpea and wheat, respectively. In all the treatments, 33% N and 100% P2O5 and K2O doses were applied at sowing in maize and wheat. Rest 67% N was applied in 2-equal doses at V5 and tasseling stages in maize, and at first and third irrigation in wheat. In chickpea, whole of the N + P2O5 were applied at the time of seeding. In all the residue management plots, about 30% of preceding crop residues was retained/incorporated and the remaining amounts of residues from these plots and full (above ground) amount of residue from non-residue management plots was removed to use as fodder and other purposes. Irrigation water was applied in all the crops based on visual crop symptoms at critical crop growth stages by flood irrigation through open channels.

column38: The site has a semi-arid climate, typically characterized by hot and dry summer andcold winter with a mean annual precipitation of about 652 mm.The soil of the experimental site is a sandy loam in texture (TypicHaplustept) of Gangetic alluvial origin, and well drained with 64.1%sand, 16.9% silt and 19.0% clay, pH 7.9, bulk density 1.63 Mg m−3,hydraulic conductivity (saturated) 0.835 cm h−1, organic carbon4.89 g kg−1 soil, EC 0.32 dS m−1. The moisture content at saturation was 0.38m^3 m^−3 and at 0.033 MPa (Field capacity) varied from 22to 27% and at 1.5 MPa (Permanent wilting point) varied from 8 to12% in different soil layers of 0–30 cm depth. designThe experiment was laid out in a split-plot design withtillage/crop establishment practices [Zero tillage with residueretention (ZT), Permanent bed with residue retention (PB), andConventional tillage with residue incorporation (CT)] as main-plotand nutrient management [Control (unfertilized), Farmers’ Fertilizer Practice (FFP), Recommended dose of fertilizers (Ad-hoc), andNutrient Expert decision support tool-based fertilizer application(Pampolino et al., 2012) (SSNM)] as sub-plot treatments. The 12 treatment combinations with a harvested subplot size of 30.15 m2(7.5 m length x 4.02 m width) were replicated thrice every year (forall the three years) of study. Maize (DHM-117)was sown with seed rate of 20 kg ha−1 at spacing of 67.5 cm × 20 cmin ZT and CT plots, while, one row of maize was established on topof the raised bed in PB by keeping plant spacing of 20 cm during 1st fortnight of July in rainy season and harvested in last week of October (in 3-years of the study). Wheat (cv. HD 2967) was sownwith a seed rate of 100 kg ha−1in the 2ndto 3rdweek of Novemberat a row spacing of 22.5 cm in ZT and CT, while two rows of wheatwere planted on the top of the PB keeping a row spacing of 18.5 cm,crop was harvested in 2ndand 3rdweek of April during all the studyyears. Mungbean (cv. Pusa Vishal) was sown using a seed rate of25 kg ha−1 in the 2nd fortnight of April with a row spacing of 30 cmin ZT and CT, while two rows of mungbean were planted on the topof the PB keeping a row spacing of 18.5 cm, harvesting/pod pickingwas done in 3rdand 4thweek of June during all the years. Fertilizers in the FFP treatment were applied based on surveyof 50 farmers’ of the area (Delhi NCR region (including the partsof Haryana, Western Uttar Pradesh, Parts of Rajasthan), and Pun-jab and plains of Uttarakhand, Supplementary Table 4) and was110:30:0 and 172:57.5:0 kg ha−1of N: P2O5: K2O for maize andwheat, respectively. The Ad-hoc recommendations were based onthe economic optima of nutrients for Delhi state by Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). The Ad-hoc recommendationswere 150:60:40 kg ha−1and 120:60:40 kg ha−1of N: P2O5: K2Ofor maize and wheat, respectively. Weed management in the ZT and PB plots was done by usingthe herbicide glyphosate was sprayed at 1.0 kg ha−1(about twodays before sowing of each crop). However, in the case of CTplots Atrazine at 1.0 kg ha−1as pre-emergence (PE) in maize,Pendimethalin at 1.0 kg ha−1as PE in mungbean and wheat andCladinofop at 60 g ha−1at 28–32 days after seeding of wheat wasapplied. In addition to chemical weed management, one handweeding was also done in all the CT plots only at 30–40 days aftersowing. In ZT and PB plots weed infestation was less than CT, excepthardy perennial weeds after the first year, which were uprootedmanually.

The moisture content at saturation was 0.38m^3 m^−3 and at 0.033 MPa (Field capacity) varied from 22to 27% and at 1.5 MPa (Permanent wilting point) varied from 8 to12% in different soil layers of 0–30 cm depth. designThe experiment was laid out in a split-plot design withtillage/crop establishment practices [Zero tillage with residueretention (ZT), Permanent bed with residue retention (PB), andConventional tillage with residue incorporation (CT)] as main-plotand nutrient management [Control (unfertilized), Farmers’ Fertilizer Practice (FFP), Recommended dose of fertilizers (Ad-hoc), andNutrient Expert decision support tool-based fertilizer application(Pampolino et al., 2012) (SSNM)] as sub-plot treatments. The 12 treatment combinations with a harvested subplot size of 30.15 m2(7.5 m length x 4.02 m width) were replicated thrice every year (forall the three years) of study. Maize (DHM-117)was sown with seed rate of 20 kg ha−1 at spacing of 67.5 cm × 20 cmin ZT and CT plots, while, one row of maize was established on topof the raised bed in PB by keeping plant spacing of 20 cm during 1st fortnight of July in rainy season and harvested in last week of October (in 3-years of the study). Wheat (cv. HD 2967) was sownwith a seed rate of 100 kg ha−1in the 2ndto 3rdweek of Novemberat a row spacing of 22.5 cm in ZT and CT, while two rows of wheatwere planted on the top of the PB keeping a row spacing of 18.5 cm,crop was harvested in 2ndand 3rdweek of April during all the studyyears. Mungbean (cv. Pusa Vishal) was sown using a seed rate of25 kg ha−1 in the 2nd fortnight of April with a row spacing of 30 cmin ZT and CT, while two rows of mungbean were planted on the topof the PB keeping a row spacing of 18.5 cm, harvesting/pod pickingwas done in 3rdand 4thweek of June during all the years. Fertilizers in the FFP treatment were applied based on surveyof 50 farmers’ of the area (Delhi NCR region (including the partsof Haryana, Western Uttar Pradesh, Parts of Rajasthan), and Pun-jab and plains of Uttarakhand, Supplementary Table 4) and was110:30:0 and 172:57.5:0 kg ha−1of N: P2O5: K2O for maize andwheat, respectively. The Ad-hoc recommendations were based onthe economic optima of nutrients for Delhi state by Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). The Ad-hoc recommendationswere 150:60:40 kg ha−1and 120:60:40 kg ha−1of N: P2O5: K2Ofor maize and wheat, respectively. Weed management in the ZT and PB plots was done by usingthe herbicide glyphosate was sprayed at 1.0 kg ha−1(about twodays before sowing of each crop). However, in the case of CTplots Atrazine at 1.0 kg ha−1as pre-emergence (PE) in maize,Pendimethalin at 1.0 kg ha−1as PE in mungbean and wheat andCladinofop at 60 g ha−1at 28–32 days after seeding of wheat wasapplied. In addition to chemical weed management, one handweeding was also done in all the CT plots only at 30–40 days aftersowing. In ZT and PB plots weed infestation was less than CT, excepthardy perennial weeds after the first year, which were uprootedmanually.

column33: 150 kg N ha-1 + 60 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 40 kg K2O ha-1 + 25 kg ZnSO4 ha-1 for Kharif maize; 150 kg N ha-1 + 80 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 60 kg K2O + 25 kg ZnSO4 ha-1
column38: The climate of the area is semi-arid, withan average mean annual rainfall of 650 mm (70–80% of whichis received during July-September) with the mean annual evap-oration of 850 mm. Annual rainfall of the cropping cycles (Julyto June) ranged from 532.8 to 1507.1 mm. The mean daily mini-mum temperature ranged from 0 to 4◦C in January and mean dailymaximum temperature ranged from 40 to 46◦C in May-June. Soil sub-samples were collected at the start of experiment inJune 2008 from 0 to 30 cm layer using auger of 5.0 cm diameter.The soil of experimental site was sandy loam in texture, very deep( > 2 m) having 64.1% sand, 12.6% silt and 23.4% clay with pH 7.8,EC 0.32 dS m−1, KMnO4oxidizable N 158.4 kg ha−1(Subbiah andAsija, 1956), 0.5 M NaHCO3extractable P 11.6 kg ha−1(Olsen et al.,1954), and 1 N NH4OAC extractable K 248.4 kg ha−1, diethylene-triamine penta acetic acid (DTPA) extractable Zn (1.6 mg kg−1), Fe(6.7 mg kg−1) and Cu (1.3 mg kg−1). The experiment was laid out in split-plot design with three replications. Each experimental unit wasrandomized and consisted of 16.5 m × 4.0 m plots. Quality pro-tein maize hybrid HQPM-1 was sown with seed rate of 20 kg ha−1during first fortnight of July in kharif season and from last week ofOctober to first week of November in winter season (in six years ofthe study). The maize crop was harvested in thelast week of October and first week of May during kharif and rabiseasons of each year, respectively. Kharif maize received a common fertilizer dose of 150 kgN + 60 kg P2O5+ 40 kg K2O + 25 kg ZnSO4ha−1and rabi maizewas fertilized with 180 kg N + 80 kg P2O5+ 60 kg K2O + 25 kgZnSO4ha−1. In both the seasons, 1/3rd N and whole P2O5,K2O and25 kg ha−1ZnSO4were applied as basal at sowing, while remaining2/3rd N was top dressed by broadcasting as urea in two equal splitsat V5and VTvegetative growth phases of maize. For managing weeds, herbicide glyphosate was sprayed @1.0 kg ha−1in the ZT and PB plots about two days before sowingof each crop. However, in case of CT plots Atrazine @ 1.0 kg ha−1as pre-emergence(PE) in maize, In addition to chemical weed management, one hand weeding was alsodone in all the CT plots only at 30–40 days after sowing. In ZT andPB plots weed infestation was less than CT except hardy perennialweeds during initial two years, which were uprooted manually. The flood irrigation was applied through open channels at crit-ical crop growth stages in the respectivecrops.

column33: ammonium nitrate + 44 kg P ha-1
column38: Three predominant soils were found on the site (Andrews and Diderikson, 1981): Webster (fine-loamy, mixed, superactive, mesic Typic Endoaquolls), Clarion (fine-loamy, mixed, mesic Typic Hapludolls), and Nicollet (fine-loamy, mixed, mesic Aquic Hapludolls). A no-till system with controlled traffic was established on the entire area in 1995. In October 2001, a chiselplow- based tillage system was established on plots comprising one-third of the area. To establish and maintain the corn–soybean rotation half of the field was planted with corn and the other half was planted with soybean each year. In the following year the crops were switched. Corn and soybean were planted in late April or early May each year with a five-row planter with a 0.76-m row spacing. At planting an ammonium polyphosphate starter fertilizer was applied in-furrow at rates of 13 and 44 kg ha-1 of N and P, respectively. At approximately 38 d after planting a urea ammonium nitrate fertilizer solution was applied 0.13 m from the row at a rate of 202 kg N ha-1. Following both corn and soybean harvest in the fall, a rye winter cover crop was planted into selected no-till plots using a no-till grain drill with 0.19-m row spacing at 3 800 000 seeds ha21. The rye cover crop was killed in the spring 7 to 10 d before planting with glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine]. Plots were 3.8 m wide by 55.8 m long.

column33: NH4NO3 + 80 kg P2O5 ha-1
column38: The soil was a well-drained humic gleysol (USA classification: clayey, mixed, mesic Typic Humaquept) (230 g kg-1 sand, 390 g kg-1 silt, and 380 g kg-1 clay) derived from a fluvial deposit and evolved from a fine-textured grayish-to-brown parent material (Lamontagne et al., 2001). At establishment of the maize–soybean rotation, soil pH was 6.3 (1:1 soil:water ratio) (Poirier et al., 2009) and soil organic carbon was 38 g C kg-1 (Larouche, 2006).  The N application rates are based on the provincial recommendation for maize, which range from 120 to 170 kg N ha-1 depending on climatic zone and soil texture (CRAAQ, 2003). Grain maize (Pioneer Hybrid 3893) was seeded on 12 May 2004 at a rate of 74 000 seeds ha-1 with 0.76 m between rows. Soybean (OAC Bayfield Hybrid) was seeded on 25 May 2005 at a rate of 450 000 seeds ha-1 and the same row spacing as maize. Immediately prior to seeding, the soybean seeds were inoculated with a commercial formulation of Bradyrhizobium japonicum. In 2004, the two fertilized treatments (1N and 2N) received 40 kg N ha-1 of mineral N (NH4NO3 [34-0-0]) at seeding applied with the seeder, followed by a sidedress, banded between the rows at 0.05–0.10 m depth at the 2- to 3-leaf stage (17 June 2004). The sidedress consisted of 40 kg N ha-1 (1N) and 120 kg N ha-1 (2N). The control treatment (0N) received no mineral N. The mineral N fertilizer was applied only in 2004 (maize year) and no N fertilizer was applied in 2005 (soybean year). Phosphorous was applied to all plots at seeding each year as triple superphosphate at 80 kg P2O5 ha-1.

column10: 2 or 3
column38: Twenty farms were chosen within the Po valley in 2013 with the first aim of evenly representing the pedoclimatic conditions and cropping systems occurring in the area addressed by the HelpSoil project. The monitoring on the demonstration farms was carried out from late 2013 to October 2016 (i.e. 32 months). The demonstration fields were set up on each farm with two or three replicates to compare production and environment-related aspects under the farm current condition (i.e. CvtA, MT or NT) and the CA alternative option (MT or NT). The farms' key features, such as site location, soil texture class, CA implementation year, crop rotation, and tillage treatments are listed in Table 2. Further details on cover crops cultivation and soil characteristics are given in Supplemental File 2. The chemical and physical parameters of soils were measured on soil sampled in early 2014. Texture classes varied from sandy loam to clay; silty loam and silty clay loam were the soil types most represented in the present study. A different code was assigned to the farms where CA was implemented before 2006 (Long-term), from 2007 and 2013 (Medium-term), and at the beginning of the experiment in 2013 (Short-term); this temporal distinction was chosen following the findings of Pittelkow et al. (2015). Machinery with varied characteristics and brands were adopted for tillage and sowing, according to the on-farm availability and the tested tillage treatments. In an attempt to picture real farm conditions, dates of tillage, sowing, harvesting, weed and pest control, and irrigation were defined by local pedoclimatic conditions and farmers' experience. Complete information about the 20 farms is given at the official project website http://www.lifehelpsoil.eu/en/demonstrative-farms/.

column33: Urea ammonium nitrate

column33: 40-50 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 90 kg K2O5 ha-1
column38: A field experiment was established in 1996 in Agramunt, NE Spain (41°48′ 36′’ N, 1°07′ 06′’ E, 330m asl) to compare two tillage types (CT, conventional tillage; NT, no-tillage) and three mineral N rates (0, 60 and 120 kg N ha−1). The area is representative of rainfed semiarid Mediterranean conditions with a mean annual precipitation of 401 mm, potential evapotranspiration (PET) of 855 mm, and annual temperature of 14.1 °C (1984–2014). The 30-yr mean precipitation received during the soil water recharge period (September to January) reaches 201mm. The experiment was based on a randomized complete block design with three replications which was run for 18 years until 2014.Prior to the establishment of the experiment, the area was devoted to winter cereal production with summer fallow managed under intensive tillage and high rates of N which correspond to the high rate of the field experiment.  Individual plot was 6m wide by 48m long. The CT treatment consisted of one moldboard plough pass (25–30 cm depth) plus one or two cultivator passes (15 cm depth) before sowing, during September and October depending on soil moisture. In the NT treatment no soil tillage practices were carried out. Three to five days before sowing, the weeds were controlled by applying 1.5 L ha−1 of glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine]. Given the medium-high levels of available P and K, applications were oriented to satisfy crop needs at an equal rate for both tillage treatments: ca. 40–50 kg P2O5 ha−1 yr−1 and 90 kg K2Oha−1 yr−1. The grain was harvested using a commercial combine at the end of June or beginning of July, which chopped and spread uniformly crop residues over the soil surface. In the CT treatment, crop residues were incorporated into the soil with tillage operations. Under NT, crop residues were maintained on the soil surface throughout the study period

column5: Texas, Temple (Grassland Soil and Water Research Lab)
column33: 145 lb N acre-1 + 135 lb P2O5 acre -1
column38: The study was conducted at the Grassland Soil and Water  Research Lab at Temple, TX, on a Houston Black clay soil.   The Houston Black  clay soil contains 4% sand, 39% silt, and 56% clay in the  surface 0 to 12 in. depth.   Field plots were established in 1991 on an area which had been in continuous no-till management for 10 yr.   No-till/rake was a slot plant with residue rakes attached to the planter to sweep crop residue away from the row. Fertilizer was applied to com plots at a rate of 145 Ib N/acre and 135 lb P20/acre prior to planting with a coulter nozzle applicator, which placed the fertilizer in the surface 2 in. of soil (Morrison and Potter, 1994). Liquid starter fertilizer (10-34-0) was applied in the furrow adjacent to the seed at planting to all tillage regimes at a rate of 5 Ib N/acre and 39 Ib P20/acre. Com (cultivar Dekalb 671 in 1992, and Dekalb 689 in 1993 and 1994) was planted into soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] residue each year at a rate of 23 800 seeds/acre in 1992 and 27 000 seeds/acre in 1993 and 1994. Planting dates were 26 Mar. 1992, 10 Mar. 1993, and 18 Mar. 1994.  Fertilizer was applied to grain sorghum plots at a rate of 120 lb N/acre and 110 lb P20S/acre prior to planting. Liquid starter fertilizer, (10-34-0), was applied in the furrow adjacent to the seed at planting to all tillage regimes at a rate of 5 lb N/acre and 39 lb P20/acre. Grain sorghum (cultivar Golden Acres TEY75 in 1992 and 1993 and Dekalb 37 in 1994) was planted into corn residue, between the old corn rows, at a rate of 140 500 seeds/acre on 26 Mar. 1992, 1 Apr. 1993, and 16 Mar. 1994.  Surface residue cover from the previous crop was determined immediately after planting by an image analysis technique. In this method, the percentage of pixels falling within residue is determined on electronic photographs (Morrison et aI., 1993).

column5: New Delhi (Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa, New Delhi)
column19: pigeon pea - groundnut - maize - soybean - cotton
column33: N + 80 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 80 kg K2O ha-1
column38: A field experiment was conducted during kharif 2007 on pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan, var P 992), groundnut (Arachis hypogaea, var. TAG 24), maize (Zea mays, var. PEMH 2), soybean (Glycine max, var. D 9814) and cotton (Gossypium hirsutum, var. SCH 22) under different tillage and crop residue management (TCRM) practices, in an on-going longterm conservation tillage field experiment on wheat-based cropping systems started in kharif-2004 at IARI, New Delhi. Above five kharif crops were raised alternately with wheat (var. PBW 343) in rabi under the main plots and the sub-plot treatments were zero tillage with residue (ZT+R), zero tillage without residue (ZT-R), conventional tillage with residue (CT+R) and conventional tillage without residue (CT-R). The residues of different kharif crops were applied @ 2 tonnes/ha before sowing of wheat and wheat residue @ 3 tonnes/ha was applied before sowing of kharif crops in the respective fields. Recommended fertilizer doses of N:P2O5:K2O at the rate of 120:60:40, 25:60:40, 25:60:40, 120:60:40, 25:60:40 and 160:80:80 were applied for wheat, pigeonpea, groundnut, maize, soybean and cotton, respectively. Weeds were controlled by application of herbicide paraquat @ 1 kg ai/ha in zero tillage plots before sowing of kharif crops. Other agronomic operations were carried out as and when required. The experimental soil was sandy loam in texture, neutral in reaction (pH 7.5), low in organic carbon (0.48%) and available nitrogen (194 kg/ha), medium in available potassium (186 kg/ha), low in available phosphorus (9.9 kg/ha) and sulphur (16.8 kg/ha), and free from salinity (0.35 dS/m). Taxonomically (USDA) it belongs to Typic Haplustept subgroup.

column38: The ploughed soil (0–20 cm) before the experiment contains SOC, total N, available N, available P, and available K were 14.79 g /kg , 1.54 g /kg , 95.1 mg /kg , 16.1 mg /kg and 74.2 mg /kg respective. Fertilizers of urea, superphosphate and potassium chloride were applied at the rates of 112.5 kg N, 39.3 kg P and 62.2 kg K ha as basal fertilizer after transplanting and thoroughly incorporated in the soils by hand. Additional urea was spread over the surface soil at a rate of 45 and 67.5 kg N ha at the tillering and heading periods respectively. Weeds were controlled by herbicides. Organophosphate insecticides were used to control asiatic rice striped borer (Chilo suppressalis) and paddy stem borer (Tryporyza incertulas). Irrigation water was pumped from an adjacent well and induced through irrigation channel to the experimental plots. Mulches also acted as insulators to downward conduction of heat into the soil. (2) Straw mulch was effective in most situations for conserving soil water.

column23: stubble left but straw removed + incorporated
column33: N + 140 kg P ha-1 + 62 kg K ha-1
column38: The soil is a Cinnamon Loess, low in organic matter (<1%) and slightly alkaline (pH 7.7). Under the USDA texture classification system, the soils are defined as silt loam and according to the FAOUNESCO soil map (FAO-UNESCO, 1974) the soil type is a Chromic Cambisol. The effects of controlled traffic and traditional tillage on winter wheat were studied from 1998 to 2005. Before the treatments were applied, the experimental area was ploughed (30 cm depth) to provide uniform soil conditions. Every season, fertilizer was applied at the rate of 150 kg N ha-1, 140 kg P ha-1 and 62 kg K ha-1 and the seeding rate was 225 kg ha-1. Wheat was sown in the last 10 days of September and harvested in the first 10 days of June. The treatments consisted of two controlled traffic treatments with full straw cover, no tillage (NTCN) and shallow tillage (STCN), and one conventional tillage treatment (CT). In this treatment, 30 cm high wheat stubble was left at harvest, and all wheat straw was returned to the plots after being threshed.  In the fallow period, there was no tillage—weeds controlled by herbicides only.

column33: with compost, 87.4 kg P ha-1
column38: The site occupied the area between two parallel steep-back sloped terraces that were established in the mid 1960s. Conversion to NToccurred in 1992 with a soybean crop. The NT rotation included small grain cereals and corn rotated with soybeans. Controlled traffic was practiced to minimize soil compaction. The crops that followed one-time tillage of NT were sorghum (2003 and 2005) and soybeans (2004). No manure had been applied previously, but cattle grazed on corn stalks. Subplots treatments were no compost applied and composted beef feedlot manure applied at 87.4 kg P ha21 shortly before tillage. In 2004, soybean (cv. Dekalb 25–51 of Maturity Group 2 at the ARDC, and cv. Asgrow 3302 of Maturity Group 3 at RMF) was sown at both sites at a rate of 494 000 seeds ha-1. Corn (cv. Pioneer 33R81, 2750 growing degrees days at physiological maturity) was sown at the ARDC in 2005 at a rate of 56 800 seeds ha21. Grain sorghum (cv. NC17R37E of Maturity Group 1) was sown at RMF in 2003 and 2005 at a rate of 190 000 seeds ha-1. The only inorganic fertilizer applied was ammonium nitrate applied to corn and sorghum at the suggested rates .

T1: Flat sowing with conventional tillage (CT) in kharif - CT in rabi (CT/CT); T2: CT - no tillage (NT); T3: NT/NT; T4: NT + wheat straw mulch @ 5 t/ha (NT+S)/ NT, T5: fresh raised beds (FB)/flat CT (FB/CT); T6: CT FB; T7 : permanent raised beds (PB) - permanent raised beds (PB/PB) and T8.: PB + wheat straw mulch @ 5 t/ha (PB+S/PB) and were replicated four times. Wheat ‘PBW 343’ was sown on 12 November, 2003 and 5 November, 2004. using a seed rate 100 kg/ha in flat and 75 kg/ha in bed planted treatments and harvested on 6 April, 2004 and 20 April, 2005. In maize, atrazine 50 WP @ 1 kg/ha was applied as preemergence to control weeds. In wheat, fenoxaprop-p-ethyl 10 EC @ 0.1 kg/ha and 2, 4-D @ 0.62 kg/ha (35 days after sowing) were applied to control grassy and broad leaf weeds. The recommended dose of fertilizers i.e. 120 + 26.4 + 25 kg N+P+K/ha were applied to both the crops in each season. Entire P and K fertilizers were applied at the sowing. In maize, N was applied in three equal splits (at sowing, knee high and tasseling stage) whereas in wheat, nitrogen was applied in two equal splits (one at sowing and other after first irrigation). After pre-sowing irrigation, maize did not receive any irrigation during 2003 but received four irrigations in flat CT and NT treatments and five irrigations in beds during 2004. Wheat received four irrigations during 2003-04 and three during 2004-05.

column33: Urea + ammonium nitrate + 154 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 322 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The experimental field was located in Agramunt, NE Spain (41°48' N, 1°07' E, 330 m a.s.l.). The area has a semiarid Mediterranean climate with an average annual temperature of 13.9 ± 0.6°C and annual precipitation of 392 ± 106 mm (period 1975–2014). During the growing season (April–October), the average precipitation is lower than 300 mm (288 ± 98 mm). The study was conducted during the years 2015 to 2017. Soils in the plots of the study were classified as Fluvisols. The study was carried out on the plots of a formerly rainfed long‐term field experiment set up in 1996, in which three tillage systems (conventional tillage, CT; reduced tillage, RT; and no‐tillage, NT) under barley monoculture were compared. The CT consisted of one pass of rototiller to 15 cm depth followed by subsoiler to 35 cm depth and finally one pass of a disk plough to 20 cm depth with almost 100% of the crop residues incorporated into the soil. The NT treatment consisted of weed control with a nonselective herbicide (i.e., glyphosate) at 1.5 L ha−1. Tillage operations were conducted at the end of March to the beginning of April of the corresponding year. The experiment lasted 3 years, in which a non‐ GMO maize hybrid (cv. Kopias, KWS SAAT SE) was planted in late April at a rate of 90,000 seeds ha−1 with a pneumatic direct drilling planter of 73 cm width between rows, regulated to plant at the same soil depth (3–4 cm) in both tillage treatments. A pre‐emergence herbicide (5 L ha−1 of Metolachlor 31.25% and Terbuthylazine 18.75%) was applied to control grasses and broad‐leaved weeds. At post emergence, Fluroxypyr 20% (at 1 L ha−1) was applied to control Abutilon theophrasti Medik. No insecticides or fungicides were needed. Mineral N fertilization was split in one pre‐planting application of 50 kg N ha−1 with urea (46% N, and two top‐dressing applications of 75 kg N ha−1 with calcium ammonium nitrate (27% N), at the V5 and V10 crop development stages (Ritchie, Hanway, Benson, & Herman, 1993). On the basis of soil analysis, P and K fertilization was applied before planting at rates of 154 kg P2O5 ha−1, and 322 kg K2O ha−1, respectively, in the first 2 years. The field was irrigated using a permanent solid‐set  sprinkler irrigation system, programmed to meet crop evapotranspiration requirements minus the effective precipitation (75% of any precipitation above 4 mm), in day and night time irrigations. Irrigation was applied from 7 days after planting to mid‐September. The amount of water applied by irrigation was 631, 672, and 696 mm for years 2015, 2016, and 2017, respectively. Harvesting was carried out by the end of October with a commercial medium‐sized combine. After harvest, crop residues were chopped and spread over the soil.

The initial (baseline) soil analysis (0–15 cm depth) after rice harvest in October 2010 revealed that soil was slightly alkaline (pH = 8.5), with soil bulk density of 1.34 Mg m−3 and soil porosity of 50%. The SOM content was 1.37%, total N = 0.07%, available P = 10 μg g−1 soil, exchangeable K = 0.19 meq 100−1 g soil, available S = 9.8 μg g−1 soil and available Zn = 0.4 μg g−1 soil; The experiment was conducted as a two-factor split-plot design, with tillage treatments assigned to main plots and residue-management treatments to subplots, in four replicates. There were five alternative tillage treatments (zero tillage – ZT, strip tillage – ST, minimum tillage – MT, permanent-raised beds – PB, and fresh raised beds – FB) compared against CT, and two alternative residuemanagement options [retention of 50% (CR50) and 100% (CR100) of the previous crop’s residue on soil surface of the succeeding crop] compared against removal of all residues (0% retention; CR0). Each sub-plot = 8.0 m × 6.0 m (48 m2). The biomass of residues of each crop in 50% and 100% residue-retention treatments were determined from the same 10 m2 sampling area that was used for grain yield in each plot, whereas in the 0% residue-retention plots, all crop residue was removed from the field . To enable residue treatments for the first maize crop in 2010, a uniform crop of monsoon season rice was grown prior to the maize crop. The rice was harvested at ground level. After emergence of the maize seedlings, straw was spread uniformly, making sure that it did not cover the plants. After harvest, the maize stalks were cut and chopped into 5–10 cm length pieces and placed in the residue-retained treatment plots after emergence of the mungbean seedlings. The maize stalks were chopped, as it was difficult to operate the bed planter or the PTOS through the standing maize plants. Mungbean residue was, however, retained on the rice plots without chopping. Fertilization:  Mungbean: Seeds were sown at 35 kg ha−1 immediately after maize harvest during the second or third week of April. Fertilizer management Fertilizers were applied to all crops using recommended practice (BARC 2012). In all crops, N, P, K, S, Zn and B fertilizers were supplied through urea, triple super phosphate (TSP), muriate of potash (MoP), gypsum, ZnSO4 and borax, respectively. Rice: Fertilizer N, P, K, S and B were applied to rice @76, 12.5, 25, 8 and 7.5 kg ha−1. In DSR, urea was applied in 3 equal splits at 10 days after seeding (DAS), 25–30 DAS, and 45–50 DAS. In TPR, urea was broadcast in 2 equal splits, at 15–20 days after transplanting (DAT) and 35–40 DAT. Maize: Fertilizers in maize were applied @250, 70, 170, 30, 5 and 1.4 kg ha−1 N, P, K, S, B, and Zn, respectively. Nitrogen was broadcast at 3 equal splits as basal (just before sowing), and at V6 and V10, while K was broadcast in 2 equal splits as basal and at V10. Fertilizer P was band-placed basally at 2–3 cm depth. Irrigation: Mungbean: Fertilizers in mungbean were broadcast just before sowing @20, 15, 20, 10 and 2 kg ha−1 for N, P, K, S and Zn, respectively. Irrigation Maize and TPR were grown with 2–3 irrigations each year, each irrigation providing around 50–60 mm water, but in DSR, whether on flats or beds, no pre- or post-sowing irrigation was provided as the soil moisture due to pre-monsoon rainfall was enough for rice seedling establishment and post-sowing rainfall enough for its growth and development. Mungbean was grown as rainfed. Weed: There were no major infestations of pest and diseases in any crops and were controlled using recommended practices if required. Weeds were controlled manually or by using recommended herbicides. No pre-planting herbicides were applied in CT. In all the alternative tillage treatments, glyphosate (Roundup) was applied to the untilled soil @ 1.0 kg a.i. ha−1 using 500 L ha−1 water 3 days before sowing. There were no major weeds in TPR, maize and mungbean but in DSR weeds were controlled using either the broad-spectrum post-emergence herbicide Pyrazosulfuron @20 g a.i. ha−1 during 1–3 DAS, or, if still some weeds left, by spraying Fenoxaprop @56 g a.i. ha−1 during 25–30 DAS. Rice was harvested during the second or third week of October while maize was harvested during the first week of April each year. Mungbean was harvested between 7–9 June each year. All crops were harvested manually. To enable residue treatments for the first maize crop in 2010, a uniform crop of monsoon season rice was grown prior to the maize crop.

column33: Ammonium nitrate + 44 kg P ha-1 as triple super phosphate + 150 kg K ha-1 as mutiate of potash
column38: Crops were seeded in the 3rd week of May in 1992 and 1993, using a 2-row John Deere planter modified with Yetter heavy duty coulters (Allan Machine Co., NV, USA). This experiment was conducted for two growing seasons at two sites, on a Ste. Rosalie clay (Site 1) and on Ormstown silty clay loam (Site 2), both Humic Gleysols and typical eastern Canadian soils adapted to corn and soybean production. Crop systems were continuous corn, corn-soybean-corn, soybean-corn-soybean, and continuous soybean in 1991, 1992 and 1993. Three rates of fertilizer N used for corn were 0, 90, and 180 kg N ha–1 and continuous soybean plots were 0, 20, and 40 kg N ha–1, rates within those recommended for crops in Quebec. No fertilizer N was applied to soybean in rotation with corn. Ammonium nitrate was broadcast on the surface of each plot at the time of seeding. Phosphorus was banded 5 cm beside and 5 cm below the seed at 44 kg P ha–1 as triple super phosphate for corn and soybean. Potassium was broadcast at seeding time at 150 kg K ha–1 for corn and 65 kg K ha–1 for soybean as muriate of potash. Weeds were controlled with diclofop-methyl (Hoechst Canada Inc., Willowdale, ON, Canada) and Atrazine (Drexel Chemical Co., Memphis, TN, USA) at a rate of 3.5 L ha–1 (480 g active ingredient L–1) in late June for both growing seasons. Roundup (Monsanto Inc., Mississauga, ON, Canada) was applied before seeding and during the growing season between rows for both crops in the 3rd week of July 1992 and 1993, at a rate of 5.0 L ha–1 (356 g active ingredient L–1). An inverted funnel (25 cm diameter) was attached over the nozzle to prevent damage to the corn or soybean plants.

column38: The experiment was conducted from April 2001 to November 2003 at the Harlaka Research Farm of Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, located 5 km southeast of Québec City (46°48′ N, 71°23′ W), Canada, on two soils from the same catena: a poorly drained Kamouraska heavy clay (Orthic Humic Gleysol or fi ne, mixed, frigid, Typic Humaquept; clay = 770 g kg−1; sand = 70 g kg−1; pH = 6.2) and a well-drained Saint-André gravelly loam (Fragic Humo-Ferric Podzol or mixed, frigid, Typic Dystrochrept; clay = 220 g kg−1; sand = 440 g kg−1; pH = 5.9) located 200 m apart. The Kamouraska soil series occupies 32,000 ha in the St. Lawrence valley, but <500 ha are characterized by a heavy clay texture (>600 g clay kg−1, Soil Classifi cation Working Group, 1998); while the St-André series covers 50,000 ha, mostly with a loam or sandy loam texture. The seeding date was between 30 April and 25 May, while harvest was between 5 and 22 August. Mineral fertilizers (32.5 kg ha−1 of N as NH4NO3, K2O, and P2O5) were applied before seeding in both tillage treatments in 2002 and 2003. In 2001, 70 kg ha−1 N was applied before seeding in the MP plots and split between planting (10 kg ha−1) and tillering (60 kg ha−1, mid-June) in the NT plots. Weeds were controlled by manual weeding and by the use of herbicides (1 L ha−1 Dyvel, containing 84 g ha−1 dicamba [3,6-dichloro-2-methoxybenzoic acid] and 336 g ha−1 MCPA [(4-chloro-2-methylphenoxy)acetic acid]). The treatments consisted in MP to 0.20 m in the fall and NT laid out in 8- by 8-m plots in a randomized complete block design with four replicates. In contrast with the clay soil, the NT/MP ratio tended to be greater before (1.44) than after tillage operations (0.44), indicating that conditions shortly after soil disturbance and residue incorporation favored N2O production and emission. High denitrifi cation rates in the fall, long after the infl uence of spring fertilizer application on soil mineral N content had disappeared (Fig. 4 and 5), were probably sustained by the mineralization of crop residue and native soil organic N. Alternatively, recently fi xed NH4 + was found to be highly dynamic in this soil.

A 4-year field experiment, begun in April 2008, was conducted in a farmer’s paddock (33o 35.212'S; 120o 48.221'E) on a nonwetting bleached sand, with slight ironstone gravel at the surface and increasing gravel with depth (Ferric mesonatric yellow sodosol: Isbell, 2002) on the south coast of Western Australia. The region has a Mediterranean-type climate characterised by hot dry summers and cool wet winters. On one section, where the paddock had previously been burnt from a lightning strike in December 2004, stubble was burnt each year during the experiment just prior to seeding. Dates of burning were 13 April 2008, 14 May 2009, 6 May 2010 and 26 May 2011. On the other section which had not been burnt during the lightning storm, stubble was retained throughout the experiment. Individual plots were harvested by a contractor using a plot harvester (Massey Ferguson 31, Germany) at maturity in late November or December each year.  Winter season crops planted were Canola cv. Surpass 501TT (1 May 2008); Barley cv. Dash (15 May 2009); Canola cv. 45y82 IT hybrid (7 May 2010); Wheat cv. Mace (28 May 2011).

column33: N + 60 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 40 kg K2O ha-1
column38: Field experiments with conventional tillage, conventional tillage plus crop residue incorporated at sowing, zero tillage where crop residues were removed and zero tillage with crop residue retained over surface at sowing, in maize–mustard cropping sequence have been continuing for 3 years (2004– 07) at the research farm of the Institute, New Delhi. In maize crop, residue of previous mustard crop was applied @ 2 tonnes/ha, while for mustard, maize residue was applied @ 3 tonnes/ha. In conventionally tilled plots, 1 disk plowing, followed by 2 cultivations by cultivator to a depth of 0.15 m was done.  The soil Typic Haplustept, ranged in texture (0–0.15 m) from loamy sand to sandy loam with pH 8.3 and organic C content of 0.6 g/kg soil. Supplementary irrigations were given as per need. Forty kg each of N and P2O5 /ha were applied as basal before sowing and rest 40 kg N/ha was applied as top-dressing (on 30 days after sowing). One pre-sowing light irrigation and 2 irrigation thereafter (on 35 and 100 days after sowing) were applied. The crop was harvested on 13 March 2007. Yield reduction under zero tillage was more pronounced in maize than mustard due to perennial weed problem and tilling the land once in 2–3 years is recommended under maize–mustard cropping system under similar set of conditions as in the present study.

column33: N + 26 kg P ha-1 + 50 kg K ha-1 + 25 kg Zn ha-1
column38: The climate of the area is semi-arid, with an average annual rainfall of 750 mm (75–80% of which is received during July to September), minimum temperature of 0–4 8C in January, maximum temperature of 41–44 8C in June, and relative humidity of 50–90% throughout the year. The experimental soil (0– 15 cm) was clay loam in texture with bulk density 1.58 Mg m-3, pH 7.8, EC (saturation extract) 0.24 dS m-1, organic carbon 0.41%, KMnO4 extractable N 141 kg ha-1, Olsen P 25 kg ha-1, and ammonium acetate exchangeable K 301 kg ha-1. The five treatments (T1 to T5) involving three tillage and two rice establishment methods were evaluated in the rice–wheat rotation. Each experimental unit consisted of 17.0 m x 8.5 m (144.5 m2) plot. After rice harvest, most widely grown wheat cultivar PBW-343 was seeded in rows 20 cm apart (using a seed-cum-fertilizer drill) at rate of 100 kg ha-1 on November 12 and 17 in year 1 and year 2, respectively, In no-till plots, existing weeds prior to the seeding of rice and wheat were killed by pre-plant application of glyphosate at 0.9 kg a.i. ha-1. The plots were kept weed-free throughout the growing season by using pre-emergence or post-emergence herbicides and hand-weeding. In rice, pre-emergence herbicides used were anilophos at 0.4 kg a.i. ha-1, 4 days after transplanting (DAT) in transplanted rice, pretilachlor plus safener at 0.5 kg a.i. ha-1 just after sowing in wet direct-seeded rice (T4) and pendimethalin at 1.0 kg a.i. ha-1 within 48 h of sowing in dry direct-seeded rice (Singh et al., 2007). Additionally, need based hand-weeding was done to keep the plots weed-free. In wheat, grassy weeds were controlled by spraying sulfosulfuron at 0.35 kg a.i. ha-1 21 days after sowing (DAS), and broadleaf weeds were controlled using 2, 4D at 0.5 kg a.i. ha-1 35 DAS followed by one hand-weeding.

column33: 67 kg P ha-1 as triple superphosphate + 84 kg K ha-1 as muriate of potash
column38: The experiment was conducted from 1997 to 1999 at the  Agricultural Research Station farm, Fort Valley State Univer-  sity, Fort Valley, GA. The soil was a Dothan sandy loam with. a pH of 6.5 and sand, silt, and clay contents of 650, 250, and, 100 g kg-1, respectively, at 0- to 30-cm depth. The clay content  increased to 350 g kg-1 below 30 cm. At 0 to 30 cm, organic  C was 8.8 g kg-1 and organic N was 620 mg kg-1. Previous (5 yr) were wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), soybean [Glycine max L. (Merr.)], and tomato. After sampling, vetch and weeds were mowed with a rotary mower to break the plants into small pieces, killed by spraying 3.36 kg a.i. ha-1 glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] in NT plots, and incorporated into the soil by harrowing in CP and MP plots. Residues were allowed to decompose in the soil for 13 to 16 d before P and K fertilization and corn planting. At two corn-planting dates, P {from triple superphosphate [Ca(H2PO4 )2]} fertilizer and K [from muriate of potash (KCl)] fertilizer were broadcast at 67 and 84 kg ha-1, respectively, to all plots based on the soil test. Following tillage, silage corn (cv. McNair 508) was planted at 70 000 seeds ha-1 in 8-row plots (0.9-m spacing). Irrigation (equivalent to 25 mm of rain at a time using reel rain gun) was applied on 12 and 27 May, 15 June, and 18 July in 1998 and on 10 and 25 Apr. Averaged across treatments, cover crop biomass was 65% higher, N concentration 13% higher, and N accumulation 101% higher in 1999 than in 1998.

The soil was a Dothan sandy loam with. a pH of 6.5 and sand, silt, and clay contents of 650, 250, and, 100 g kg-1, respectively, at 0- to 30-cm depth. The clay content  increased to 350 g kg-1 below 30 cm. At 0 to 30 cm, organic  C was 8.8 g kg-1 and organic N was 620 mg kg-1. Previous (5 yr) were wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), soybean [Glycine max L. (Merr.)], and tomato. After sampling, vetch and weeds were mowed with a rotary mower to break the plants into small pieces, killed by spraying 3.36 kg a.i. ha-1 glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] in NT plots, and incorporated into the soil by harrowing in CP and MP plots. Residues were allowed to decompose in the soil for 13 to 16 d before P and K fertilization and corn planting. At two corn-planting dates, P {from triple superphosphate [Ca(H2PO4 )2]} fertilizer and K [from muriate of potash (KCl)] fertilizer were broadcast at 67 and 84 kg ha-1, respectively, to all plots based on the soil test. Following tillage, silage corn (cv. McNair 508) was planted at 70 000 seeds ha-1 in 8-row plots (0.9-m spacing). Irrigation (equivalent to 25 mm of rain at a time using reel rain gun) was applied on 12 and 27 May, 15 June, and 18 July in 1998 and on 10 and 25 Apr. Averaged across treatments, cover crop biomass was 65% higher, N concentration 13% higher, and N accumulation 101% higher in 1999 than in 1998.

column33: N + 16 kg P ha-1 + 11 kg S ha-1
column38: In both years, the two experiments were on adjacent 3-ha  parcels where the previous crops were winter wheat and spring  barley, respectively. Stubble from the previous crops was left  undisturbed fromharvest inAugust through February. In early  March, 0.32 kg a.e. ha-1 glyphosate herbicide [N-(phosphono-  methyl)glycine] was applied to both plot areas to control winter annual grassy weeds and volunteer from the previous crop. Fertilizer injection with shanks spaced 300 mm apart and 100 mm deep with an attached five-bar harrow. Barley seed was treated in both years with a broad-spectrum fungicide and insecticide formulation of tebuconazole {a-[2-(4-chlorophenyl)ethyl]-a-(1,1-dimeth- ylethyl)-1H-1,2,4-triazole-1-ethanol} thiram [bis(dimethylthi- ocarbamoyl)disulfide], and lindane [1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachloro- hexane]. The fertilizer rate (based on soil test with a yield goal of 4000 kg ha-1) was 78 kg N, 16 kg P, and 11 kg S ha-1 in 1996 and 84 kg N, 15 kg P, and 10 kg S ha-1 in 1997. In the CT treatment, all N and S were applied as liquid in either aqua NH (double disk) 139b 111b 3 plus ammonium thiosulfate (1996) or urea– ammonium nitrate solution (320 g N kg-1) plus ammonium thiosulfate (1997). Phosphorus was applied with the seed as granular monoammonium phosphate at the time of sowing in 1996, and before sowing as ammoniumpolyphosphate solution in 1997 All NT drills delivered seed and all fertilizer in one pass through the plots. Plots were sown to barley at 78 kg ha-1 with ‘Baronesse’ between 28 and 31 March in 1996, andwith ‘Camelot’ on 7 and 8April in 1997.

column5: Kansas State University Southwest Research-Extension Center near Tribune, Kansas
column33: Urea + 12 kg P ha-1 ammonia polyphosphate
column38: This long-term dryland (non-irrigated) tillage intensity study was conducted at the Kansas State University Southwest Research-Extension Center near Tribune, KS (38°28'13'' N, 101°45'16'' W, 1095 m asl) from 1991 through 2015 on a deep silt loam soil (Richfi eld silt loam [fi ne smectitic, mesic Aridic Argiustoll]). Tribune, KS, is in a semiarid environment with average annual precipitation of 455 mm. Th e NT system relied solely on herbicides to control weed growth during the fallow periods. Herbicides used for weed control in NT fallow varied across years but relied primarily on glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] (0.84 kg acid equivalent ha–1), dicamba (3,6-dichloro-2-methoxybenzoic acid) (0.14–0.28 kg a.i. ha–1), and 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxy-acetic acid) (0.28–0.56 kg a.i. ha–1). On average, this resulted in four to fi ve herbicide applications prior to each crop. All tillage systems used herbicides for weed control during the growing season. All phases of each rotation were present each year. The experimental design was a randomized complete block with four replications. The experimental plots were 15.2 m wide and 30.4 m long. Planting dates were from late May to early June for grain sorghum and from the second week of September to second week of October for winter wheat. Seeding rate was 80,000 to 100,000 seeds ha–1 for sorghum and 45 to 60 kg ha–1 for wheat. Sorghum was planted with a John Deere model 7300 planter (Moline, IL) in 76 c rows and wheat was planted with a single disc drill (John Deere 752 drill with 19 cm row spacing) for the NT plots and a hoe drill (John Deere 9400 drill with 30 cm row spacing) for the RT and CT plots. Urea ammonium nitrate (UAN, 28% N) was applied at average rates of 67 and 90 kg N ha–1 for wheat and sorghum, respectively, with a liquid fertilizer applicator (Melroe model 220 Spra Coupe, Bismarck, ND) that dribble-banded the UAN on the surface in late winter to early spring. Starter fertilizer (ammonia polyphosphate, 10–34–0) was surface dribbled (5 cm from the row) to sorghum with the planter at planting to supply about 8 kg N ha–1 and 12 kg P ha–1. For wheat, monoammonium phosphate (11–52–0) was applied with the seed at planting to supply about 7 kg N ha–1 and 15 kg P ha–1.  An annual yield advantage with reduction of tillage, often in the order NT > RT > CT, is perhaps a result of increases in the yield components due to conservation of water, improved surface residue, improved soil biological activity, and soil structure

column5: Kansas, Tribue (Southwest Research and Extension Center)
column33: 60 lb/acre NPK-28-0-0
column38: The predominant cropping system in the region is WF. The cropping systems evaluated were WF, WSF, and WW. All crop rotations were grown using NT, and the WF and WSF also were grown under RT. The RT systems used a combination of herbicides and tillage for weed control during fallow, whereas NT relied solely on herbicides. Weed control programs for each system are outlined in Table 1. A sweep plow with three 5 ft Vblades was used for all tillage operations. Plot size was 30 by 80 ft. The experimental design was a randomized complete block with four replications. All phases of each rotation were present each year. Winter wheat (‘TAM 107’) was planted at 45 Ib/acre in September. A John Deere 8300 hoe drill with 14-in. row spacing was used in 1991 and 1992. A John Deere 750 single disc drill with 7.5411. row spacing was used from 1993 to 1995. Grain sorghum (‘Pioneer 8771’) was planted at 28 000 seeddacre in late May or early June in 30-in. rows with a John Deere 7300 planter. Fluid fertilizer N (28-0-0) was applied prior to planting of sorghum (60 Ib N/acre) and in the spring to wheat (50 Ib N/acre for WF and WSF and 35 Ib N/acre for WW). No fertilizer P was applied because soil test P levels were high. An economic analysis compared the relative costs and returns for each system. Costs for tillage, herbicide applications, planting, and harvest were based on average custom rates for western Kansas. Compared with conventional tillage (CT) systems, maintaining surface crop residue cover with RT or NT systems can reduce evaporation and enhance soil water storage.

column33: UAN + 0/20 kg P ha-1 as ammonium polyphosphate
column38: All selected sites had been in reduced tillage (disc and field cultivation) for several years before initiation of the study. Site 1 is mapped as a Parsons silt loam (fine mixed, thermic Mollic Albaqualfs), and Sites 2 and 3 are mapped as Catoosa silt loams (fine-silty, mixed, thermic Typic Argiudolls). All sites were in soybean production in the previous year (1996). Crop rotations and other cultural practices employed during the study were determined by the cooperator and are listed in Table 1. Results from Site 1 for 1999 are not reported due to poor plant emergence. Three tillage practices were the whole plots and P fertilizer management was the subplot factor. Tillage practices were no-till (NT), reduced till (RT), and plow (PL). Subplots were (i) 0 kg P ha-1 (CK), (ii) 20 kg P ha-1 as ammonium polyphosphate (10–34–0) applied as a surface broadcast (BC), (iii) 20 kg P ha-1 applied as a starter (ST) 5 cm to the side and 5 cm below the seed, and (iv) 20 kg P ha-1 applied in deep bands (DB), 15 cm deep and 0.7 m apart. Broadcast applications were made before plowing and before disking in the tilled treatments. Nitrogen (13 kg N ha21 UAN) was applied as a starter to all check plots to balance N fertilizer with P treatments. Except when soybean was grown, additional N fertilizer (UAN) was surface broadcast to the entire study area at the rate recommended by Kansas State Soil Testing Laboratory for each crop (Whitney, 1983). Glyphate was applied to all NT plots before planting; other herbicides applied for weed control depended on weed pressure and cooperator discretion. Excellent chemical weed control was obtained at all locations, and post-emergence cultivation for weed was not performed or necessary of any of the treatments. In subsequent years, reduced tillage was used on plowed treatments to assess the residual value of moldboard plowing. all treatments were no-till planted into the corn residue so that planting was completed in a timely fashion.
