column33: ammonium nitrate + 8.9 kg P ha-1
column38: A tillage study initiated in 1981 in southwestern Saskatchewan, at Swift Current, on a Swinton silt loam, an Orthic Brown Chernozemic soil (Aridic Haploboroll in the U.S. classification) (Ayres et al., 1985), was used to study the effect of crop rotations and tillage on the distribution of P in the surface 10 cm of the soil profile. The ZT treatment consisted of chemical weed control during the fallow year, and seeding directly into the standing residues of the previous crop. For the CW cropping system, CT consisted in seeding the crop after a preseeding tillage with a heavy-duty cultivator, while ZT consisted of seeding directly onto the standing stubble of the previous crop. Spring wheat was grown in fallow-wheat (FW) and in continuous-wheat (CW) rotations, under cultivator-tillage (CT) and zerotillage management. For the FW cropping system, CT consisted of one-to-four tillage operations up to 5± 10 cm depth with a chisel plow equipped with sweeps (heavy-duty cultivator) during the summer of the fallow year, and one tillage operation with the heavy duty cultivator before seeding in the crop year. Spring wheat cv. Canuck (from 1981 to 1989), and cv. Lancer (from 1990 onwards) were sown at a rate of 67 kg ha -1. Fertilizer N, as ammonium nitrate, was applied to each treatment (combination of tillage and cropping system) at the average soil test recommendation for all the plots of each specific treatment. Until 1989, N was broadcast prior to seeding. Starting in 1990, up to 45 kg N ha -1 was seed-placed together with P. Any N in excess of 45 kg ha -1 was broadcast. Fertilizer P was placed with the seed as monoammonium phosphate; typically, the depth of seeding and P placement was 5 cm for the ZT system and 6 cm for the CT system. Until 1989, all treatments received a fixed rate of 8.9 kg P ha-1. Starting in 1990 all treatment received P at rates based on the average Olsen-P for each particular treatment. Phosphorus application rates since 1990 varied from 5.5 to 8 kg ha -1, and averaged 7.2 kg P ha -1.

column5: ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi
column33: N + 26 kg P ha-1 + 33 kg K ha-1
column38: A field experiment was conducted at the farm of Division of Agronomy at ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute (280 400 N, 77012 E at an altitude of 228 masl), New Delhi during 2010, 2011 and 2012. The experimental site falls in the agro-climatic zone of “Trans Indo-Gangetic Plains”, having a sub-tropical and semi-arid climate, with hot summers and cold winters with mean annual maximum and minimum temperatures of 40.5° C and 6.5° C, respectively. The mean annual rainfall is 670 mm and its distribution is unimodal. Approximately 70–80% of rainfall is confined to three months from July to September. The quantity of rainfall received during the years of experimentation was 535 mm, 931 mm and 538 mm during 2010, 2011and 2012, respectively. The soil of the experimental field has a sandy loam texture up to 30 cm soil depth and can be classified as Typic Haplustept or Inceptisol. The surface soil layer of 0-15 cm has a neutral pH of 7.5, an organic C (Walkley and Black 1934) content of 0.32%, KMnO4-oxidizable N (Subbiah and Asija 1956) of 172 kg/ ha, and NaHCO3-extractable P (Olsen et al. 1954) of 12.8 kg/ha, and NH4OAc-exchangable K (Hanway and Heidel 1952) of 289 kg/ha. The experiment was conducted in split-plot design with three replications during kharif season of 2010, 2011 and 2012. In main plots, tillage systems, viz. conventional tillage (CT), CT + residues at 3 t/ha, zero-tillage (ZT) and ZT+ residues at 3 t/ha were allotted. column33: 300+200 kg ha-1 urea + 500 kg superphosphate
column38: The study was established in 2004 at the Zong Ai village in Shouyang County (37º54´N, 113º10´E), located on the Loess Plateau, characterized by a semiarid climate. The soil had a silt loam textureaccording to the USDA classification , and was classified as a Chromic Cambisol according to the FAO-UNESCO soil map. Before the experiment, the mean texture particle size distribution for the surface layer (0–20 cm) included 455 g kg−1 sand, 340 g kg−1 silt and 205 g kg−1 clay. The soil pH was 8.4 (in a 1:2.5 soil/water suspension), the SOC content was 17.6 g kg−1, the total N content was 1.03 g kg−1, the total P was 0.10 g kg−1 and the total K was 2.52 g kg−1. Two different soil management treatments were conducted in a randomised block design (RBD) with three replicates. Each plot was 6.0 m × 10.0 m in size with a buffer zone of 0.6 m between each other.CT: Most residues from the prior maize crop were removed for fodder, leaving 10–15 cm of stubble on the field after harvest in October. The field was tilled at a depth of 20–25 cm using a tractor-drawn plough. NT : Maize was harvested and standing stubble, approximately 15 to 20 cm in height, was retained with all maize residues left as mulch cover (average 3.75 t ha−1). The maize breed (cv Jindan34) was sown on approximately 25 April each year using a holesowing tool (3 cm diameter). The continuous maize crops were planted using 60 cm row spacing and 30 cm row spacing planting, and a seeding rate of 60,030 plants ha−1 in total. An herbicide (2,4-D-butylate) and insecticide (40% dimethoate) were applied at the three-leaf stage in June. Three hundred kg ha−1 urea (46% N) and 500 kg ha−1 superphosphate (16% P2O5) were applied as basal fertiliser, and another 200 kg ha−1 urea (46% N) was applied as a top dressing each year during the jointing stage of maize. This cropping system provided a seven-month fallow period between the maize harvest in October and planting during the following year.

(i) conventional tillage-based management with incorporation of crop residues into the soil (CT), and (ii) no-tillage management with retention of crop residues from the previous maize crop on the soil surface, but without a cover crop (NT). Two field experiments were conducted during the 2001/2002 growing season on the experimental station of Embrapa Cerrados (15.59°S, 47.70°W), located near Planaltina, Federal District of Brazil, at an altitude of 1175m. There was no previous cover crop. The maize crop was directly seeded (05/11/2001) in the resulting mulch (about 4 t dry matter ha−1) without any tillage operation using a direct seeder pulled by a tractor. Sowing density was the same as in the CT treatment. In the two treatments maize was fertilized at planting with 400 kg ha-1 of compound NPK (4-30-16) fertilizer and 19 kg ha−1 of ZnSO4 and two leaf applications of 1.5 kg ha−1 MnSO4. At 20 days after planting, 65 kg N ha−1 was applied in the form of urea. Weed control was done with glyphosate (1080 g ha−1) and 2.4 D (1612 g ha−1) before maize planting, followed by applications of 1480 g ha−1 of atrazine and 1160 g ha−1 of S-metolachlor. column5: Iowa, Ames, Boone (Iowa State Agronomy and Ag Engineering Research Farm)
column33: urea ammonium nitrate + compost
column38: The experimental site had been in continuous corn production since 1987, with tillage main plots consisting of MP, chisel plow, and no-till since 1988. In 1997, the entire site was planted to soybean. Soil samples collected from the top 18 cm in 1997 indicated that tillage had not affected soil pH (6.7), OM (63 g kg-1), P (Bray-1, 54mg kg-1), or K(ammoniumacetate extraction, 210 mg kg-1) levels. In 1998, a corn–soybean–wheat/clover rotation was initiated with all phases represented each year. Subplots, 7.6 m (10 rows with a 76-cm row spacing) wide by 13.1 m long, consisted of the application of bedded swine manure compost (amended) or no compost. Compost application rate during the first crop rotation cycle (1998–2000) was set at 8000 kg C ha-1 per application and reduced to 4000 kg. C ha-1 thereafter. Compost rates to achieve the C application target were 61.6, 74.7, 54.1, and 22.3 Mg dry matter ha-1 in 1998, 1999, 2000, and 2001, respectively.Corn (‘Pioneer Brand 3563’) was planted in late April of each year at a seeding rate of 81 510 seeds ha-1. In 1999, 2001, and 2002, 151, 174, and 123 kg N ha-1 were applied to no-compost plots, and 118, 151, and 67 kg N ha-1 were applied to compost plots. In 2000, 162, 106, and 106 kg N ha-1 were applied to the no- compost plots in no-till, chisel plow, and MP systems, respectively, while the compost plots received 146, 84, and 62 kg N ha-1 for the three tillage systems. All sidedress N was 32% urea ammonium nitrate (UAN) applied using a point-injector applicator. Clover was chemically killed each fall. Typical management practices were used for corn and soybean weed control. No herbicide was applied to wheat. in 1998, 1999, 2000, and 2001, the straw residue after wheat harvest was allowed to remain on the compost plots but was removed from the no-compost plots.  Soybean (‘Pioneer Brand 9294’) was planted in mid-May in all years at a rate of 444 600 seeds ha_1 in 76-cm rows. No fertilizer was applied during the soybean phase of crop rotation.

column33: urea+ 33 kg P ha-1 as single superphosphate + 66 kg K ha-1 as muriate of potash
column38: The soil of the experimental field was very deep (>20 m), well-drained sandy loam (158 g clay and 657 g sand kg-1) with 1% slope and classified as Typic Ustochrept. The top-soil (0–15 cm layer) at the start of experiment was non-saline (electrical conductivity 0.35 dS m-1) with pH 8.10, and contained 4.61 g kg-1 Walkley-Black carbon, 76.9 mg kg-1 available N (Subbiah and Asija, 1956), 7.72 mg kg-1 0.5 M NaHCO3-extractable P (Olsen et al., 1954) and 111 mg kg-1 1 N NH4OAc-extractable K. The decennial monthly minimum temperature fluctuates from 6.9 to 21.8 -C and maximum temperature from 23.7 to 42.6 -C at the experimental site. The average annual rainfall is 831 mm, and over 75% of this is received through northwest monsoon during July to September. Rice was fertilized with a uniform dose of 150 kg N + 33 kg P +66 kg K +30 kg S + 5 kg Zn ha-1, whereas maize received 175 kg N + 33 kg P + 66 kg K ha-1. The N, P and K were applied through urea (46% N), single superphosphate (7% P), and muriate of potash (49.8% K), respectively. Rice received S from single superphosphate (12% S) used as a source of P and the balance was made using gypsum (12% S). Zinc was applied as zinc sulphate (21% Zn) in all the years. To both TPR and DSR, fertilizer N was applied in 3 equal splits, at sowing/transplanting; at maximum tillering (25–30 days after transplanting in TPR/40–45 days after sowing in DSR); and at panicle initiation (50–55 days after transplanting in TPR/ 65–70 days after sowing in DSR). Half dose of K was applied as basal (incorporated into soil for transplanted rice and banded for DSR) and remaining half of K was top-dressed manually at panicle initiation. Entire amounts of P, S and Zn were applied at sowing. To maize, 1/3 of N and entire dose of P and K was band applied at sowing. The remaining 2/3 of N was applied in two equal splits at V6–V8 (vegetative stage when 6th–8th leaves appeared) and V10–V12 (when 10th –12th leaves appeared) stage. Basal applica-tion of fertilizers under CTDSR, ZTDSR and ZTM plots was banded at sowing through multi-crop planter cum fertilizer drill (model; NMCT-ZT) manufactured by National Agro-Industries, Ludhiana, Punjab, India. Main plot treatments were three combinations of tillage and crop establishment methods and the sub-plot treatments were two residue management options: removal of residues (-R) of both the crops, and partial residue (5 Mg ha-1) either retained at soil surface in zero-till plots or incorporated into the soil in conventional till plots (+R) for both rice and maize. Three crop establishment methods included: puddled transplanted rice (TPR) followed by conventional till maize (TPR/CTM); conventionally till dry direct-seeded rice (CTDSR) followed by CTM (CTDSR/CTM); and zero-tilled DSR followed by zero-tilled maize (ZTDSR/ZTM). DSR was sown with commercially sold zero-till maize/multi-crop planter cum fertilizer drill having inclined plate seed metering system (model: NMCT-ZT) at 20 cm row spacing using a seed rate of 25 kg ha-1.   Weeds in ZT plots were smothered by spraying glyphosate at 900 g (a.i.) ha-1 using flat fan nozzle (Knapsac sprayer, model AGM/ 001). In DSR, pendimethalin 1000 g (a.i.) ha_1 was sprayed at two days after sowing (DAS), followed by one post-emergence spray of chlorimuron ethyl + metsulfuron methyl at 4 g (a.i.) ha-1 at 21 DAS for controlling broadleaf weeds. In TPR, butachlor 1000 g (a. i.) ha-1 was broadcasted manually two days after transplanting. One manual weeding was also done in rice (TPR and DSR) and CTM to keep the plots weed-free. Rice and maize were grown under assured irrigated conditions.

column33: ammonium nitrate
column38: This study was initiated in 1998 on a Zanesville silt loam soil (Fine-silty, mixed, mesic Typic Fragiudalf) with 0–2% slope in Princeton, Kentucky in Caldwell county. The nutrient application treatments consisted of a control, which was fertilized only with chemical fertilizers, and two rates of broiler litter at 11 and 22 Mg ha-1 on a wet weight basis. For the chemical fertilizer treatment, P and K were applied according to soil test results on samples taken every spring prior to planting using University of Kentucky fertilizer recommendations. The amount of fertilizer nitrogen applied was 169 kg N ha-1 applied as ammonium nitrate. For CT, fertilizer or litter was applied and then incorporated with tillage, while for NT, treatments were surface applied on the plots. These methods of fertilizer and litter application are the practices that farmers normally use in the region. A commonly used litter application rate for corn is 11 Mg ha-1.With an average nitrogen content of 26.6 g (kg wet)-1 in the litter and the estimation that about half of the nitrogen is available to the crop (Rasnake, 2002), the available nitrogen with 11 Mg ha-1 of litter was 146 kg N ha-1. This value was similar to the chemical fertilizer application of 169 kg N ha-1. The nitrogen application rate recommended for corn using University of Kentucky recommendations is 157–196 kg ha-1 (University of Kentucky, 2006). The litter rate of 22 Mg ha-1 provided available nitrogen of 292 kg ha-1. The 22 Mg ha-1 litter rate evaluated effects of a high application rate used more as a disposal rate for the litter that would exacerbate potential problems with increased levels of P, Cu and Zn in the soil. Corn was planted in plots consisting of four 0.75 m wide rows that were 15 m long in early May and harvested as grain in September by picking the two center rows for a harvest area of 1.5 m x 9 m (13.5 m2). The same treatments were applied on the same plots and corn was planted each year from 1998 to 2001. In 2002 and 2003, corn was planted using NT, but no broiler litter was applied. The entire experiment was fertilized only with nitrogen at 202 kg N ha-1 each year using ammonium nitrate. In 2004 and 2005, corn was not planted and fertilizer was not applied. The plots were mowed periodically.

column33: lime ammonium nitrate(LAN)
column38: Since the beginning of the experiment, the trial site has been planted to dry maize continuous monocropping, in summer and left fallow during the winter months. In NT and RT treatments about 10–12 t ha−1 yr−1 of maize residues were left on the soil surface, thus forming permanent soil cover, while in CT treatments residues were removed on the soil surface after harvest.  The considered rates of N (0, 100 and 200 kg N ha−1) were applied as lime ammonium nitrate (LAN). Nitrogen was applied as top dressing four weeks after planting. Potassium (K) and phosphorous (P) were applied at planting in the band at a rate of 50 and 20 kg ha−1, respectively. Lime (Calcitic) was applied at a rate of 2 Mg ha−1 every second season to the entire treatments. Weeds were controlled chemically using a combination of mesotrione, atrazine, Smetolachlor and 2,4-D. The only pesticide applied at planting was pyrethroid (Decis Forte) to control cutworms. Leaf fungal disease (grey leaf spot, northern corn leaf blight and rust) were controlled using carbendazim plus flusilazole and azoxystobin.

column38: Since the beginning of the experiment, the trial site has been planted to dry maize continuous monocropping, in summer and left fallow during the winter months. The considered rates of N (0, 100 and 200 kg N ha−1) were applied as lime ammonium nitrate (LAN). Nitrogen was applied as top dressing four weeks after planting. Potassium (K) and phosphorous (P) were applied at planting in the band at a rate of 50 and 20 kg ha−1, respectively. Lime (Calcitic) was applied at a rate of 2 Mg ha−1 every second season to the entire treatments. Weeds were controlled chemically using a combination of mesotrione, atrazine, Smetolachlor and 2,4-D. The only pesticide applied at planting was pyrethroid (Decis Forte) to control cutworms. Leaf fungal disease (grey leaf spot, northern corn leaf blight and rust) were controlled using carbendazim plus flusilazole and azoxystobin.

column33: UAN + DAP
column38: There was a total of eight blocks of each treatment for the corn– soybean plots. Th e corn–soybean plots measured 10 by 20 m, with the predominate soils being Octagon silt loam (a fi ne-loamy, mixed, active, mesic Mollic Oxyaquic Hapludalf ) and Th rockmorton silt loam (a fi nesilty, mixed, superactive, mesic Mollic Oxyaquic Hapludalf ). When the corn–soybean plots were established, the northern 20 plots were planted to soybean in odd years and to corn in even years. The treatments were: (i) conventional tillage (defi ned as fall chisel, spring disk) with all N fertilizer applied at the time of planting; (ii) no-till with all N fertilizer applied at the time of planting; (iii) no-till with all N fertilizer applied at the time of planting and annual ryegrass (Lolium multifl orum Lam.) planted as a winter cover crop; (iv) no-till with half of the N fertilizer applied at the time of planting and the remainder sidedressed post-emergence; and (v) precision tillage with all N fertilizer placed at the time of planting. The bare-soil plots were located in the grassed buff er strips between the plots, with glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine] used to remove grass and other vegetation. Pesticide used: roundup, bicep; and pesticide application data is 17 Apr. plant cover in winter.

column33: 400 kg ha-1 superphosphate + 100 kg ha-1 K2O
column38: The site had a mean annual rainfall of 850 mm and evaporation of about 1000 mm (Linacre and Hobbs, 1977). It had a uniform slope of 8%. Superphosphate was applied at a rate of 400 kg ha-1 four weeks prior to the sowing of the soybeans, and an additional 100 kg ha-1 was applied at sowing. The experiment began in 1981, and consisted of two tillage treatments (Conventional Tillage—CT and No-till—NT) within a crop rotation consisting of rainfed summer soybean (Glycine max (L.) cv Manta) and a winter cereal of oats (Avena sativa). Each treatment was replicated 3 times and each replicate consisted of a field plot measuring 60 m x 20 m. Potassium fertiliser was applied in some years according to soil test requirements, at rates of up to 100 kg ha-1 K2O. Molybdenum was applied as a seed dressing. A four row no-till planter was used on both treatments.

column33: Nitro-chalk fertilizer
column38: The original sub-plot treatments were 0, 50, 100 and 150 kg Nrha as ‘Nitro-Chalk’ fertiliser per hectare. In 1975 the latter three rates were increased to 60, 120 and 180 kg N/ha, but the zero treatment was retained. The experiment was conducted under continuous barley (Hordeum Íulgare L.) (with 1 yr of oilseed rape (Brassica spp.) in 1988/1989) until 1992 but, due to weed control problems, no grain yield data were recorded for 1992. by 1974 couch grass could be controlled by use of the then newly developed herbicide glyphosate. The next major infestation occurred in 1988 when sterile brome (Bromus mollis) affected the nonploughed plots, especially the long-term zero tillage plots. Because of the delayed germination of this species, the infestation could not be controlled by herbicides alone and required the sowing of oilseed rape as a break crop in 1988/1989 to allow appropriate herbicide usage. In the last season of the experiment (1992), a serious outbreak of sterile brome again occurred on zero tillage plots which proved difficult to control as no suitable herbicide was yet available. Nevertheless, at the end of the experiment, the broad-leaved weed seed bank was smaller and contained fewer species under long-term zero tillage than under long-term conventional ploughing.

column33: urea + superphosphate + potasium chloride + pig manure
column38: This investigation was conducted at Sanxing Experimental Station (SES) on Chongming Island (31°41′20″N, 121°33′47″E, altitude ranging from 3.5–4.5 m), China, with a rice (Oryza sativa L.) – wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) cropping rotation system. The soil in the experimental field was estuarine alluvial soil, with 15.21 g·kg−1 soil organic matter, 0.94 g·kg−1 total N, 81.62 mg·kg−1 alkali-hydrolysable N, 53.53 mg·kg−1 available P, 109.35 mg·kg−1 available K, and pH 8.30. The straw returned in the wheat season was the rice straw harvested from the previous season (C/N = 53.11, in which the contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were 36.43%, 22.52%, and 18.69%, respectively). The straw returned in the rice season was the wheat straw harvested from the previous season (C/N = 81.72, in which the contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were 33.62%, 22.53%, and 18.45%, respectively). N, P and K were supplied through urea (N-46%), calcium superphosphate (P2O5–46%), and potassium chloride (K2O-60%). Organic fertilizer was decomposed pig manure. The contents of N, P, and K in the organic fertilizer were 10.52 mg·kg−1 N, 20.47 mg·kg−1 P2O5, and 15.13 mg·kg−1 K2O, respectively. The experiment began in October 2012 and included a total of nine treatments combining different tillage systems, fertilization types, and the presence/absence of straw return (Table 1). Each treatment included three replications and was set up in a single-factor random block design. Each plot was 40 m long and 6 m wide, with an area of 240 m2. The ridges between the plots and the irrigation/ drainage ditch ridges between the blocks were separated by plastic film. The chemical fertilizer application rates in the rice season were 225 kg·hm−2 N, 90 kg·hm−2 P2O5, and 90 kg·hm−2 K2O, and the application rates in the wheat season were 270 kg·hm−2 N, 60 kg·hm−2 P2O5, and 90 kg·hm−2 K2O. The application rate of organic fertilizer was 12,500 kg·hm−2 in both the rice and wheat seasons. Straw, organic fertilizer, P fertilizer, and K fertilizer as base fertilizers were applied once before planting in each crop season. The N fertilizer included two parts, base fertilizer and topdressing. To each plot, 60% of the N and all of the P, K and organic fertilizers were applied before sowing in the rice season. The remaining N was applied in two equal parts 20 and 60 days after sowing. In the wheat season, 60% of the N and all of the P, K and organic fertilizers were applied before sowing. The remaining N was applied in equal amounts 10, 30 and 60 days after sowing. Field management and pest control were performed according to the local management routines. The soil samples were collected in September 2012 before the start of the experiment. During the experiment, soil samples were collected in the topsoil (0–20 cm) and subsoil (20–40 cm) by a 5-cm-diameter corer in each plot after the wheat harvest (in June 2013, June 2014, and June 2015) and after the rice harvest (in November 2013, November 2014, and November 2015).

The soil in the experimental field was estuarine alluvial soil, with 15.21 g·kg−1 soil organic matter, 0.94 g·kg−1 total N, 81.62 mg·kg−1 alkali-hydrolysable N, 53.53 mg·kg−1 available P, 109.35 mg·kg−1 available K, and pH 8.30. The straw returned in the wheat season was the rice straw harvested from the previous season (C/N = 53.11, in which the contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were 36.43%, 22.52%, and 18.69%, respectively). The straw returned in the rice season was the wheat straw harvested from the previous season (C/N = 81.72, in which the contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were 33.62%, 22.53%, and 18.45%, respectively). N, P and K were supplied through urea (N-46%), calcium superphosphate (P2O5–46%), and potassium chloride (K2O-60%). Organic fertilizer was decomposed pig manure. The contents of N, P, and K in the organic fertilizer were 10.52 mg·kg−1 N, 20.47 mg·kg−1 P2O5, and 15.13 mg·kg−1 K2O, respectively. The experiment began in October 2012 and included a total of nine treatments combining different tillage systems, fertilization types, and the presence/absence of straw return (Table 1). Each treatment included three replications and was set up in a single-factor random block design. Each plot was 40 m long and 6 m wide, with an area of 240 m2. The ridges between the plots and the irrigation/ drainage ditch ridges between the blocks were separated by plastic film. The chemical fertilizer application rates in the rice season were 225 kg·hm−2 N, 90 kg·hm−2 P2O5, and 90 kg·hm−2 K2O, and the application rates in the wheat season were 270 kg·hm−2 N, 60 kg·hm−2 P2O5, and 90 kg·hm−2 K2O. The application rate of organic fertilizer was 12,500 kg·hm−2 in both the rice and wheat seasons. Straw, organic fertilizer, P fertilizer, and K fertilizer as base fertilizers were applied once before planting in each crop season. The N fertilizer included two parts, base fertilizer and topdressing. To each plot, 60% of the N and all of the P, K and organic fertilizers were applied before sowing in the rice season. The remaining N was applied in two equal parts 20 and 60 days after sowing. In the wheat season, 60% of the N and all of the P, K and organic fertilizers were applied before sowing. The remaining N was applied in equal amounts 10, 30 and 60 days after sowing. Field management and pest control were performed according to the local management routines. The soil samples were collected in September 2012 before the start of the experiment. During the experiment, soil samples were collected in the topsoil (0–20 cm) and subsoil (20–40 cm) by a 5-cm-diameter corer in each plot after the wheat harvest (in June 2013, June 2014, and June 2015) and after the rice harvest (in November 2013, November 2014, and November 2015).

column33: urea + 15-20 kg P ha-1 as monoammonium phosphate
column38: The soil, a Hythe clay loam (Odynsky et al. 1961), is a Gray Luvisol (a fine montmorollinitic, frigid Mollic Cryoboralf in the USDA soil taxonomy). The surface (0–15 cm) soil pH (in 0.01 M CaCl2) was 5.1 at initiation of the study, however, 0.02 M CaCl2-soluble Al [determined according to Webber et al. (1977)] was <0.05 mg L–1. The organic C concentration was 32 g kg–1, and base saturation was 82%. Annual temperature and precipitation of the area average 2°C and 452 mm, respectively. Moisture deficit is usually the growth-limiting factor for the region. The experiment started in 1991 as a 2 ×2 ×2 factorial, randomized complete block design with four replications to study the effect of lime (0 vs. 7.5 Mg ha–1) and tillage practices (NT vs. CT) on crop production under two crop rotations (pea-barley-barley vs. canola-barley-barley). Weeds in NT plots were killed with glyphosate (N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine) prior to seeding. In 1997, the crop rotations were changed to a single rotation comprising a pea-barley-canola sequence. This entailed aligning the three new subplots (each 5 m by 18 m) that now comprised the three crop phases of the new rotation across the previous six subplots. This was the straw removed (–straw) vs. straw retained (+straw) comparison made possible by reducing the replications per treatment to two. Each spring barley received 22.5 kg N ha–1 and canola 65 to 68 kg N ha–1. Monoammonium phosphate was placed with the seed at a rate of 15 to 20 kg P ha–1. The balance of the N fertilizer was banded below and beside the seed row as urea. Sulphur was applied to pea and canola at 11 to 17 kg S ha–1 as potassium sulphate. Field pea was inoculated with Rhizobium in a granular-based carrier, and received no N other than that co-applied in ammonium phosphate fertilizer.

column33: urea + PCU
column38: Two field experiments were conducted near Beaverlodge (2004–2007), Alberta (55o 11'N, 119o 32'W), and Star City (2004–2006), Saskatchewan (52o 81'N, 104o 51'W), on Dark Gray Luvisolic soils (Typic Cryoboralf). At Beaverlodge, the soil had a loam to clay loam texture, a pH of 5.8, and contained 29 g organic C kg-1 and 3.1 g total N kg-1 soil in the top 15 cm. At Star City, the soil was a clay loam, had a pH of 6.3, and contained 38 g organic C kg-1 and 3.0 g total N kg-1 soil in the top 15 cm. For this site, the mean annual precipitation is 425 mm and growing season (May–August) precipitation is 244 mm. The mean annual and growing season precipitations at Beaverlodge are 468 and 247 mm, respectively. Tillage systems (CT and NT) were assigned to the main plots; combinations of type of N fertilizer (urea and PCU), time of application (spring-banded [SB] or fall-banded [FB]), and N rates (0–90 kg N ha-1) were applied to the subplots. Nitrogen application rates were: 0, 0.5x 1.0x and 1.5x where the base rate x = 60 kg Nha-1 at Star City for all three experimental years, and at Beaverlodge, x = 60 kg N ha-1 in 2004 and 2007, 50 kg N ha-1 in 2005 and 55 kg N ha-1 in 2006. At Star City, wheat was grown in 2004, canola in 2005, barley in 2006; at Beaverlodge, barley was grown in 2004 and 2007, canola in 2005, and wheat in 2006.

The field studies were conducted from 1987 to 1990 at the Bradford AgronomyR esearch Farm near Columbia and the Greenley Memorial Farm near Novelty, MO. At the Columbia site, the soil is a somewhat poorly drained Mexico silt loam (fine, montmorillonitic, mesic Mollic Endoaqualf); at the Novelty site, it is a poorly drained Putnam silt loam( fine, montmorillonitic, mesic Vertic Albaqualf). Both are typical claypan soils of central and northeast Missouri. The studies at both sites were sprinkler irrigated. Phosphorus and potassium applications were based on soil tests and University of Missouri recommendations to maintain adequate nonlimiting corn production. Thee experiment design was a split-split plot arranged within a randomized completeb lock. Whole plots were tillage system (chisel-disk and no-till). Subplot treatments were crop rotation (continuous corn and corn following soybean). Sub-subplots were N rates (0, 67, 135, 202, and 269 kg ha-1). The sub-subplot dimensions were 3 by 12 m and consisted of four rows spaced 76 cm apart. Treatments were replicated four times and were applied to the same plots each year. The study was established in 1987. In 1986, both sites were cropped to soybean using conventional tillage. Consequently, the no-till blocks and all rotations were begun in 1987, and by 1988 the continuous corn blocks were actually second-year corn and the no-till blocks were in their second year of no-till cropping. Yield and other measurement are reported for 1988 through 1990. In 1990, the Columbia site experienced excessive rainfall during the planting season. After two planting attempts failed to establish an adequates tand, the Columbia site was abandoned. For the chisel-disk tillage treatment, all tillage was done in April, prior to application of N treatments. Primary tillage was done with a chisel to a depth of 15 cm, and secondary tillage consisted of one pass with a tandem disk. Both soybean and corn blocks were maintained each year for the corn-soybean rotation, so that each year corn was grown on ground that had been cropped to soybean the year prior and to corn 2 yr prior. Pioneer 3377 corn hybrid was planted with a double-disk planter. In 1989 and 1990, starter fertilizer (5.6 kg N ha-1 and 8.4 kg ha-1 P) was applied 5 cm to the side and 5 cm below the seed with a ripple coulter mounted ahead of the double-disk opener. The N applied in the starter was not considered part of the treatment N. Seeding rates (kernels ha-1) were 59 300 in 1988, 71 600 in 1989 and 79 100 in 1990. Planting dates varied from 24 April to 11 May. The only exception was the Novelty 1990 location, where planting was delayed until 30 May because of wet weather. In most cases, the N treatments were applied no more than 7 d prior to planting. At the Columbia site in 1988, plots were replanted due to poor stand establishment from the first planting. In that case, nearly a month separated the N application and the planting date. The N source was anhydrous NH3 in 1987 and 1988. Nitrogen source was changed to knife injected UAN so lution in 1989 and 1990. The change was for safety and convenience of application, with the assumptionth at N source had no bearing on rotation and tillage effects, provided the N was injected. column33: 100 kg ha-1 basal NPK fertilizer (23-21-0 + 4S)
column38: A long-term CA trial was established in 2007 at Chitedze Research Station (CRS), Malawi (latitude -13.9738°, longitude 33.6527°, altitude 1147 m.a.s.l.) on a sandy clay loam soil (Chromic Luvisol, for more details see Table 1) where rainfed cropping is standard practice. The site was under maize (Zea mays L.)- pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan (L.) Millsp.) trials prior to cropping season 2005/2006. In cropping season 2006/2007 it was planted to a uniform fertilized maize crop, before it was converted into the conservation agriculture long-term trial in 2007. The experiment consisted of eight management treatment plots in a randomized complete block design with four replications. Plots were 24m×12.75 m, accommodating 18 rows of maize. The management treatments manipulated with rainout shelters in this study were: 1) CP (conventional control plot): Maize was planted as a continuous monocrop in a ridge and furrow system prepared by hand hoes with no surface crop residues (Fig. A.1A in Supplementary material); 2) NT (no-tillage, crop residue mulching and maize monoculture): Maize was direct-seeded as a continuous monocrop using dibble sticks with crop residues retained from the previous season (Fig. A.1B in Supplementary material); 3) CArot (no-tillage, crop residue retention and crop rotation): Maize was direct-seeded as a continuous monocrop using dibble sticks with crop residues retained from the previous season. Maize rotated with cowpea, both phases of the rotation alternated annually across two plots in each replicate block (Fig. A.1C in Supplementary material); and 4) CAint (no-tillage, crop residue retention and intercropping): Maize and cowpea were direct-seeded using dibble sticks with crop residues retained from the previous season. The cowpea intercrop was seeded between maize rows (Fig. A.1D in Supplementary material).   Legumes in rotation were cowpea, variety Sudan, planted at one seed per station in rows spaced at 75 cm with stations spaced at 10 cm (target population 133,333 plants ha−1). Groundnuts, ICRISAT variety CG 7, were planted one seed per station in rows spaced at 37.5 cm with stations spaced at 15 cm (177,777 plants ha−1). The cowpea variety Sudan, was also planted in the intercropped treatment in 75 cm rows between maize lines, two seed per station, and 50 cm between stations (53,333 plants ha−1). Weeds were removed three times per season across all treatments using shallow hoeing or hand removal. No herbicides were applied on the trial in both cropping seasons. The insecticides, Cypermethrin 200EC and Dimethoate, were applied using knapsack sprayers to control aphid outbreaks on cowpeas only, no other chemicals were sprayed during in the duration of the trial. All treatments received top-dressings of 100 kg ha−1 basal N-P-K fertilizer (23-21-0+4S) approximately two weeks after planting and 100 kg ha−1 urea approximately five weeks after planting based on the recommended fertilizer rate for Malawi. As per treatment, all crop residues were retained and spread over the surface of experimental treatments at the end of the growing season. They were re-distributed before planting as some had been moved by strong winds during the dry winter season.

In cropping season 2006/2007 it was planted to a uniform fertilized maize crop, before it was converted into the conservation agriculture long-term trial in 2007. The experiment consisted of eight management treatment plots in a randomized complete block design with four replications. Plots were 24m×12.75 m, accommodating 18 rows of maize. The management treatments manipulated with rainout shelters in this study were: 1) CP (conventional control plot): Maize was planted as a continuous monocrop in a ridge and furrow system prepared by hand hoes with no surface crop residues (Fig. A.1A in Supplementary material); 2) NT (no-tillage, crop residue mulching and maize monoculture): Maize was direct-seeded as a continuous monocrop using dibble sticks with crop residues retained from the previous season (Fig. A.1B in Supplementary material); 3) CArot (no-tillage, crop residue retention and crop rotation): Maize was direct-seeded as a continuous monocrop using dibble sticks with crop residues retained from the previous season. The cowpea intercrop was seeded between maize rows (Fig. A.1D in Supplementary material).   Legumes in rotation were cowpea, variety Sudan, planted at one seed per station in rows spaced at 75 cm with stations spaced at 10 cm (target population 133,333 plants ha−1). Groundnuts, ICRISAT variety CG 7, were planted one seed per station in rows spaced at 37.5 cm with stations spaced at 15 cm (177,777 plants ha−1). The cowpea variety Sudan, was also planted in the intercropped treatment in 75 cm rows between maize lines, two seed per station, and 50 cm between stations (53,333 plants ha−1). Weeds were removed three times per season across all treatments using shallow hoeing or hand removal. No herbicides were applied on the trial in both cropping seasons. The insecticides, Cypermethrin 200EC and Dimethoate, were applied using knapsack sprayers to control aphid outbreaks on cowpeas only, no other chemicals were sprayed during in the duration of the trial. As per treatment, all crop residues were retained and spread over the surface of experimental treatments at the end of the growing season. They were re-distributed before planting as some had been moved by strong winds during the dry winter season.

column5: Clarke County (University of Georgia Horseshoe Bend LTREB Agroecosystem)
column33: N + 49 kg P ha-1 + 107 kg K ha-1
column38: The area selected for the cropping systems was last cultivated in 1966, and prior to May 1978 was in old-field vegetation (Solidago canadensis L., Rubus spp., Ambrosia artemisiifolia L., and Andropogon spp.) typical of a 12-year fallow. Prior to 1965, the majority of HSB was pasture.  The soil belongs to the Hiwassee series and is a typic Rhodudult, It is a well-drained sandy~clay loam. This area is considered to be prime agricultural land with moderately high fertility relative to the southern Piedmont. Both treatments received 47 kg N/ha, 49 kg P/ha and 107 kg K/ha granular fertilizer, which was broadcast before planting. Fertilizer recommendations were made by the University of Georgia Extension Service. Conventional tillage plots were disk plowed to a depth of 18 cm and then drag harrowed prior to planting. Funk's 522 grain sorghum was planted in 76 cm rows (15 kg of seeds/ha) using a coulter no-tillage planter. The sorghum was seeded directly into the soft without any seedbed preparation. Atrazine (5 1 active ingredient/ha) was applied at the time of planting for weed control. Glyphosate (8 1 active ingredient/ha) was used as a post-emergence herbicide. On August 20, the sorghum was side-dressed with ammonium nitrate (84 kg N/ha). Conventional and no-tillage plots were subjected to the same fertilizer and herbicide applications throughout the study. The old field had less litter than the no-tillage systems which reflects higher net primary production and subsequently larger amounts of plant residues in the latter systems. The large litter component in notillage and old-field treatments probably contributed to lower nitrate-- ammonium ratios in these systems compared to conventional systems, presumably, in part, because heterotrophic bacteria in the surface litter competed with the nitrifying bacteria for ammonium. Plant residue was left on the surface in no-tillage (NT) plots and incorporated into the soil in conventional tillage (CT) plots. On 30 April 1979, glyphosate (6 1 active ingredient/ha) was applied as a contact herbicide. The rye was mowed on 16 May. On 12 June, sorghum was again planted. Cultural procedures for summer 1979 and winter 1980 were basically the same as those used in 1978 and 1979. After harvest, rye was planted on 20 November.

column33: N + 105 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 45 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The tillage treatments included reduced tillage, in which a 10–15-cm-high wheat stubble was left when the winter wheat was harvested, and the wheat straw was not returned to the plots after the wheat was threshed. With no tillage, a 30-cm-high wheat stubble was left at harvest, and the wheat straw was returned to the plots. For subsoil tillage (ST), a 25–30-cm-high wheat stubble was left at harvest, and the wheat straw was returned to the plots. With conventional tillage, a 5–6-cm wheat stubble was left at harvest, but the wheat straw was not returned to the plots. The time of planted and harvested is different from 1999 to 2005, which may be attributed to the rainfall and temperature in different years. Every year, the same quantity chemical fertilizer (150 kg ha-1 N, 105 kg ha-1 P2O5, and 45 kg ha-1 K2O) was applied to the top 20 cm before planting. A chemical herbicide was used to control weeds during the summer fallow, and weeds were hand-hoed during the growing period. Winter wheat (T. aestivum L. ‘‘Yumai 48’’) was planted on 27 September in 1999, 30 September in 2000, 29 September in 2001, 25 September in 2002, 5 October in 2003, 2 October in 2004, and 1 October in 2005, respectively. The winter wheat was planted at 120 kg ha-1 at a fixed seeding rate .The winter wheat was harvested 28 May in 2000, 27 May in 2001, 2 June in 2002, 5 June in 2003, 30 May in 2004, and 25 May in 2005, respectively.

column33: ammonium nitrate + 70 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 105 kg K2O ha-1
column38: Field tests were carried out in 2013 and 2014 in the Agricultural Experimental Station of Osiny, belonging to the Institute of Soil Science and Plant Cultivation – State Research Institute in Puławy. The experiment was established using the method of random blocks, in three replications, on soil belonging to the good wheat complex, quality class II and III b. The pseudobacterial soil was characterized by neutral pH (pHKCl 6.77), and contained 19.3 mg P2O5 and 16.3 mg K2O in 100 g of soil. In plough cultivation after harvesting the forecrop, straw was crushed, and ploughing to a depth of 10 cm with a disc aggregate, and ploughing to a depth of 20-22 cm, were performed. The sowing density of common wheat grains of Kandela cultivar and SMH 87 durum wheat was respectively: 5,5 and 6,5 mln・ha-1. Nitrogen fertilization in the form of ammonium nitrate was applied at a dose of 50 kg N・ha-1 before sowing, 50 kg N・ha-1 in the stem formation stage, and 30 kg N・ha-1 in the earing stage. Phosphorus and potassium fertilization was applied in spring before wheat sowing at the rates of 70 kg P2O5 ha-1 and 105 kg K2O ha-1, respectively. The plot area for harvesting was 45 m2.

column33: N + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 90 kg K2O ha-1
column38: After the tillage, wheat was sown on 20 September in the WWC system and MWR system, whereas a scheduled fallow lasted several months in SMC, until the seeding date of 23 April 2008. The soils contain 27% clay, 39% silt, and 34% sand and have weak cohesion, good waterstorage capacity and negligible drainage below 2 m. In 2007, one season of maize was cultivated in the experimental field using CT and no fertilizer, and after the harvest, the experiment commenced with the scheduled first tillage. The drill also banded full rate chemical fertilizers 5 cm below the seeds, while in CT the one-time application of a full amount of fertilizers was conducted by broadcast before sowing. The wheat harvesting was performed in the first fortnight of the following June, followed by one scheduled tillage. Fertilizers were applied after seeding: for all treatments, fertilizers at full rate were broadcasted evenly to corresponding plots before the first rainfall. The harvest of maize was performed in the first fortnight of September, followed by the scheduled tillage. To compare the fertilizer use efficiency and productivity of different tillage and cropping systems, all tillage and cropping systems had the same chemical fertilizer application rate: 150 kg N, 120 kg P2O5, and 90 kg K2O ha−1. To coincide with the local conventional practice, plots under CT applied the method of seeding following a 0–10-cm rotary tillage. To minimize the field surface disturbance and retain the straw mulch, the NT seeding method was used in the ST and NT plots. For winter wheat, the conventional fertilization by broadcast before rotary tillage and sowing aimed to incorporate the fertilizers into soils under CT treatment, similar to the method in NT and ST with respect to the fertilization time and depth. For all treatments, weeds were controlled by spraying chemical herbicides before crop emergence and at the initial fallow stage, as well as by hand one to two times in the growth season based on visual estimates of weed populations.

column33: N + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 90 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The field experiment was carried out at the Heyang Dryland Agricultural Research Station (latitude 35°19′N; longitude 106°04′E; altitude 877 m) in the southeast Loess Plateau, Heyang County, Shaanxi Province, China. The climate is semiarid and continental monsoon with mean air temperature, aridity index and evaporation of 11.5 °C, 1.5 and 1832.8 mm, respectively. The annual average sunshine duration is 2528.3 h with a frost-free period of 180–190 days. The 30- year average annual precipitation is 527 mm, concentrated from July to September. The experimental fields are level, and the typical dark loessal soil, classified as Chromic Cambisol according to the FAO/UNESCO Soil Classification, with middle loam texture (27% clay, 39% silt, and 34% sand). The field study was conducted in a winter wheat continuous cropping system. The experimental design was a split-plot design with three replications, where fertilizer application rates of recommended (150 kg N, 120 kg P2O5 [52.4 kg P], and 90 kg K2O [74.7 kg K] ha−1, RF), conventional (255 kg N, 180 kg P2O5 [78.6 kg P] ha−1, CF), and low amounts (75 kg N, 60 kg P2O5 [26.2 kg P], and 45 kg K2O [37.3 kg K] ha−1, LF) were assigned to the main plots, and tillage treatments (CT, NT, and ST) were assigned to the subplots. Each subplot measured 22.5m in length and 5m in width with a 60-cm interval between adjacent plots. Urea, ammonium phosphate and potassium sulfate were employed for the application of NPK fertilizer, respectively. There were no other nutrients applied in this experiment. Tillage was performed following the previous wheat harvest in mid to late June. For CT practice, the soil was tilled to a depth of 20–25 cm accompanied by incorporation of wheat straw using a moldboard plow, and rotary tillage was applied before the sowing stage. For ST practice, the soil was tilled to a depth of 30–35 cm with 60-cm intervals using a subsoiling chisel with adjustable wings, which allowed less soil disturbance under it than in CT. For NT practice, soil disturbance was avoided until sowing. The straw was retained evenly on the soil surface as mulch after harvest under NT and ST, whereas the soil surface under CT lay bare in the fallow period. A common commercial wheat variety, Jinmai 47, was sown in late September, using a fixed seed rate of 150 kg ha−1 and row spacing of 20 cm. Weeds were controlled by spraying chemical herbicides after tillage and before crop emergence for all treatments, as well as manually during the growth season based on visual estimates of weed populations. Other management practices were the same for all plots except for the treatment practices.   Prior to the research, winter wheat was cropped annually at this site under CF and CT practice, with the crop residue removed every year after harvest.

column33: 38 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 75 kg K2O ha-1
column38: A 7-year field study was established at the Wenxi Dryland Wheat Agriculture Station (35°20′N, 111°17′E), Shanxi Province of China between 2009 and 2015. The site represents the typical semiarid climate of Northeast Loess Plateau. Winter wheat is staple crop for the people lived in this area, which was usually planted in the early October. Rainfed agriculture is popular owing to scarce rainfall and unavailable irrigation condition. More than 60% rainfall fell in the fallow season, i.e. July to September. This unmatched rainfall distribution regarding to crop water consumption is main limiting factor for wheat production in this area. In this experiment, three different tillage methods in fallow season were designed as: 1) deep ploughing to 25–30 cm; 2) deep subsoiling to 30–40 cm and 3) no tillage in fallow season as control. In each year, previous wheat was harvesting in end of June. Thereafter, tall stubble (20–30 cm) was remained to reduce water evaporation and increase soil organic carbon for next season. All treatments were arranged in a randomized, complete block design with three replicates in each experimental season. Each plot was 50m long and 6m wide consisting of 30 rows of wheat spaced 0.2m for all treatments. Before sowing, pure nitrogen, P2O5 and K2O were applied at the rate of 150, 38 and 75 kg ha−1 respectively.  All plants were machine harvested in late June. During whole growing season, weed was well controlled by hand and no irrigation was applied in each experimental year.

column33: N + 50 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 40 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The field experiments were conducted under natural weed infestations in maize (rainy season)-wheat (winter) cropping system in 2010–11 and 2011–12 at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi. Soil (Inceptisol) was a sandy loam with pH 7.9 and organic carbon 0.52%, and medium available P (18.4 kg ha−1) and available K (191.6 kg ha−1) and low available N (272.6 kg ha−1). The climate of the experimental field is semi-arid, sub-tropical with hot and dry summers and cold winters. annual rainfall, 80% is received during July–September, and rest is received during December to February. Pan evaporation varies from 3.5 to 13.5mmd−1 and reference evapo-transpiration from 9 to 15mmd−1. The experimental site had even topography and was irrigated with a good drainage system. In maize, eight weed control/herbicide treatments (Table 1) were laid out in a randomized complete block design with three replications. These treatments were considered as main plots during the winter in wheat crop. No herbicides were applied during winter in wheat in the six (T2–T7) herbicide-treated/brown manuring plots, but their residual/carry-over effects were evaluated in combinations with three sub-plot treatments, namely, conventional tillage (CT), zero tillage (ZT) with 100% maize residue (R) retention (ZT+R), and ZT without residue (ZT−R), imposed in each main plot. The experiment was laid out in a split plot design. In both maize and wheat crops, weeds were allowed to grow with crops throughout the crop-growing period in unweeded control (UWC) plots. Weeds were removed manually on their emergence from the weed-free control (WFC) plots. The CT plots in maize and wheat had no crop residue retention/incorporation and were ploughed once by a tractordrawn disc plough followed by three passes with a harrow to have a pulverized soil. Land was leveled after each ploughing by a soil leveler. In wheat, the plots were not ploughed under the ZT treatments. The whole residue of previous maize crop was retained on the ZT+R plots, whereas removed from the ZT−R plots. For brown manuring, Sesbania seed @10 kg ha−1 was uniformly broadcast over the entire plot at the time of sowing of maize. 2,4-D @ 0.75 kg a.i. ha−1 was applied at 25 DAS for killing Sesbania plants, which on gradual drying up served as mulch for initial 35–40 DAS. Mustard residue @ 5 Mg ha−1 was retained on soil one day after atrazine application in the atrazine+ mustard residue treatment. The pre-emergence application of tank-mixture of atrazine (0.75 kg a.i. ha−1)+pendimethalin (0.75 kg a.i. ha−1) is recommended for weed control in maize in India. It was applied singly and in combination with KNO3 (6%w v−1), the concentration was optimized in earlier studies (Authors’ observation). KNO3 was applied with 400 L ha−1 water before the application of the tank-mixture of pendimethalin+imazethapyr. For the tank-mixtures treatments, partner herbicides at required quantities were mixed in the spray-tank before application. All herbicides were applied with 400 L ha−1 water using a knapsack sprayer fitted with a flat fan nozzle (Sukun Agencies India, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India). The plot size was 10.0m×5.0m in maize. In wheat, the main and sub-plot sizes were 10.0m×5.0m and 5.0m×3.0 m, respectively. A recommended dose of 120 kg N, 60 kg P2O5 and 40 kg K2O per ha in the form of urea, single superphosphate and muriate of potash, respectively was applied to both crops. Half dose of N and full dose of P and K were applied at sowing, and the remaining N was top-dressed after irrigation in equal amounts at 30 and 60 DAS of maize; and at 25 (crown root initiation/CRI) and 60 (flowering) DAS of wheat. No fungicide, but insecticide carbofuran 3G @ 25 kg ha−1 was used to control stem borer and shoot fly in maize.

column38: Kulumsa is located on a clay soil (an intergrade between a eutric Nitisol and a luvic Phaoezem), while the Asasa soil is a clay loam (calcic Chernozem). The mechanized trial consisted of 12 treatments comprising the complete factorial combination of: (a) three levels of post-harvest SM—stubble burning, partial stubble removal (50%), and complete retention of stubble; (b) two levels of tillage—zero tillage (ZT) and conventional tillage (CT) at Kulumsa, and minimum. In the mechanized trials, CT consisted of one pass with a tractor-drawn disc plow followed by two passes with a disc harrow during the “short rains” fallow period in order to maximize weed control. For the MT and ZT treatments, chemical fallow was substituted for tillage during the “short rains” period each year: glyphosate was applied at 720 g active ingredient (a.i.) per hectare as required during the “short rains” season to prevent weeds from attaining a height of 20 cm with a maximum of two applications per season. Partial stubble removal simulated grazing by removing 50% of post-harvest crop stubble. Thus, approximately 500 kg ha−1 of stubble remained on the soil surface at sowing time. Stubble burning was carried out during late January each year before the “short rains” began. Plots with complete stubble retention were left undisturbed until spraying or tillage operations began; more than 2 t ha−1 of stubble remained on the soil surface at sowing time. two levels of CS—continuous wheat and 1 year of faba bean (Vicia faba) followed by 2 years of wheat. Over the trial period (1992–2000), sowing dates ranged from 11 June to 19 June at Asasa and from 26 June to 7 July at Kulumsa. Due to the risk of damage by spray drift, hand weeding was used to control weeds during 1992, 1995, and 1998 when both wheat and faba bean were sown. During 1993, 1994, 1996, 1997, 1999 and 2000, when all plots were sown to wheat, weed control entailed a post-emergence spray application of a tank mix of fenoxaprop-P-ethyl + fluroxypyr + MCPA at 0.069 + 0.175 + 1.0 kg a.i. ha−1, respectively. Thus, over the trial duration, the bread wheat cultivars Enkoy (1992–1993), Mitike (1994), and Qubsa (1995–2000) were sown using a seed rate of 150 kg ha−1. From 1992 to 1994, bread wheat received a basal N application of 41 kg ha−1 at Kulumsa and 18 kg ha−1 at Asasa. From 1995 to 2000, newly recommended fertilizer rates were implemented, and bread wheat received a basal N application of 82 kg ha−1 at Kulumsa and 41 kg ha−1 at Asasa. During 1992, 1995, and 1998, faba bean cultivar CS20DK was sown using a seed rate of 200 kg ha−1; for faba bean, basal N was applied at the rate of 18 kg ha−1 at both Kulumsa and Asasa. Both crops received a basal application of 20 kg P ha−1 each year. SM treatments were initiated in main plots of 20m × 20 m, tillage in sub-plots of 10m × 20 m, and CS in sub–sub-plots of 5m × 20m in 1992. All treatments were applied to permanent plots maintained over the trial duration.

column24: direct planted into the chopped residues of previous crop
column38: The soil was a fine-loamy, mixed, mesic Ultic Haplustalf, (Soil Survey Staff, 1996), previously under processing tomato. The main factor was the soil management system (conventional tillage vs no-tillage, hereafter indicated as CT and NT, respectively), with the rate of applied nitrogen (0, 250 and 300 kg N ha-1 year-1) as the secondary factor, for a total of 24 sub-plots. Results are shown in the way of N mixed. Each sub-plot was 4.5 m wide and 12 m long. The fertilizer was top dressed twice, in equal quantities. The first application was immediately after plant emergence with 0, 125 and 150 kg N ha-1, as Ca(NO3)2 (15.5% N); the second application was at the V6-V8 stage. The NT plots were treated with Glyphosate before maize planting. In all years, the hybrid PR34N43, FAO 500 (Pioneer Hi-Bred Italia) was used, with a row spacing of 70 cm. Seed density was 9.2 and 8.9 seeds m-2 for NT and CT, respectively. When necessary, maize crop has been irrigated by flood technique. During 2004 rainfall was near normal up to the first ten days of May (Tab. 2), then a lack of rainfall occurred during the growing season (-26%, as compared with the 20-yr average), reducing yields despite the three irrigations.

column33: N + 70 kg P ha-1 + 100 kg K ha-1
column38: A field experiment (winter wheat and summer maize rotation) was initiated in October 2009 at the China Agricultural University Experimental Station in Huantai County, Shandong Province (36°58′ N, 117°59′ E). In this region the annual mean air temperature is 13.4 °C and the annual precipitation is 584 mm. The soil is classified as Aquic Inceptisol, consisting of 38% clay (< 0.002 mm), 32% (0.002–0.02mm) silt and 30% (0.02–2 mm) sand. The bulk density is 1.4 g cm−3 and pH is 7.7 (water/soil=2.5/1). Soil properties in October 2009 were: 10.0 g kg−1 soil organic carbon, 1.1 g kg−1 total N, 13 mgkg−1 available P and 111 mg kg−1 available K. The field experiment is a 2×2 × 3 factorial experiment, with two types of tillage (CT and NT), two types of straw management (SI and SR) and three fertilizer N rates (control without N fertilization [0 kg N ha−1 yr−1, control (CK)], optimized N fertilization [450 kg N ha−1 yr−1, OPT] and local conventional N fertilization [690 kg N ha−1 yr−1, conventional N fertilization (CON)]. The triple replicated treatment plots (6m×11 m) were randomly arranged. Winter wheat (var. Luyuan 502) was sown on 5 October and 10 October in the 1st (2013–2014) and 2nd (2014–2015) wheat seasons, respectively, and harvested on 5 June 2014 and 10 June 2015, respectively. Summer maize (var. Zhengdan 958) was inter-crop sown 2 weeks before the wheat harvest and harvested at the end of September in 2014 and 2015. For all N-fertilized treatments, N fertilizer was broadcast at a ratio of 6:4 as basal fertilizer and at top-dressing stage in both the wheat and maize seasons. Phosphorous (70 kg P ha−1) and potassium fertilizers (100 kg K ha−1) were also applied as basal fertilizer in each crop season. For SI treatment, straw was pulverized (2–5 cm for wheat straw and 5–10 cm for maize straw) and spread on the soil surface by a harvester without disturbing the soil. For SR treatment, wheat and maize were manually harvested and straw was also removed manually. Seeding and fertilization took place simultaneously using a seeding machine, and the field immediately received 75mm of irrigation. In addition to irrigation during seeding, during the wheat season the field received 75mm irrigation four times in 2013–2014 and twice in 2014–2015. During the maize season the field was irrigated twice (75mm each time) in 2014 and 2015. Herbicide was applied in all treatments according to the practice of local farmers.

column33: ammonium nitrate
column38: This study showed that herbicides could be used to control weeds in NT as effectively as CT. In 1962, a field study was established at the experimental site to assess various weed control strategies in a 3-yr winter wheat–sorghum–fallow (WSF) rotation. Grain sorghum was grown in the rotation following winter wheat from 1962 to 1992, and corn was substituted for grain sorghum from 1993 to 2003. Both tillage treatments received identical annual N fertilizer inputs from 1962 to 1989 before planting wheat and sorghum as ammonium nitrate at an average annual rate of 48 kg N ha21. Fertilizer application rates were based on typical rates adopted by producers using the WS/CF system. The NT treatment used herbicides as the primary weed management strategy and has not been tilled since 1962. In 1989, the CT treatment was converted to NT (called the CT to NT treatment). The original NTweed management regime was maintained continuously in the NT treatments from 1962 to 2003. Crop residues were not removed from the plots. In general, numerous studies have demonstrated that increased crop yields from NT were attributed to greater soil moisture storage due to residue cover in cropping systems in arid and semiarid environments

column33: anhydrous ammonia
column38: Two experimental sites were established in the fall of 2000, one near Stillwater, OK at the Agronomy Research Station (Easpur loam fineloamy, mixed, superactive, thermic Fluventic Haplustoll), and one in Lahoma, OK at the North-Central Oklahoma Research Station (Grant silt loam fine-silty, mixed, thermic Udic Argiustoll). Individual plots measured 3.0x4.6 m. Anhydrous ammonia (82-0-0) was applied at rates of 0, 61, 123, and 185 kg N ha-1 using two different methods of injection. At the Lahoma site, a seeding rate of 95 kg ha-1 was planted the initial year and increased to 125 kg ha-1 the second year and was sustained through the third and fourth years in 19 cm rows within wheat stubble from the previous year as well as conventionally worked ground. Triple super phosphate (0-46-0) was applied pre-plant at a rate of 39 kg P ha-1 the first two years at Lahoma to alleviate possible phosphorous deficiencies. However, starting in 2002 at both locations, triple super phosphate was banded with the seed at a rate of 12 kg P ha-1. At the Efaw site, a seeding rate of 125 kg ha-1 was planted in 15 cm rows in grain sorghum stubble from the previous summer as well as conventionally worked ground the first two years, but beginning in 2002 the same seeding rate was planted in 18 cm rows within wheat stubble from the previous year as well as conventionally worked ground. In this case, conventional tillage at both sites consisted of disking throughout the summer, and preparing the seedbed with a field cultivator. Wheat residue cover was measured before and after AA applications on the no-till starting in 2002, using a modified, line-intercept method (Morrison et al., 1997) as a means of determining residue disturbance (residue disturbance = residue cover (%) before AA - residue cover (%) after AA) by AA application method.

column5: Saskatchewan, Swift Current (clay site, 50 km north of Swift Current)
column33: ammonium nitrate + 20 kg P2O5 ha-1 as monoammonium phosphate
column38: On the silt loam, the five treatments were spring wheat ( Triticum aestivum L. ) grown on three summer fallow tillage systems (conventional, minimum, and zero tillage (i.e. chemical fallow)), and two continuous crop systems, one with preseeding tillage (conventional) and the other without preseeding tillage (zero tillage ). Fall applications of 2,4-D ester (all treatments) or chlorsulfuron (minimum and zero-tillage fallow) were used each fall to control winter annual weeds such as flixweed (Descuraina sophia L. Webb ) and stinkweed ( Thlaspi arvense L.). Weed control on minimum and zero-tillage fallow plots was achieved with broad-spectrum herbicide tank-mixes which included herbicides such as glyphosate, dicamba, or 2,4-D alone or in combination as required, with a first application in mid to late June. A single herbicide application with residual herbicides such as chlorsulfuron and dicamba in combination with glyphosate sufficed for weed control in zero-tillage fallow. Broadcast fertilizer. Spring wheat (cv. 'Canuck' or 'Leader') was sown at a rate of 67 kg haon the silt loam and clay, while durum wheat (Triticum turgidum L. cv. 'Wakooma' ) was sown at a rate of 101 kg ha- 1 on the sandy loam. All tillage treatments received 20 kg ha-I P205 (monoammonium phosphate) placed with the seed. N fertilizer amendments (ammonium nitrate), based on soil nitrate levels measured in the upper 0.60 m of the soil in the fall and regional soil test recommendations, were applied with the seed in 1984 and broadcast applied prior to seedbed preparation or seeding in all other years. The average rate of N fertilizer applied to wheat grown continuously was 43, 37, and 33 kg ha- 1 on the silt loam, clay, and sandy loam soils, respectively. Wheat grown on fallow received an average N rate of 22 kg ha -1. In late October each year, crop residues in 1 m 2 frames were collected and surface soil taken with a spade to approximately 50 mm depth to determine wind erodibility index (% surface aggregate < 0.84 mm) by dry sieving (Anderson and Wenhardt, 1966 ). Total aboveground yield (straw plus grain), and grain yield from a 1 m 2 equivalent area were measured after air drying of the samples (approximately 8% grain moisture content). When spring wheat was grown continuously, yields were similar whether sown directly in stubble or after preseeding tillage. However, zero-tillage seeding on stubble significantly enhanced soil water recharge relative to preseeding tillage (333 vs. 302 mm, respectively) on the clay.

column33: urea + monoammonium phosphate
column38: Research trials were established at two sites in western Manitoba on two orthic Chernozems, a clay loam (CL) and a fine sandy loam (FSL), representing a moderate-to-high moisture and drought-prone soil, respectively. Herbicide application was according to recommendations in the provincial Guide to Chemical Weed Control (Anonymous 1995). Nitrogen and phosphate fertilizer, as urea and monoammonium phosphate respectively, was applied according to soil testing recommendations for moist soil conditions. Plots were sown on land previously cropped to canola, with the exception of the summer fallow treatments in years 2 and 3. Three tillage effects were imposed, namely summer fallow (SF), conventional tillage (CT), and direct drill (DD). The SF tillage treatment consisted of rototilling the soil to remove all trash in the first season, while in the second and third season, fallow plots prepared the previous season were cultivated as the CT treatment. The CT treatment consisted of a single pass of a conventional cultivator, with rear-mounted tine harrows, once in the fall and prior to seeding in the spring, whereas the seed was sown directly into canola stubble with the DD treatment.

column33: NPK
column38: A 4 year field experiment on irrigated RWS was established in 2011 starting with rice on a Typic Ustochrept sandy loam soil (13.5% clay, 16.0% g silt and 70.5% sand)) at the experimental farm of the Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, Punjab (30o 56'N and 75o 52'E) in the Indo-Gangatic plains in the northwestern India. The experimental field was under conventional RW system for more than 10 years. The long-term average (30 years) mean minimum and maximum temperatures in wheat (November to April) are 6.7 oC and 22.6 oC while in rice (June to October) are 18 oC and 35 oC, respectively. The surface soil (0–15 cm) layer at the initiation of experiment was non-saline (electrical conductivity (EC) 0.34 dS m-1) with pH 7.81 (1:2 soil:water) and contained 0.351% easily oxidizable organic carbon, 11.3 mg kg-1 0.5 M NaHCO3-extractable P  and 46.3 mg kg-1 1 N NH4 OAc-extractable K. Before imposing treatments in rice in 2011, the experiment was laid out in November 2010 and a crop of wheat was raised in all the plots by applying recommended dose of fertilizers. The experiment was laid out in a split plot design with three replications and consisted of four treatment combinations of wheat stubble and Sesbania aculeata green manure (GM) management: PTRw0, puddled transplanted rice (PTR) with no wheat stubble retained; PTRw25, puddled transplanted rice with 25% anchored wheat stubble (12–15 cm high stubbles) retained; PTRw0- + GM; and PTRw25 + GMin main plots. There were three combinations of tillage and rice residue management in sub plots in subsequent wheat:CTWr0, conventional till (CT) wheat with rice residue removed; ZTWr0, ZT wheat with rice residue removed; and ZTWr100, ZT wheat with 100% rice residue retained as mulch. The sub-plot size was 3.6 m 9 19.0 m. The same treatments were assigned to same experimental plots in all the years of the study. After harvesting wheat, all the designated plots were irrigated and GM (Sesbania aculeata) was sown under zero tillage conditions using a seed rate of 50 kg ha-1. Green manure was sown in the third week of April. The amount of wheat stubble left in these plots ranged from 1.51 to 1.70 Mg ha-1 in different years. The stubble N, P and K nutrients averaged 5.2–5.6 kg, 0.48–0.69 kg and 11.7–14.2 kg ha-1 - year-1 in different treatments, respectively. The amount of dry matter of GM ranged from 3.46 to 4.1 Mg ha-1 and total N, P, K and carbon added ranged from 84 to 99 kg ha-1, 11–13 kg P ha-1, 51.2–60.7 kg K ha-1 and 1.31 to 1.56 Mg ha-1 in different years and under different treatments. Thirtyday- old rice seedlings (variety PR 115) were transplanted manually at 15 cm 9 20 cm spacing in the second week of June each year. At the same time, non-GM treatments plots were tilled using two diskings followed by planking to keep the plots weed free.

column38: The soil at Mfou is classified as clayey, kaolinitic, Typic Kandiudult (Hulugalle and Ndi, 1993). Annual mean maximum air temperature ranges from 29.6 to 31.9 8C and the mean minimum air temperature from 21.2 to 23.5 oC. The relative humidity ranges from 73.8% to 88.0%. The site has a bimodal rainfall distribution: the first and second rainy season typically last from mid-March to mid-July and from mid- August to end of November, respectively. The mean total annual rainfall is around 1500 mm. Conventional suckers of the local plantain cultivar Essong were treated in boiling water (Hauser, 2007) and planted in 2002 in a 4– 5-year-old bush dominated by Chromolaena odorata ([L.] King and Robinson, 1987). Maize was sown at 0.50 x 0.50 m spacing and thinned to one plant per stand. At 2 and 4 weeks after seeding urea was applied at the rate of 30 kg ha-1 N, per application, on one tilled and on one no-till sub-plots per plot.

column2: Soil Science Society of America Journal
column38: Soil of the study area was Pullman clay loam (fine, mixed, thermic Torrertic Paleustolls) with a uniform 0.3% slope. The study involved an irrigated winter wheat-dryland grain sorghum-dryland sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.) rotation. Wheat was planted 30 to 60 d after sunflower harvest. The furrow-irrigated wheat, which was grown before plot establishment on a given area, yielded 2.63, 3.95, and 3.16 Mg of grain/ha and 5.4, 6.3, and 5.2 Mg of residue/ha in 1978,1979, and 1980, respectively. Irrigation furrow spacing for the wheat was 1.0 m and drill row spacing was 0.25 m. On no-tillage plots, weeds were controlled with atrazine [2-chloro-4-(ethylamino)-6-(isopropylamino)-s-triazine]3 and 2,4-D[(2,4-dichlorophenoxy) acetic acid]3 applied at rates of 0.34 and 0.11 g/m2, respectively, soon after wheat harvest, Terbutryn [2-(tert-butylamino)-4-(ethylamino)-6-(methylthio)- 5-triazine]3 was applied at a 0.34-g/m2 rate to all plots for additional weed control during the sorghum growing season. Residue level treat ments consisted of no removal of residues and removal of most of the standing wheat residues before imposing the tillage treatments. Residues were removed with a flail-type forage harvester with the blades operated 30 to 50 mm above the soil ridges. None of the plots was plowed during the period from sorghum harvest to sunflower planting. Weeds were not a problem during late fall and winter; however, 2,4-D at 0.06 g/m2 and metolachlor [2-chloro-N-(2-ethyl-6-methylphenol)- N-(2-methoxy-l-methylethyl) acetamide]3 at 0.34 g/ m2 were applied in spring for weed control. Sorghum was planted 13, 26, and 4 June in 1979, 1980, and 1981, respectively. The sorghums were DeKalb medium maturity hybrids 'C46+', 'C42y+', and 'DK42y' in the respective years and were planted on the ridges with unit planters having double-disk openers. Depth bands on the openers resulted in seed placement at about a 38-mm depth. The intended plant population was about 96 000 plants/ha, but extra seed drop resulted in higher populations in some cases (Unger, 1984).

column33: N + 16 kg P ha-1 +94 kg K ha-1 + N from residual of oat
column38: A non-irrigated oat (Avena sativa L.)/soybean multiple cropping, tillage experiment was initiated in 1976 and continued through 1984 near Gainesville, FL. Date of planting in 1984 was 28 May. Plant density was 360 000 soybean plants ha- 1. The soil was classified as an Arredondo fine sand (loamy, siliceous hyperthermic Grossarenic Paleudults). The mechanical analysis for the 0-60-cm depth of an Arredondo soil, close to the experimental site, was as follows: 3.4% clay, 4.6% silt and 92.0% sand. The sand fraction was: 12% very fine sand, 52% fine sand, 26% medium sand and 2% coarse sand (Carlisle et al., 1981). Pesticides were applied for weed control at planting and when plants were 30-40-cm tall and for insect control twice after pod formation. In the spring of 1984, soybean plants received residual fertilizer from the oat crop, which had received a broadcast application of 20, 16 and 94 kg ha-1 of N, P and K, respectively, after planting in December 1983, and 67 kg of N ha-1 in February 1984.

column33: urea + 9 kg P ha-1 + 4.5 kg K ha-1
column38: the soil is a naturally drained Waukegan silt loam (fi ne-silty over skeletal mixed, superactive mesic Typic Hapludoll) with sand, silt, and clay contents of 220, 550, and 230 g kg−1, respectively, and organic carbon of 26 to 30 g C kg−1 in the upper 0.2 m. Mean annual precipitation and temperature are 879 mm and 6.4°C, respectively. Th e current study examined the corn phase of the corn–soybean rotation at two levels of tillage intensity. Corn (37L11; Pioneer, Mankato, MN) was planted in all plots at seeding rates of 79,000 ha−1 on 9 May 2008, 5 May 2009, and 6 May 2010 using a John Deere model 7100 MaxEmerge planter. Row cleaning coulters (Yetter Mfg., Colchester, IL) were used in the NT treatments to produce a more desirable seed bed. Liquid starter fertilizer was applied within 5 cm of the seed row at planting at 4.5, 9.0, and 4.5 kg ha−1 of urea-N, P, and K, respectively. Additional P and K fertilizers were applied periodically to the entire plot areas. Fertilizers were applied on 11 June 2008, 18 June 2009, and 10 June 2010 when the corn was at stage V4 to V6. In each case, fertilizer application was timed to minimize ammonia volatilization losses. In 2008 and 2010, fertilizers were applied before at least 17 mm of precipitation occurring within the next 12 h. In 2009, fertilizers were applied within 6 h after 11 mm of precipitation when the soil surface was very wet. All fertilizer products were hand-applied (broadcast) uniformly on the surface at 146 kg N ha−1. No-till plots received additional glyphosate applications occasionally as needed. Stover was obtained by cutting plants just above the crowns for all plants where ears were removed. All stover was weighed, and six plants were subsampled and ground, dried, and weighed for moisture content. Grain and stover samples were further ground with a grinding mill and analyzed with an elemental N analyzer (VarioMax; Elementar, Hanau, Germany) for total N.

column33: urea + 52 kg P2O5 ha-1
column38: The soil has beenclassified as a Hyposodic Vertisol (Calcaric, Chromic)according to the World Reference Base System(Verhulst et al. 2009; IUSS Working Group WRB2007). The soil is characterised by low soil organicmatter (SOM<12 g kg−1) and slight alkalinity (pH 8)(Limon-Ortega et al. 2008). The soil has a clay texture(on average 300 g kg−1 sand, 200 g kg−1 silt and500 g kg−1 clay in the top meter of the profile) inapproximately the top 1.2 m and a lighter textureunderneath up to 2 m (clay loam to sandy clay loam).Bulk density is around 1.3 Mg m-3 in the ploughlayer and somewhat higher in the Vertic horizon. The crop was irrigated at planting inboth the full and reduced irrigation treatments. Auxiliary irrigations were applied to the fullirrigation treatment when plant available soil watercontent to 0.6 m soil depth was about 70% of thesoil’s plant available water holding capacity; thisresulted in three to four auxiliary irrigations perseason and a total of approximately 520 mm ofirrigation water applied. An auxiliary irrigation wasapplied to the reduced irrigation treatment atheading each year. Approximately 240 mm ofirrigation water was applied in total to the environmentswith reduced irrigation. Two wheat rows were sown on top of the bed with0.27 m between the rows at a seeding rate of 130 kg ha−1. Before planting, 103 kgN ha−1 and 52 kg P2O5 ha−1 was band applied in the center of the beds. At theend of the tillering stage, 175 kgN ha−1 and 100 kgN ha−1 was banded as urea in the bottom of thefurrow in the full and reduced irrigation treatments,respectively. Pest, diseases and weeds were controlledwith common on-station measures. In the2008/09 study season, wheat was sown on 27/28 November 2008. During this season, auxiliary irrigations were applied 43, 66, 89 and 109 days after sowing under full irrigation and 77 days after sowing in the reduced irrigation treatment. Rainfall received during the three growing seasons considered in this study was negligible: 20 mm in 2006/07 (in the third week of January), 6 mm in 2007/08 and 3 mm in 2008/09.
