column33: N + 46 kg P ha-1 + 62 kg K ha-1
column38: The soil was slightly calcareous chernozem with 47% clay and silt. The 0–30 cm layer of soil contained 3.3% organic matter, 0.21% total N, 1.9% organic C, and 14 and 31 mg per 100 g soil of available P and extractable K, respectively, 9.7% total CaCO3 and pH 7.8, on average. Planting of all treatments was realized with a four row planter for direct maize planting, John Deere 7200. The plant density was 64 935 plants/ha. The following tillage systems were investigated (fac¬tor B): NT – no-tillage, RT – reduced tillage and CT – conventional tillage. Fertilizers treat¬ments were (factor C): F0 = control, F1 = 258 kg/ha (N 150 kg/ha, P 46 kg/ha and K 62 kg/ha) and F2 = 516 kg/ha (N 300 kg/ha, P 92 kg/ha and K 124 kg/ha). Prior to planting on NT, total herbicide Roundup (glyphosate 480 g a.i.) was applied as necessary to control vegetation in amounts of 5 L/ha. Pre-emergence application of herbicide Atrazine 500 SC in amount 1 L/ha (atrazine 500 g a.i.) and Harness 2 L/ha (acetochlor 900 g a.i.) were carried out on all treatments, until 2007 when atrazine was replaced with terbuth¬ylazine. During vegetation, inter-row cultivation was applied to control weeds so they would not affect growth and development of the plants or depress the maize yields. Every year the preceding crop was winter wheat and the harvest residues were removed from the plots in or¬der to prevent Fusarium infection

column38: The soils were classified as a Listowel silt loam (medium, mixed weakly to moderately calcareous Typic Hapludalf) at Kirkton and a Toledo silt loam to silty clay loam (medium, burnmixed weakly to moderately calcareous Typic Humaquept) at Belmont. The preceding year’s crop was soft white winter wheat, which was grown using recommended production practices for Ontario. Wheat was harvested using commercial harvesting equipment, and straw was baled leaving a standing stubble height of 20 cm. Fall K was applied as muriate of potash [KCl] (0–0–60) at rates of 0, 42, and 84 kg K ha21. Fall K was applied in a manner that was specific to each of the tillage practices. Corn was planted using a John Deere (Moline, IL) Model 7000 row crop planter in 1996 and 1997 and a John Deere Model 1760 row crop planter in 1998. Spring K was applied as part of a starter fertilizer blend including urea [(NH2 )2CO] (46–0–0), monoammonium phosphate [NH4H2PO4] (11–52–0), and muriate of potash (0–0–60). The low K application rate was either 8 (1996) or 0 (1997 and 1998) kg K ha21. The high K application rate was either 50 (1996) or 42 (1997 and 1998) kg K ha21. Each of the two starter fertilizer formulations applied 30 and 13 kg ha21 N and P, respectively. Corn (cv. Pioneer 3752) was planted in 76-cm wide rows at a seeding rate of 74 000 seeds ha21. The planting dates were 30 May 1996, 30 May 1997, and 8 May 1998 at Kirkton and 30 May 1997 and 8 May 1998 at Belmont. Weed control consisted of a pre-emergence broadcast application of cyanazine {2-[[4-chloro-6-(ethylamino)-1,3,5-triazin-2-yl]amino]-2-methylpropionitrile} at 2.0 kg a.i. ha21 and metolachlor [2-chloro-N-(2-ethyl-6-methylphenyl)-N-(2-methoxy-1-methylethyl)acetamide] at 2.6 kg a.i. ha21. Dicamba (3, 6-dichloro-2-methoxybenzoic acid) was applied postemergence, whenever necessary, at a rate of 0.3 kg a.i. ha21 to control broadleaf weed escapes.

column33: ammonium nitrate + 16-40 kg P ha-1
column38: Plot size for the sandy loam and clay loam sites was 7.4 mX 12.3 m. Corn hybrid 'Pioneer 3950' (Pioneer Hi-Bred Ltd., Chatham, Ont., Canada) was planted in 1982 and 1983 on the sandy loam and silt loam soils at a rate of approximately 65 000 seeds ha-1. In 1984, 'Pioneer 3925' was used at the sandy loam location. Ammonium nitrate was broadcast at rates of 100-150 kg N ha- 1, 136-170 kg N ha- 1, and 119-136 kg N ha- 1 on the sandy loam, silt loam and clay loam sites, respectively. Potash (0-0-60) was broadcast as required on the sandy loam and silt loam soils. In most years, monoammonium phosphate was applied as a starter fertilizer to achieve phosphorus rates of 16-40 kg ha- 1, depending on soil requirements. The following herbicides were used for weed control: alachlor (2-chloro-N- (2,6-diethylphenyl)-N- (methoxymethyl) acetamide), pre-emergence at 2.15- 2.25 kg ha-1 in 1982 and 1983; metolachlor (2-chloro-N-(2-ethyl-6-methylphenyl )-N- ( 2-methoxy- 1 -methylethyl ) acetamide ), pre-emergence at 1.92- 2.64 kg ha- 1 in 1984; cyanazine (2- [ [ 4-chloro-6- (ethylamino)- 1,3,5-triazin- 2-yl]amino]-2-methylpropanenitrile), pre-emergence at 2.0-2.25 kg ha- 1 from 1982 to 1984; dicamba (3,6-dichloro-2-methoxybenzoic acid), postemergence at 0.34 kg ha-1 when necessary. One of the following insecticides was banded at planting for corn rootworm control: Counter 15G (S-( ( ( 1,1- dimethylethyl)thio)methyl)0,0-diethyl phosphorodithioate) at 7.5-9.9 kg ha- 1; Furadan 10G (2,3-dihydro-2,2-dimethyl-7-benzofuranyl methylcarbamate) at 14.6 kg ha- 1, Dyfonate 20G (O-ethyl S-phenyl ethylphosphorodithioate) at 7.0 kg ha- 1. Surface residue %: sandy loam plot, NT 70.1% MP 16.4%; Clay loam site, NT 40.1% MP 4.9%.

column33: UAN + 100 kg K ha-1
column38: The fields had been in a 3-year crop rotation consisting of soybean–winter wheat–corn for at least 15 years prior to initiating these field trials. The soils were classified as a Brunisolic Gray Brown Luvisol according to Canadian soil classification (Albic Luvisol based on FAO soil classification). The soils during both years were classified as moderately well drained. Corn was planted following soybeans in 1997 and following winter wheat in 1998. Wheat straw was baled shortly after harvest leaving a standing stubble height of approximately 20 cm. glyphosate was applied at a rate of 1.1 kg a.i. ha−1 to control volunteer wheat and (or) weeds. The four fertilizer treatments applied to each tillage system were: 1. Deep band. Potash fertilizer (100 kgKha−1) was band applied 15 cm deep on 76 cm centres. Banding of K fertilizer occurred following completion of spring tillage, and corn rows were positioned directly on top of the fertilizer bands. 2. Broadcast. Potash fertilizer (100 kgKha−1) was broadcast applied just prior to spring tillage operations. 3. Broadcast + shallow-band. Half (50 kgKha−1) of the potash fertilizer was surface broadcast just prior to tillage operations. The other half was applied through the planter in a band positioned 5 cm to the side of the row, 5 cm below corn seeding depth. 4. None applied. No potassium fertilizer was applied. In treatments 1–3 above, K fertilizer was either deep band or broadcast applied within 1 day prior to corn seeding as muriate of potash (KCl). Corn ‘Pioneer 3820’ was planted in 76 cm wide rows at a seeding rate of 80,000 seeds ha−1. In 1997, corn was planted using a John Deere (Moline, IL, USA) model 7000 MaxEmerge row crop planter. Corn seeding dates were 21 May 1997 and 10 May 1998. Weed control consisted of a pre-emergence broadcast application of cyanazine {2-[[4-chloro-6- (ethylamino)-1,3,5-triazine-2-yl]amino]-2-methylpropanenitrile} at a rate of 2.1 kg ha−1 and metolachlor [2-chloro-N-(2-ethyl-6-methylphenyl)-N-(2-methoxyl- 1-methylethyl)acetamide] at a rate of 2.4 kg ha−1. Nitrogen was injected as urea-ammonium-nitrate (28% N) between rows when corn was at the seven- to nine-leaf stage at a rate of 150 kgNha−1.

column2: Soil Science Society of America Journal
column33: NH4NO3 + P + K
column38: The soil types were a Rion-Pacolet sandy clay loam complex (2-6% slope) at the Piedmont location and an Eunola sandy loam (0-3% slope) at the Coastal Plain location. Selected physical and chemical properties of the surface 0.20 m of each soil prior to the initiation of the experiment were as follows: (i) Rion-Pacolet: 48% sand, 25% silt, 27% clay, 5.2 cmolc kg-1 CEC, and pH 5.7; (ii) Eunola: 70% sand, 21% silt, 9% clay, 3.3 cmolc kg-1 CEC, and pH 6.1. Both sites had been in CT corn the previous year. Lime and P and K fertilizers were broadcast on the soil surface as needed, based on North Carolina Department of Agriculture soil-test recommendations. Dolomitic lime was applied in the fall, and P and K were applied in the spring prior to chisel plowing. DeKalb-Pfizer 789 corn1 was planted at a seeding rate of =59 000 kernels ha-1 on 26 Apr. 1984, 9 Apr. 1985, 14 Apr. 1986, 1 May 1987, and 26 Apr. 1988 at the Piedmont location, and 16 May 1984, 2 Apr. 1985, 26 Mar. 1986, 7 May 1987, and 24 Apr. 1988 at the Coastal Plain location. At planting, 34 kg N ha-1 as NH4NO3 was banded on the soil surface 10 cm from the row. An additional 166 kg N ha-1 as NH4NO3 was applied in the same manner 4 to 5 wk after corn emergence. The experimental area was sprayed with 4.7 L ha-1 glyphosate [isopropylamine salt of N-(phosphono- methyl) glycine], mixed with 3.5 L ha-1 alachlor [2-chloro-2'-6'-diethyl-N-(methoxymethyl)-acetanilide] and 4.7 L ha-1 atrazine [2-chloro-4-ethylamino-6-isopropylamino- 1, 3,5-triazine] for weed control. Terbufos (S-[[(l,ldimethylethyl) thio]methyl] O,O-diethyl phosphorodithioate) granules were banded over the row at 8 kg ha-1 (1.2 kg a.i.) for insect control. Weeds were controlled postemergence with linuron [3-(3, 4-dichlorophenyl)-l-methoxy- 1-methylurea] sprayed at 2.9 L ha-1. Corn grain yield was measured by machine harvesting the two center rows of each plot. Grain yield was adjusted to a 155 g kg-1 moisture basis. 'RingAround 604' soybean was planted at a rate of = 96 000 seeds ha-1 on 15 May 1984, 9 May 1985, 27 May 1986,18 May 1987, and 23 May 1988 at the Piedmont location, and 16 May 1984, 8 May 1985, 14 May 1986, 7 May 1987, and 24 May 1988 at the Coastal Plain location. Weed control was provided with a spray application at planting of 4.7 L ha-1 each of glyphosate and alachlor. Weeds were controlled postemergence with a spray application of 2.3 L ha-1 acifluorfen (sodium 5-[2-chloro-4- (trifluoromethyl) phenoxyl]-2-nitrobenzoate) or 1.2 L ha-1 sethoxydim (2-[l-(ethoxyimino) butyl-5-[2-(ethylthio) propyl]- 3-hydroxy-2-cyclohexen-l-one). Soybean yield was determined by machine harvesting the two center rows of each plot. Grain yield was adjusted to a 130 g kg-1 moisture basis. Surface residue cover percentage was estimated in all corn plots each year =2 to 3 wk after crop emergence using a 7.6-m transect with 25 points (Sloneker and Moldenhauer, 1977).

column33: Urea(46% N) + 75 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 150 kg K20 ha-1
column38: The field experiments were conducted in Xinxiang Experiment Station of Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Henan Province, China (35°18'N, 113°54'E). Soil textural class for studied site is classified as clay loam (ISSS Classification, International Soil Science Society), with percentage composition of sand, silt and clay as 32.95, 34.2 and 32.85%, respectively (saturation: 38.5%). Soil bulk density was 1.29 g cm-3, 1.34 g cm-3, 1.55 g cm-3 and 1.52 g cm-3 at 0-10 cm, 10-20 cm, 20-30 cm and 30-40 cm soil depth, respectively. Major soil nutrient contents analyzed were: organic matter 12.55 g kg-1, total nitrogen 1.13 g kg-1, available phosphorus 16.15 mg kg-1, and 109.95 mg kg-1 available potassium (pH = 8.21, EC = 1.2 dSm-1, slope gradient with negligible risk of soil erosion). Usual crop rotation for this area is double cropping system with winter-wheat and summer-maize, in that rotary tillage (15-20 cm) is practiced for wheat and no-tillage farming for maize crop is followed usually. The experiment was conducted from 2011 to 2012. Randomized complete block design was used with split plot arrangement and three replications. The maize variety Zhengdan-958 was planted at the density of 67500 plants ha-1 with an 80-40 cm wide/narrow row spacing pattern. N fertilizers at 225 kg N ha-1 (Urea: 46% N) were applied in two split applications: 1/3 as basal application before planting, and the remaining 2/3 as side-dressing at the V8-V9 growth stage. Phosphate (P2O5) and Potassium (K2O) fertilizers were applied at 75 kg/ha and 150 kg/ha before sowing, respectively. in subplots two soil tillage treatments just before the maize sowing were conducted viz. SS: subsoiling tillage management involved complete soil inversion and burial of crop residues to a depth of 30 cm using a stripe deep loosening machine

column33: Urea + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 90 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The experimental was established in 2007 at a tableland ((35°19′54.45′′N latitude, 110°05′58.35′′E longitude; altitude 877 m) site, located in Heyang county, Shaanxi Province, China, during 2007–2016. The experimental fields are level and the soil is classified as middle loam based on the FAO/UNESCO Soil Classification. All the fields had been plowed for several years at the start of the experiment in 2007, and the soil in 0–20 cm layer had a pH of 8.2, an SOC of 9.94 g kg−1，a soil total nitrogen content of 0.74 g kg−1，a soil total phosphorous content of 0.59 g kg−1, and an available potassium content of 110.6 g kg−1. The soil bulk density was 1.43 g cm−3 and soil porosity was 46.76%. In this study, we chose year 2013 to represent a dry year, 2014 as a normal year and 2016 as a humid year. A homogeneous area of 2025m2 was selected in 2007 for the establishment of the experimental plots. The experimental area was a randomized block design with three replications. Each plot was 5m wide and 22.5m long. In this study, six tillage treatments were applied in the fallow period of spring maize field. NT (no-tillage) was applied every year, ST (sub-soiling was applied every year), CT (conventional tillage was applied every year), NT/ST rotation (no-tillage was applied in first year and rotated with sub-soiling in second year), ST/CT rotation (sub-soiling was applied in first year and rotated with conventional tillage in second year), CT/NT rotation (conventional tillage were applied in first year and rotated with no-tillage in second year). In the CT treatment, the soil was tilled to 20–25 cm depth using a tractor-mounted moldboard plow, and the crop straws were returned and buried into the arable layer. The straws were retained evenly on the plot surface as mulch under NT and ST. A common spring maize variety Zhengdan 958 was sown in middle or late April, the local popular sowing time. For NT and ST, maize was drill seeded at a plant density of 5.3 plants m−2, while for CT, sowing with the same plant density was conducted using a rotary cultivator seeder. The distance within and between rows of maize was 30 cm and 60 cm, respectively. The one-time application of the full amount of fertilizer was conducted by broadcast before sowing with rates of 150 kg N ha−1,120 kg P2O5 ha−1 and 90 kg K2Oha−1. The fertilizer types for N, P2O5 and K2O were urea, ammonium phosphate and potassium sulfate, respectively. The harvest of maize was performed in the first fortnight of September. After the scheduled tillage, the field was kept fallow until the seeding of next maize season in next April. For all treatments, weeds were controlled by spraying chemical herbicides before crop emergence and at the initial fallow stage, as well as by hand one to two times in the growth season based on visual estimates of weed populations.

In the CT treatment, the soil was tilled to 20–25 cm depth using a tractor-mounted moldboard plow, and the crop straws were returned and buried into the arable layer. The straws were retained evenly on the plot surface as mulch under NT and ST. A common spring maize variety Zhengdan 958 was sown in middle or late April, the local popular sowing time. For NT and ST, maize was drill seeded at a plant density of 5.3 plants m−2, while for CT, sowing with the same plant density was conducted using a rotary cultivator seeder. The distance within and between rows of maize was 30 cm and 60 cm, respectively. The one-time application of the full amount of fertilizer was conducted by broadcast before sowing with rates of 150 kg N ha−1,120 kg P2O5 ha−1 and 90 kg K2Oha−1. After the scheduled tillage, the field was kept fallow until the seeding of next maize season in next April. For all treatments, weeds were controlled by spraying chemical herbicides before crop emergence and at the initial fallow stage, as well as by hand one to two times in the growth season based on visual estimates of weed populations.

column33: litter
column38: The soil was a Hartsells fine sandy loam. The Hartsells series consists of moderately deep, well-drained, moderately permeable soils that formed in loamy residuum weathered from acid sandstone containing thin strata of shale or siltstone. Climate in this region is subtropical with no dry season; mean annual rainfall is 1325 mm, and mean annual temperature is 16°C (Shaw, 1982). Before field study initiation in 1980, the site had been under intensive row crop production for more than 50 yr. Rotation treatments were continuous corn–wheat cover, continuous soybean–wheat cover, corn–wheat cover–soybean–wheat cover, and soybean–wheat cover–corn–wheat cover. The rotational corn–wheat cover– soybean–wheat cover and soybean–wheat cover–corn–wheat cover treatments alternated yearly to evaluate the impact crop rotations had on corn or soybean grain yield each year. Wheat cover crops were established the preceding fall of each year and seeded at a rate of 100 kg ha-1. After wheat emergence, 112 kg N ha-1 as NH4NO3 and poultry litter were applied to the wheat cover of the corn and soybean crops. A day or two after tillage operations occurred, the subsequent corn and soybean crops were planted at a rate of 57,000 seed ha-1 and 32 seed m-1, respectively. Corn was planted in mid-April, and soybean was planted in early June of each year. Corn received 56 kg N ha-1 at planting and an additional 168 kg N ha-1 as NH4NO3 (no poultry litter was applied to corn) 2 to 3 wk after emergence. No fertilizer was applied to the soybean crop. Both poultry litter and NH4NO3 were surface-broadcasted by hand. The average poultry litter nutrients applied each year from 1991 to 2001 was 112 kg N ha-1, 6.5 kg P ha-1, 96 kg K ha-1, 86 kg Ca ha-1, and 6 kg Mg ha-1 to the wheat cover crop. Dolomitic lime, KCl (0–0–60) ,and P were applied in the fall according to Auburn University soil test recommendations. Phosphorus was not applied to plots receiving poultry litter to prevent P buildup. Lime and K application rates varied across years, but all plots received the same amount when applied. No additional micronutrients other than those contained in the poultry litter were applied during the 10-yr study period. Weed control initially consisted of atrazine followed by glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] applied post-emergence for the corn plots. Weed control in soybean plots was accomplished by applying Imazaquin {2-[4,5-dihydro-4-methyl-4-(1- methylethyl)-5-oxo-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-3-quinoline-carboxylic acid} at planting; Linuron [(N-3,4-dichlorophenyl)-N-methoxy- N-methyl-urea] and 2,4-DB (4-(2,4-dichlorophenoxy)butanoic acid) were tank-mixed and applied post-directed to soybean for weed control. Additional weed control was achieved by hand weeding and cultivation as needed in the NT and CT, respectively, for corn and soybean plots. The tillage treatments (main plots) consisted of conventional tillage (CT; moldboard plowing and disking followed by rototiller in the spring), no-tillage (NT; planting into crop residue with a double disk-opener planter), and strip tillage (planting behind a strip-till shank to a 35- to 40-cm depth).

The Hartsells series consists of moderately deep, well-drained, moderately permeable soils that formed in loamy residuum weathered from acid sandstone containing thin strata of shale or siltstone. Climate in this region is subtropical with no dry season; mean annual rainfall is 1325 mm, and mean annual temperature is 16°C (Shaw, 1982). Before field study initiation in 1980, the site had been under intensive row crop production for more than 50 yr. Rotation treatments were continuous corn–wheat cover, continuous soybean–wheat cover, corn–wheat cover–soybean–wheat cover, and soybean–wheat cover–corn–wheat cover. The rotational corn–wheat cover– soybean–wheat cover and soybean–wheat cover–corn–wheat cover treatments alternated yearly to evaluate the impact crop rotations had on corn or soybean grain yield each year. Wheat cover crops were established the preceding fall of each year and seeded at a rate of 100 kg ha-1. After wheat emergence, 112 kg N ha-1 as NH4NO3 and poultry litter were applied to the wheat cover of the corn and soybean crops. A day or two after tillage operations occurred, the subsequent corn and soybean crops were planted at a rate of 57,000 seed ha-1 and 32 seed m-1, respectively. Corn was planted in mid-April, and soybean was planted in early June of each year. Corn received 56 kg N ha-1 at planting and an additional 168 kg N ha-1 as NH4NO3 (no poultry litter was applied to corn) 2 to 3 wk after emergence. No fertilizer was applied to the soybean crop. Both poultry litter and NH4NO3 were surface-broadcasted by hand. The average poultry litter nutrients applied each year from 1991 to 2001 was 112 kg N ha-1, 6.5 kg P ha-1, 96 kg K ha-1, 86 kg Ca ha-1, and 6 kg Mg ha-1 to the wheat cover crop. Dolomitic lime, KCl (0–0–60) ,and P were applied in the fall according to Auburn University soil test recommendations. Phosphorus was not applied to plots receiving poultry litter to prevent P buildup. Lime and K application rates varied across years, but all plots received the same amount when applied. No additional micronutrients other than those contained in the poultry litter were applied during the 10-yr study period. Weed control initially consisted of atrazine followed by glyphosate [N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine] applied post-emergence for the corn plots. Weed control in soybean plots was accomplished by applying Imazaquin {2-[4,5-dihydro-4-methyl-4-(1- methylethyl)-5-oxo-1H-imidazol-2-yl]-3-quinoline-carboxylic acid} at planting; Linuron [(N-3,4-dichlorophenyl)-N-methoxy- N-methyl-urea] and 2,4-DB (4-(2,4-dichlorophenoxy)butanoic acid) were tank-mixed and applied post-directed to soybean for weed control. Additional weed control was achieved by hand weeding and cultivation as needed in the NT and CT, respectively, for corn and soybean plots. The tillage treatments (main plots) consisted of conventional tillage (CT; moldboard plowing and disking followed by rototiller in the spring), no-tillage (NT; planting into crop residue with a double disk-opener planter), and strip tillage (planting behind a strip-till shank to a 35- to 40-cm depth).

column5: Quebec, Ste. Anne de Bellevue (MacDonald Farm)
column33: urea + liquid dairy manure
column38: The soil was a mixed, frigid Typic Endoaquent classified as a Courval sandy-loam, containing 15.4 g organic C kg–1 and pH 6.1 in the 0- to 15-cm layer. From 1991 to 2000, when this study began, the site was a CT system under grain corn (Zea mays L.) production. Annual nutrient applications included about 30 m3 ha–1 of liquid dairy manure as well as 100 to 140 kg N ha–1 from urea fertilizer. In May 2000, a factorial (tillage x crop rotation) experiment was established with two tillage treatments (NT or CT) and three crop rotations (corn/soybean, soybean/corn or continuous corn; only one crop per year), for a total of six factorial treatments. All plots were directly seeded with a John Deere 7100 Max Emerge seeder. Silage corn (Zea mays L. ‘Cargill 2610’) was treated with Maxim and Captan and planted with 75 000 seeds ha–1 in 0.75-m rows. Soybean (Glycine max L. Merr. ‘Cargill A0868TR’) treated with Soy Select was planted at a rate of 400 000 seeds ha–1 in 0.75-m rows. Seeding was completed between mid-May and the first week of June during five growing seasons (2000–2004). Weed populations were determined in six 30 cm ×30 cm quadrats at about 1.5-m intervals along four 10-m transects in each plot on 2000 Jun. 20 and 2001 Jun. 12, prior to the application of post-emergence herbicides. Weed control in plots under corn production was achieved with post-emergence herbicide applications of 25 g a.i. ha–1 of nicosulfuron and 280 g a.i. ha–1 of bromoxynil (2000 Jun. 27 and 2001 Jun. 18, about mid-June during the 2002–2004 growing seasons). Plots under soybean production received post-emergence applications of bentazon (1.1 kg a.i. ha–1) on 2000 Jun. 28 . Diclofop-methyl (1.0 kg a.i. ha–1) was applied on 2001 Jul. 04 and early July of 2002–2004. No insecticides were applied in any study year (2000–2004). Sticky traps and pitfall traps were placed in 12 random locations throughout each plot on two sampling dates in 2000 (Jul. 07 and Aug. 02) and two sampling dates in 2001 (Jul. 09 and Aug. 02). In August, sticky traps were between 0.75 and 1.0 m below the corn canopy. Pitfall traps were 120 cm3 specimen cups containing 60 mL of 5% glycerol solution placed in the soil so the opening (6-cm diameter) was level with the soil surface. After 48 h, traps were removed from the field and stored in plastic bags. At harvest, silage corn yield was determined by harvesting the grain and stover (stems and leaves) of 80 plants from each plot. carabid beetles move faster, or more easily, when there are fewer surface residues, as in cultivated systems. During 2001, the generalist predator population collected from NT plots contained a larger proportion of Araneae and Opiliones per treatment than the CT plots. Spiders tend to be more numerous in agroecosystems where surface residue cover is diversified by planting intercrops and cover crops, retaining weeds or conserving crop residues.

column38: Treatments consisted of two tillage systems for wheat (NT and CT) and four N rates applied to the previous cotton crop (0, 67, 134, and 202 kg N ha-1). Inc., Assaria, KS) on 24 November in 1995 and 1996. The subplots were 6.1 m long and 3.7 m wide. all wheat treatmentswere broadcastwith ammoniumnitrate (34–0–0 of N–P–K) fertilizer at 78 kg N ha-1 at the end of January in both years. Herbicides were applied to control winter annual grasses. The study was broadcast sprayed with diclofop-methyl {methyl 2-[4-(2,4-dichlorophenoxy) phenoxy] propanoate} at 0.83 kg a.i. ha-1 on 4 March 1996 and thifensulfuron-methyl + tribenuron-methyl {methyl 3-[[[[4-methoxy-6methyl-1,3,5-triazin-2-yl) amino]carbonyl]amino]sulfonyl]-2-thiophenecarboxylate + methyl2-[[[[N-(4-methoxy-6methyl-1,3,5-triazin- 2-yl)methylamino]carbonyl]amino]sulfonyl] benzoate} at 27 g a.i. ha-1 on 11 February 1997. Wheat was harvested with a small plot combine on 22 and 19 May in 1996 and 1997, respectively. Nitrogen application to a previous cotton crop increased plant residues and therefore residual N due to plant decomposition.With the application of 0 to 202 kg N ha-1 to cotton, plant N ranged from 73 to 155 kg ha-1 for NT and from 71 to 140 kg ha-1 for CT in 1995. In 1996, plant N varied from 90 to 161 kg ha-1 for NT and from 71 to 151 kg ha-1 for CT. Moreover, residual soil N increased with increasing N application to the previous cotton crop from 99 to 119 kg ha-1 for NT and from 103 to 120 kg ha-1 for CT in 1995. In 1996, the residual soil N increased from 107 to 135 kg ha-1 for NTand from 105 to 127 kg ha-1 for CT.

column33: ammonium nitrate
column38: This field research was conducted at the Rogers Memorial Farm over 16 yr (1986–2001) on a silty clay loam soil (deep, moderately well-drained upland Sharpsburg soil formed in loess; fine, smectitic, mesic Typic Argiudolls) near Lincoln, NE, under natural rainfall conditions. Subplot treatments were continuous corn, continuous soybean, soybean–corn, and corn–soybean so that each phase of all crop sequences was presented each year. Planting population for corn ranged from 40 000 kernels ha_1 in the early years of the study to 58 000 kernels ha-1 in more recent years (since 1996). Soybean was planted at rates between 250 000 and 375 000 seeds ha-1. Insecticides (which varied over years) were applied to corn at planting according to label procedures to reduce rootworm damage. For both corn and soybean, a combination of pre- and postemergence herbicides (again products varied over the years of study), cultivation, and hand weeding were used to control weeds. Nitrogen was broadcast to corn at 113 kg N ha-1 as ammonium nitrate at about the V3 growth stage. Other plant nutrients were within optimum levels for corn and soybean production. Residue was chopped in spring for the disk, no-till, and ridge-till treatments. After grain harvest from 1986 through 1999, corn stover was chopped on the chisel, plow, and subsoil treatments. These treatments were then tilled.

column33: NH4NO3
column38: Whole plots were 22.9×18.3 m; sub-plots were 22.9×6.1 m. Manure was applied on designated treatments by hand, or with a farm spreader, prior to primary tillage each year. Nitrogen fertilizer at rates of 0, 70, or 140 kg ha -1 N was broadcast as NH4NO3 and incorporated with secondary tillage except in NT and NM treatments. According to soil test, no P or K was needed, and none was applied. Maize cultivar Neb 620 was planted from 1977 through 1981; Pre- and post-emergence surface-applied herbicides were used at labeled rates. The specific herbicides used varied from year to year, but were uniform over the entire experiment within each year. Chemicals used included: alachlor; atrazine; cyanazine; dicamba; glyphosate; metolachlor; paraquat; pendimethalin; 2,4-D. Weeds not controlled by herbicides were hand-weeded. For soil insect control, carbofuran or terbufos was applied at planting at labeled rates over the seed row in a 0.20-m band to control northern maize rootworm (Diabrotica longicornis (Say)). In 1982, carbaryl was applied at 0.91 kg hafor control of European maize borer (Ostrinia nubilalis Hubner). ). In 1978, grain production of treatments with more complete residue incorporation (plow and disk) was significantly greater than that for the chisel treatment, which incoporated little residue but disturbed the soil to a greater extent.

Three separate crop residue measurements were taken and averaged from individual plots within 2 weeks after planting with a pin-type apparatus.

The soil was a Sharpsburg silty clay loam (fine, smectitic, mesic Typic Argiudolls) with a 3% slope at RMF and a Yutan silty clay loam (fine-silty, mixed, superactive, mesic Mollic Hapludalfs) with a 1 to 2% slope at ARDC. The main plots were 24 m long and 4.6 and 6.1 m wide at RMF and ARDC, respectively. Soybean (cultivar Dekalb 25-51 of maturity group 2 at ARDC, and cultivar Asgrow 3302 of maturity group 3 at RMF) was sown at a rate of 494,000 seeds ha–1. Corn (cultivar Pioneer 33R81, 2750 growing degrees days at physiological maturity) was sown at ARDC at a rate of 56,800 seeds ha–1. Grain sorghum (cultivar NC+7R37E of maturity group 1) was sown at RMF at a rate of 190,000 seeds ha–1. The only inorganic fertilizer applied was N applied to corn and sorghum at the suggested rates with a mean of approximately 95 kg ha–1 (Ferguson, 2000). Planting date varied but was typically completed by 30 April for corn, 5 to 15 May for grain sorghum, and 10 to15 May for soybean. The MMP has a reduced moldboard, causes less soil inversion, and leaves more crop residue cover than the MP. Within a few days, the fi eld-moist soil was passed through a 4-mm sieve and visible crop residues removed. Crop P uptake from throughout the measured soil depth and P deposition on the soil surface with decomposition of the crop residues was expected to restore the stratifi cation of available P and appears to have occurred in these trials.

Main plots were a combination of tillage and percentage of the total aboveground residue (referred to as straw) returned from the previous crop (CT0 = conventional tillage + no straw return; CT100 = conventional tillage + 100% straw return; ZT50 = zero tillage + 50% straw return; and ZT100 = zero tillage + 100% straw return). Subplots were three N treatments: zero-N control, sitespecific N management (SSNM), and farmers’ N-fertilizer practice (FFP). For N topdressing at MT and PI, if the SPAD reading was greater than 39, the base N rate minus 4 and 6 kg ha-1 was applied, respectively; if the reading was less than 37, the base N rate plus 4 and 6 kg ha-1 was applied, respectively; if the reading was between 37 and 39, the base N rate was applied. The base N rate was 21 kg ha-1 at MT and 31 kg ha-1 at PI. At HD, only if the SPAD reading was less than 37, was 17 kg N ha-1 applied. Because SPAD readings were greater than 39 at MT and PI, 17 and 25 kg N ha-1 in the form of urea was applied at MT and PI, respectively. No N was applied at HD because SPAD readings were greater than 37. For FFP, N was applied in two splits with 102 kg ha-1 as basal and 48 kg ha-1 at 7 days after transplanting (DAT). Herbicide was used to control weeds. In both years, phosphorus (90 kg P2O5 ha-1 as calcium superphosphate), potassium (75 kg K2O ha-1 as KCl), and zinc (5 kg ZnO ha-1 as zinc sulfate heptahydrate) were applied together with basal N.

column38: Field experiments were performed at the Wenxi Dryland Wheat Agriculture Station (35°20´N, 111°17´E), Shanxi Province of China in the 2009–2015 growing seasons. This site is located in the southeast of the Loess Plateau, and its environmental conditions represent the typical semiarid, warm temperate continental climate with annual mean precipitation of 491 mm, annual mean temperature of 12.9 °C, annual sunshine duration of 2242 h and open pan evaporation of 1839 mm. This experiment was set as single factor completely randomized design with three replicates. column33: N + 27 kg P ha-1 + 34 kg K ha-1
column38: A 2-year field experiment was conducted at Agronomy Experimental Plot, Indian Council of agricultural Research (ICAR), Research Complex for North Eastern Hill Region, Tripura Centre, Lembucherra, Tripura (W), India (23o 54'24.02''N and 91o 18'58.35''E), and altitude of 162 m ASL (metres above mean sea level) during 2012–13 and 2013–14. Prior to initiation of the experiment, winter pea was grown (2011) uniformly in the proposed land configuration for treatment stabilization. The soil of the experimental field was sandy loam in texture, and the initial soil sample had 6.9 g kg-1 organic C, 121.3 mg kg-1 available N, 26.2 mg kg-1 available P and 119.5 mg kg-1 available potassium (K). The pH of soil was 5.2 (1:2.5, soil-to-water ratio). The experiment was laid out in a randomized block design (RBD) with three replications. The sizes of gross and net plot were 594 m2 and 493 m2, respectively. A popular hybrid of summer maize (DMH-849) was sown manually at 60 9 30 cm spacing on 8 April 2012 and on 4 April 2013. Glyphosate (@ 2 ml litre-1) was applied 7 days before the sowing in no-till-based plots. In both the years, all the treatments received 120 kg N ha-1, 27 kg P ha-1 and 34 kg K ha-1. Fifty per cent of N and full doses of P and K were applied at the time of sowing in furrow below the seed. Rest of the N was applied in two split doses, 25 per cent at knee high stage and remaining 25 per cent at tasselling stage. Green cobs and fodder were harvested on 28–30 June in both the years. As the crop residues were mostly concentrated in the 0–15 cm soil profile under NT, the pore space increase which may help to proliferate the roots, and hence, higher RLD is recorded under NT.

column33: N + 18 kg P ha-1 + 33 kg K ha-1
column38: A field experiment was conducted on upland direct-seeded rice during 2012–2013 under different tillage andmulch systems at Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) Complex for the NEHR, Lembucherra, Tripura, India. The site is located at 23°54ʹ24.02” N and 91°18ʹ58.35” E at an altitude of 52 m ASL (meter above sea level). The region is characterized by sloping (~5%) upland, hot and humid weather during summer, andmild and dry climate during winter. The average annual rainfall of the region is 2200 mm. A detailed description of weather parameters is provided in Figure 1. The soil of the experimental site was sandy loam in texture. Based on the analysis of initial soil sample (average of three samples), the soil had 6.2 g kg−1 SOC determined by Walkley and Black method (Nelson and Sommers 2005), 130.3mg kg−1 available N determined by alkaline potassium permanganate method (Subbiah and Asija 1956), 24.4 mg kg−1 available phosphorus (P) determined by Bray & Kurtz No. 1 method (Olsen and Sommers 1982), 135.7 mg kg−1 available potassium (K) determined by ammonium acetatemethod (Knudsen et al. 1982), and pH of 5.2 by glass electrode method (Kalra 1995) (1:2.5, soil and water ratio). The experiment was laid out in the split-plot design, with two tillage treatments with residue management as the main plot and four types of mulches as a subplot with three replications with plot-location fixed over the years. The sub-plot size was 4.5 × 2.9 m. Thus, in total, there were six main plots and 24 sub-plots. Tillage treatments included CT-RI: conventional tillage (CT) with 100% residue incorporation (RI) and NT-RR: no-till (NT) with 100% residue retention (RR). Mulches included rice straw (SM), Gliricidia (GM), brown manuring (BM) and none (NM). Residues of the crop were retained on the surface after harvest under NT, while these were incorporated under CT. Mulch treatments were applied at the time of sowing in between the rows of rice. The rate of mulch application was different depending on mulch. SM was collected from nearby field and was applied 2.5 Mg ha−1 on a dry weight basis, and GM was applied by cut and carry methods. The leaves and twigs of Glyricidia were cut and carried from Cocotila farm of the Institute and applied 2.5 Mg ha−1 on dry weight basis. For the BM treatment, a row of cowpeas was sown between every 2 rows of rice at the rate of 10 kg ha−1, 2 days after the rice planting. Cowpea was killed by the spray of 2,4-D at 0.5 kg a.i. ha−1 at 40 days after sowing (DAS) and retained on the surface as mulch. A uniform level of mulch at the beginning of each season was supplemented, if needed, 2 Mg ha−1 in all BM plots. Cowpeas as the sole crop was grown in adjoining plots to provide the additional biomass. In the main plots, disc harrowing (5–10 cm depth) was done with a tractor-mounted disc harrow, followed by tilling with power tiller and leveling in the case of CT, while soil was left undisturbed in the NT treatment. A short duration (105–110 days) and drought tolerant rice variety Sahbhagi was seeded at 50 kg ha−1at row spacing of 25 cm. Seeding was done manually on the 2nd fortnight of June and harvested in the 2nd fortnight of October each year. A nutrient of dose (i.e., 60:18:33 kg N:P:K ha−1) was applied as urea, single super phosphate (SSP) and muriate of potash (MOP), respectively. All the P, K and half of N were applied as a basal application. Remainder of the 50% N was applied through two split applications at 30 and 75 DAS. In NT plots, glyphosate, a systemic herbicide, was applied 3 litre ha−1 about a week before sowing. Further, pre-emergence herbicide, pendimethalin was applied at 1 kg a.i. ha−1 within two days after sowing in all the plots of NT-RR and CT-RI. Also, one hand weeding along with thinning was performed at 20 DAS to maintain plant to plant spacing of 5–10 cm. The initial flush of weeds was counted at the time of thinning.

column38: Field experiments, involving the rice–rapeseed system during 2012- 13 to 2013-14 and rice–rapeseed–cowpea system during 2014-15 to 2015-16 under different tillage and mulch systems, were conducted at the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) Complex for North Eastern Hill Region, Tripura Centre, Lembucherra, Tripura, India. The site is located at 23o 54′ 24o 02″ N and 91o 18′ 58o 35″ E latitude at an altitude of 52m above sea level. Soil of the experimental site was sandy loam in texture, fine, Kaolinitic, Typic Kandiudults, and classified as Acrisols. Mulching treatments included: (1) rice straw mulch (SM), (2) Gliricidia sp. mulch (GM), (3) brown manuring mulch (BM), and (4) no mulch (NM). Tillage treatments were imposed on all crops and mulch treatments only on rice at the time of sowing. Cowpea and rice crops were grown during the pre-rainy (April to June) and rainy season (July to October), respectively without any irrigation. A fertilizer dose of 60:18:33 kg N:P:K per hectare was applied in rice. Total amount of P and K, and half of N were applied at the time of sowing of rice. The remainder (50%) of N was applied through two equal split applications at 30 and 75 DAS, respectively. The same amount of fertilizer was also applied to the rapeseed in a similar manner but the remaining N was applied in two equal splits at 30 and 60 DAS. The cowpea was grown on residual fertility without any additional fertilizer. Glyphosate, a general vegetation killer herbicide, was applied as 5 ml l−1 about a week before sowing of all crops under NT plots. The pre-emergence herbicide, pendimethalin was applied at the rate of 1 kg ha−1 in rice and rapeseed within 2–3 DAS under both CT and NT systems. One hand weeding was given at the time of thinning at 20 DAS in rice and rapeseed to maintain the required plant population and manage the weeds. Neither weeding nor thinning was done in cowpea. The observation on the growth parameters, above and below ground biomass, and the yields were recorded in all crops at harvest.

column38: A 3-year study (2013–2015) on RRS was conducted in the two rice ecologies at the Agronomy experimental farm (Cocotilla farm) of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)-Research Complex for NEH Region, Tripura Centre, Lembucherra, Tripura (W), India (23o 54’24.02”N, 91o 18’58.35”E; altitude 52 m above mean sea level). The soil (Typic Kandihumults) of the experimental field is clay loam. The soil pH was 5.1 (1:2.5 soil:water ratio) and bulk density (qb) was 1.33Mg m-3. The wet season rice (WR) was grown in a nursery during June and transplanted in the main field during July and harvested during November. The dry season rice (DR) was transplanted during winter (January) and harvested in summer (May–June). The experiment was laid out in a split plot design with three replications. The gross and net plot size were 6.0x5.0 m2 and 5.0x4.0 m2, respectively. ECO 1: This is unsubmerged, rainfed irrigated ecology. WR was grown under rainfed conditions in the lowlands. Drainage channels were provided around the field to drain excess water in the case of heavy rains. Therefore, submerged conditions did not last continuously for more than a week. DR was grown under irrigated conditions in the lowlands. Irrigation was applied as per the needs of the crop. ECO 2: Both rice crops (WR and DR) were grown under rainfed conditions in the lowlands. The WR crop depended on rainfall and DR depended on seepage water from the surrounding hills. The rice field was submerged throughout the experimental period and no irrigation was applied under this condition. Conventional tillage (CT): To plow CT plots, 4 times manual spading was performed and then they were puddled with two more spadings under both rice ecologies . No-till (NT): No spading or puddling was done under NT plots and 30% of the rice residue of previous rice crops was retained on the soil surface under both ecologies and in both seasons. Glyphosate (N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine) at 5ml -1 was sprayed on NT plots using a flat fan nozzle (Knapsac sprayer, model AGM/001) to control the weeds a week (7 days) prior to transplanting. Rice seedlings, 21 days old, of the popular high-yielding varieties Naveen (DR) and Gomati Dhan (WR) were manually transplanted at 20 cmx20 cm spacing with two seedlings per hill. DR was raised in a nursery during the first week of January and transplanted during the last week of January. Similarly, WR was nursery-raised during the third week of June and transplanted in the first week of July. The recommended dose of nutrients (i.e. 60:18:33 kg N:P:K ha-1) was applied through urea, single superphosphate (SSP) and muriate of potash (MOP), respectively, in both crops during the two respective seasons. The full amounts of P and K and half of N were applied as basal fertilizer and the other 50% N applied in two equal splits at 30 and 75 days after transplanting (DAT). Weeds in NT plots were controlled by spraying of glyphosate (N-(phosphonomethyl) glycine) @ 5 ml l-1 using a flat fan nozzle (Knapsac sprayer, model AGM/001) 7 days before transplanting of the succeeding rice crop. Irrespective of tillage, pretilachlor (2-Chloro- N-(2,6-diethylphenyl)-N-(2-propoxyethyl) acetamide at 1200 g a.i. (active ingredient ) ha-1 was applied manually 2 DAT to minimize the weed infestation. The DR plots were kept flooded (5 cm of standing water) for the first 2 weeks, followed by irrigation (to 5 cm depth) at the appearance of cracks on the soil surface till maturity. On average, total irrigation water used in DR ranged between 800 and 900 hamm across the treatments under ECO 1. In order to avoid moisture stress in crops, irrigation water was applied to the rice at all critical growth stages in the different treatments.

column38: The soil of the Experiment 1 was sandy loam (59% sand, 13% silt and 28% clay), alkaline in reaction (pH 7.85, 1:2), with cation exchange capacity (CEC) 14.7 cmol kg-1, low in organic carbon (0.36%), medium in Olsen P (10.9 mg P kg-1) and low in NH4OAc-extractable K (37.5 mg K kg-1). The soil of the second experimental field was silt loam in texture (32% sand, 18% silt and 50% clay) with pH 8.55 and CEC 14.7 cmol kg-1, and tested medium in organic carbon (0.56%), high in Olsen P (16.3 mg P kg-1) and medium in NH4 OAc-extractable K (65.4 mg K kg-1). The four straw and tillage treatments were: T1 Straw burned-conventional tillage (CT); T2 Rice straw burned-zero tillage (ZT) ;T3 Rice straw incorporated (3–4 weeks before sowing of wheat)-CT; T4 Rice straw retained at surface as mulch-ZT. Four rates of N were: 0 (control), 90, 120 and 150 kg N ha-1 were applied in the sub-plots. In wheat, all the plots received a basal dose of 26 kg P ha-1 as single super phosphate and 25 kg K ha-1 as muriate of potash prior to sowing. Wheat (variety PBW 343) was sown using a seed rate of 100 kg ha-1 between 09 and 16 November during 3 years in all the treatments the same day to avoid differences in yield due to date of sowing. Wheat was irrigated (3–4 irrigations each of 75 mmwere required) according to irrigation schedule recommended for wheat crop in the region.

column38: The field experiment component of this study was conducted at the Qingyang Loess Plateau Research Station of Lanzhou University (35°40′N, 107°52′E; altitude 1298 m) in Xifeng, Qingyang City, in Gansu Province of China. The soil is classified as Heilu (a very deep loess sandy loam of the Los Orthic Entisols based on the FAO soil classification. The average annual precipitation is 546 mm, with an average of 255 frost-free days per year. The mean annual temperature ranges from 8 °C to 10 °C, and the mean annual total sunshine hours ranges from 2300 to 2700 h. During the seven growing seasons (2001–2007, meanwhile the seventh maize, winter wheat and soybean seasons were harvested in 2007, 2008 and 2007, respectively; Each treatment was replicated four times in a randomized complete block design with a total of 16 plots. Each plot was 52 m2 (4m×13 m) in area. There were 2-m spaces between adjacent blocks and 1-m spaces between adjacent plots. Maize was sown in late April and harvested in late September, followed by winter wheat, which was harvested in the early July of the next year. Soil organic matterin cultivation layer was 12.3 g kg−1, total nitrogen was 0.80 g kg−1,water-soluble nitrogen was 47.82 mg kg−1, rapidly available phos-phorus was 6.66 mg kg−1and rapidly available potassium was114.8 mg kg−1. Its seed weresowed at density of 187.5 kg hm−2in October 10–20 in 2014–2016.Urea (N 46.3%), calcium superphosphate (P2O512%) and potassiumchloride (K2O 60%) were selected as N, P and K fertilizers, respec-tively, and applied at the levels of 225 kg hm−2(N), 70 kg hm−2(P2O5) and 75 kg hm−2(K2O), respectively. Among them, 50% ofnitrogen fertilizer was applied as the bottom application, and 30%and 20% of nitrogen fertilizer were applied at jointing stage and fill-ing stage as the additional application, respectively. No irrigationwas applied during the whole wheat growth period in the threeyears period of 2014–2017

Herbicides (pendimethalin and fluometuron to the CT plots; and pendimethalin, fluometuron and paraquat to the NT and RTC plots ) were broadcast 1 day after planting to control weeds and the winter cover crop. column33: urea + 150 kg P2O5 ha-1 as diammoium phosphate + 150 kg K2O ha-1 as potassium sulfate
column38: The long-term field experiment was established in June 2006 as a demonstration site at the Fengqiu State Key Agro-Ecological Experimental Station (35°00′N, 114°24′E) in Fengqiu, Henan Province, China. The soil is classified as an Aquic Inceptisol (USDA classification), has a sandy loam texture with 52% sand, 33% silt and 15% clay. The area belongs to semi-arid with a warm temperate continental monsoon climate. The mean annual precipitation was 615mm (mainly from July to September) and the mean annual temperature was 13.9 °C in last 30 years. The field trial was set up in a well-drained area where winter wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) has been annually rotated with summer maize (Zea mays L.). In 2006, soil had an average pH of 8.31, 6.09 g organic C kg−1, 0.55 g total N kg−1, 0.81 g total P kg−1, 18.08 g total K kg−1, 57.39 mg alkalihydrolyzale N kg−1, 9.67 mg available P kg−1 (extracted by 0.5 mol L−1 NaHCO3), and 36.14 mg available K kg−1 (extracted by 1.0 mol L−1 CH3COONH4). The experiment was performed in a completely randomized design with six treatments in triplicates including two factors. The first factor was tillage regime including T (continuous tillage), RT (tillage every four years or reduced tillage) and NT (no-tillage); and no residue (-S) or all crop residues (+S) were added to the soils of three tillage practices and regarded as the second factor. The plot size was 7m×6.5 m. After harvesting, residues were crushed into 2–3 cm pieces for maize residue and 6–7 cm pieces for wheat residue, and were then returned to the soil surface under +S treatments. The residue amounts were related to the crop yield in each plot. And under −S treatments, all crop residues were removed from the plots. Each treatment plot received the same amount of fertilizer. amounts of seed and irrigation water were also recorded in this experiment and kept the same among treatments.

column33: n + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 90 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The field experiment was conducted over ten growth seasons, from September 2007 to June 2016, at the Dryland Agricultural Research Station of Northwest A&F University, which is located in Ganjing (35°19′N, 106°4′E), Heyang County, Shaanxi Province, China. Before the experiment of 2007, continuous spring maize was planted annually, and conventional tillage (mouldboard plowing) with crop residue removal was applied every year after crop harvest. The field experiment was conducted on level terrain with dark loessal soil, which is a typical soil type in the Loess Plateau, and is classified as middle loam soil based. Each sub-plot was 5m wide and 22.5m long (112.5m2) with a 60-cm interval between plots. Winter wheat and spring maize were sown at a density of 3.3 million plants ha−1 and 60 thousand plants ha−1, respectively. The row spaces for winter wheat and spring maize were 20 cm and 60 cm, respectively. All fertilizers were once manually and evenly spread on the ground both before the sowing time of winter wheat and spring maize each year. The quantities of fertilizers were the same of winter wheat and spring maize. For the balanced fertilization (BF), 150 kg N ha−1, 120 kg P2O5 ha−1, and 90 kg K2O ha−1 were applied before sowing each year to the soil as urea, diammonium phosphate, and potassium chloride, respectively. For the low fertilization (LF), 75 kg N ha−1, 60kg P2O5 ha−1, and 45 kg K2O ha−1 were applied before sowing each year to the soil as urea, diammonium phosphate, and potassium chloride, respectively. For the conventional fertilization (CF), 255 kg N ha−1 and 180 kg P2O5 ha−1 were applied before sowing each year to the soil as urea and diammonium phosphate, respectively. For the NT treatment, the crop straw was chopped and spread evenly on the surface of the experiment plots after the harvest of the previous crop using a combine harvester. No other soil disturbance was applied before crop sowing. For the ST treatment, the crop straw was left on the soil surface as mulch, and the soil was then subsoiled to a depth of 30–35 cm with an interval of 60 cm by a subsoiler with adjustable wings. The surface soil had little disturbance with the ST treatment. For the CT treatment, the crop straw was incorporated into the soil layer and plowed to a depth of 22–25 cm. All tillage practices were applied after the crop harvests. Winter wheat and spring maize were harvested by a Guwang TB60 (ZOOMLION Co. Ltd., Hebei, China) and CC40 (ZOOMLION Co. Ltd., Hebei, China), respectively. For the NT and ST practices, all crop straw was chopped and left on the soil surface as mulch in each plot, and the amount of crop residues retained on the surface was approximately 40–70% during fallow period. At the sowing time of spring maize, the extent of the surface cover was approximately remained 15–20% in NT and ST practices. The crop straw in the CT treatment was all chopped and incorporated into the soil layer with a bare soil surface in each plot. There was a one-time herbicide sprayed in late July during the fallow period, and no other soil disturbance was applied before sowing. To reach a good soil condition for crop emergence and fertilizer mixing, rotary tillage was applied at the crop sowing, one time each year. In each plot, there were three replications for yield measurements, and each sample plot was undisturbed.

column33: urea + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 as dimmonium phosphate + 90 kg K2O ha-1 as potassium chloride
column38: This study was performed over ten crop growing seasons (from September 2007 to June 2016) on the Loess Plateau, China. The research station is located in Ganjing Town (35°19′ N, 106°4′ E), Heyang County, Shaanxi Province, China, which is characterized by a temperate, semi-arid, continental monsoon climate at an altitude of 877 m. Over the last 30 years, the annual mean temperature was 11.5 °C and the total yearly frost-free period was 210 days. The mean annual precipitation was 526 mm, and the evaporation was 1833 mm. The annual precipitation was uneven, and 60% of the total precipitation was distributed over the summer season (July, August, and September), which deviated from the winter wheat growth season. Before the experiment, continuous spring maize was planted, and conventional tillage with crop residue removal was applied after the crop harvest every year. The experimental fields are level, and the soils derived from loess are Cumuli-Ustic Isohumosols (Chinese Soil Taxonomy). The soils contain 27% clay, 39% silt, and 34% sand and have weak cohesion, good water storage capacity and negligible drainage below 2 m. All tillage practices were applied after both winter wheat and spring maize harvests. For the NT practice, the crop straw was chopped and spread evenly over the surface of the experimental plots following the harvest of the previous crop using a combine harvester. For the ST practice, the crop straw was left on the soil surface as mulch, and the soil was then subsoiled to a depth of 30–35 cm at intervals of 60 cm using a subsoiler with adjustable wings. There was a one-time application of herbicides, sprayed on the fallow soil, and no other soil disturbance or management practices were applied before sowing. These three tillage practices were combined into four tillage systems: ST/CT, CT/NT, NT, and CT. For the tillage rotation of ST/CT, tillage practices were rotated using the sequence of ST in the first year and CT in the second year. In this study, there were five complete cycles of two-year tillage rotations over the ten-year period (2007–2016). There were three replications for each treatment, and all plots were 5m in width and 22.5m in length (112.5m2), with an interval of 60 cm between plots. In the first experimental year, 2007, winter wheat was planted in September. The sowing dates for winter wheat and spring maize were late September and late April, respectively. Before sowing, 150 kg ha−1 N, 120 kg ha−1 P2O5, and 90 kg ha−1 K2O were manually applied once to the soil each year in the forms of urea, diammonium phosphate, and potassium chloride, respectively.

column33: n + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 + 90 kg K2O ha-1
column38: The field experiment was conducted over ten growth seasons, from September 2007 to June 2016, at the Dryland Agricultural Research Station of Northwest A&F University, which is located in Ganjing (35°19′N, 106°4′E), Heyang County, Shaanxi Province, China. Before the experiment of 2007, continuous spring maize was planted annually, and conventional tillage (mouldboard plowing) with crop residue removal was applied every year after crop harvest. The field experiment was conducted on level terrain with dark loessal soil, which is a typical soil type in the Loess Plateau, and is classified as middle loam soil based. Each sub-plot was 5m wide and 22.5m long (112.5m2) with a 60-cm interval between plots. Winter wheat and spring maize were sown at a density of 3.3 million plants ha−1 and 60 thousand plants ha−1, respectively. The row spaces for winter wheat and spring maize were 20 cm and 60 cm, respectively. All fertilizers were once manually and evenly spread on the ground both before the sowing time of winter wheat and spring maize each year. The quantities of fertilizers were the same of winter wheat and spring maize. For the balanced fertilization (BF), 150 kg N ha−1, 120 kg P2O5 ha−1, and 90 kg K2O ha−1 were applied before sowing each year to the soil as urea, diammonium phosphate, and potassium chloride, respectively. For the low fertilization (LF), 75 kg N ha−1, 60kg P2O5 ha−1, and 45 kg K2O ha−1 were applied before sowing each year to the soil as urea, diammonium phosphate, and potassium chloride, respectively. For the conventional fertilization (CF), 255 kg N ha−1 and 180 kg P2O5 ha−1 were applied before sowing each year to the soil as urea and diammonium phosphate, respectively. For the NT treatment, the crop straw was chopped and spread evenly on the surface of the experiment plots after the harvest of the previous crop using a combine harvester. No other soil disturbance was applied before crop sowing. For the ST treatment, the crop straw was left on the soil surface as mulch, and the soil was then subsoiled to a depth of 30–35 cm with an interval of 60 cm by a subsoiler with adjustable wings. The surface soil had little disturbance with the ST treatment. For the CT treatment, the crop straw was incorporated into the soil layer and plowed to a depth of 22–25 cm. All tillage practices were applied after the crop harvests. Winter wheat and spring maize were harvested by a Guwang TB60 (ZOOMLION Co. Ltd., Hebei, China) and CC40 (ZOOMLION Co. Ltd., Hebei, China), respectively. For the NT and ST practices, all crop straw was chopped and left on the soil surface as mulch in each plot, and the amount of crop residues retained on the surface was approximately 40–70% during fallow period. At the sowing time of spring maize, the extent of the surface cover was approximately remained 15–20% in NT and ST practices. The crop straw in the CT treatment was all chopped and incorporated into the soil layer with a bare soil surface in each plot. There was a one-time herbicide sprayed in late July during the fallow period, and no other soil disturbance was applied before sowing. To reach a good soil condition for crop emergence and fertilizer mixing, rotary tillage was applied at the crop sowing, one time each year. In each plot, there were three replications for yield measurements, and each sample plot was undisturbed.

column33: urea + 120 kg P2O5 ha-1 as dimmonium phosphate + 90 kg K2O ha-1 as potassium chloride
column38: This study was performed over ten crop growing seasons (from September 2007 to June 2016) on the Loess Plateau, China. The research station is located in Ganjing Town (35°19′ N, 106°4′ E), Heyang County, Shaanxi Province, China, which is characterized by a temperate, semi-arid, continental monsoon climate at an altitude of 877 m. Over the last 30 years, the annual mean temperature was 11.5 °C and the total yearly frost-free period was 210 days. The mean annual precipitation was 526 mm, and the evaporation was 1833 mm. The annual precipitation was uneven, and 60% of the total precipitation was distributed over the summer season (July, August, and September), which deviated from the winter wheat growth season. Before the experiment, continuous spring maize was planted, and conventional tillage with crop residue removal was applied after the crop harvest every year. The experimental fields are level, and the soils derived from loess are Cumuli-Ustic Isohumosols (Chinese Soil Taxonomy). The soils contain 27% clay, 39% silt, and 34% sand and have weak cohesion, good water storage capacity and negligible drainage below 2 m. All tillage practices were applied after both winter wheat and spring maize harvests. For the NT practice, the crop straw was chopped and spread evenly over the surface of the experimental plots following the harvest of the previous crop using a combine harvester. For the ST practice, the crop straw was left on the soil surface as mulch, and the soil was then subsoiled to a depth of 30–35 cm at intervals of 60 cm using a subsoiler with adjustable wings. There was a one-time application of herbicides, sprayed on the fallow soil, and no other soil disturbance or management practices were applied before sowing. These three tillage practices were combined into four tillage systems: ST/CT, CT/NT, NT, and CT. For the tillage rotation of ST/CT, tillage practices were rotated using the sequence of ST in the first year and CT in the second year. Xian-yu 335, a popular local hybrid) was planted at 87,000 plants ha−1 according to local production practices, with inter-row spacing of 40 cm and at a distance of 29 cm between plants in the row.
